Sports.title: Chelsea hand Pedro Neto new deal in wake of his rejecting Manchester City
Sports.content:
Chelsea have rewarded Pedro Neto’s strong start to the season and commitment to the club by handing the winger a new contract. The Portugal international had summer interest from several Premier League clubs including Manchester City, but indicated a desire to stay and play for Xabi Alonso. He has signed a five-year deal with the option of an extra year and is to receive a pay rise.

Alonso has used Neto as an attacking wingback and the 26-year-old has scored twice in five appearances. Neto, who has registered 40 goal involvements since joining from Wolves for £54m in 2024, follows other leading players at Chelsea in signing new deals. João Pedro, Reece James and Moisés Caicedo have received improved terms this year, and Cole Palmer signed a new deal in 2024 and committed his future to the club in an interview with the Guardian last season.

Chelsea’s owners have a strategy of giving lengthy incentivised contracts. However, the club have demonstrated that being on those multi-year deals will not stop players from receiving pay increases as reward for good performances. Further contract renewals are expected to be announced soon.

Neto’s determination to stay contrasted with the stance of Enzo Fernández, who was sold to City for £125m during the closing hours of the transfer window.

He was not handed a new contract after initial discussions were held. The Argentina midfielder raised questions over his future in March, criticising January’s departure of Enzo Maresca as head coach and sparking talk of a move to Real Madrid by expressing a desire to live in the Spanish capital. Chelsea responded by banning Fernández for two games.

Madrid downplayed their interest in Fernández but the 25-year-old continued to push for a new challenge. City, who appointed Maresca as Pep Guardiola’s replacement, emerged as Fernández’s strongest suitors. Chelsea were prepared to hold on to him if their valuation were not met but concluded that selling was the right long-term move. There was disappointment that one of the team’s senior players did not show better leadership when Chelsea were struggling. They missed out on European qualification after finishing 10th.

View image in fullscreen Enzo Maresca and Enzo Fernandez during their time at Chelsea. They have been reunited at Manchester City. Photograph: Mark Pain/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

Chelsea sacked Liam Rosenior in April and announced Alonso’s appointment in mid-May. They were willing to reintegrate Fernández but he is understood to have submitted a written transfer request. It is understood he also informed Chelsea he had been in contact with a former coach, believed to be Maresca, at the end of last season and during the transfer window.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Stamford Bridge hierarchy concluded that Fernández’s relationship with his teammates was broken after his public comments. Fernández’s representatives have been approached for comment.

Sources have dismissed the idea that Chelsea were bullied into selling Fernández. Neto’s renewal is viewed as the latest evidence that key players have bought into the project and will be rewarded.

Sports.title: Maresca backs Anderson over ‘kings of Manchester’ dig before derby clash
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca has backed Elliot Anderson’s assessment that ­Manchester City are the “kings of Manchester” as he prepares for his first derby in charge of the club.

City travel to Old Trafford seeking to continue their perfect start to life under Maresca and further prove Anderson’s point. The 23-year-old midfielder made his claim on signing from Nottingham Forest for £116m in the summer and having witnessed City win eight Premier League titles during the past 14 years, compared with United’s one.

“I think Manchester City was unbelievable what they achieved. It’s normal when Elliot said that,” said Maresca. “If you go back it’s a different picture, but for me the reason he said that is because when he grew up Manchester City was dominant.”

Meanwhile, Michael Carrick suggested the short turnaround after United’s Champions League win over Sabah on Thursday night was “not ideal”, especially given City had a further two days to prepare for the fixture, having beaten Porto away on Tuesday. Pep Guardiola was often vocal on the subject of fixture scheduling but Maresca has taken it more in his stride and offered little sympathy to his opposite number.

“The club mentioned to me that it happened exactly the same last year when the club played Napoli and then after two days played Arsenal,” he said. “Sometimes it happens in football. I don’t have any doubt that Man United are going to be ready for that. It just matters to adapt. It happened last year with us, this season with them, next season it will happen with a different team.”

Maresca will welcome back Nico O’Reilly after the midfielder was a late withdrawal from the win over Coventry last week and missed the trip to Portugal with a back problem, but Jérémy Doku is not fit to return from a calf injury picked up in the Community Shield defeat to Arsenal.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Across his career as a player and coach, Maresca has been involved in some of the game’s biggest rivalries, enjoying the Manchester derby as part of Guardiola’s backroom staff. “I promise you the worst one is Olympiakos-Panathinaikos [in Athens]. That is very hot.” Maresca said. “I think they [derbies] are all special games for everyone. For the fans, first of all, for the club, for the players, for the coaching staff.”

Sports.title: Olid’s United on back foot due to late business and unforgiving WSL start
Sports.content:
It was tough watching Manchester United’s players labour ineffectively against the hungry and aggressive press of London City Lionesses in the Women’s Super League’s opening match. Simi Awujo’s late consolation goal did little to ease the mounting concern for a side that have several teams nipping at their heels.

Don’t panic; that has to be United’s message. To an extent, it is very early to be writing the team’s obituary. The new head coach, Eva Olid, had only three weeks to try to implement her ideas about the way the team should play before that match in Bromley on Friday 4 September. That is not long enough for her to peel away Marc Skinner’s imprint on the team.

The forward Monica Jusu Bah did not arrive from the Swedish side Häcken until 28 August and Rebeca Bernal signed from Washington Spirit on 2 September. United’s late business, in regards to their managerial change and transfer activity, has put the team and coaching staff on the back foot, playing catch-up with clubs who got most of their business done early in the window, the better to capitalise on the opportunity for a full pre-season presented by the lack of a major international tournament.

The problem is the spotlight is harsh on the red side of Manchester. The minority owner Jim Ratcliffe’s dismissive comments relating to the women’s team and the lack of serious investment in the squad provide reasons to be somewhat forgiving of the head coach and her charges, their struggles an indictment of a club that seemingly do not fully care.

The focus is said to be on a sustainable investment model recruitment-wise and on developing younger players. In isolation they are admirable goals, but in the context of investment gathering pace at other WSL teams and the relative pocket change required at a club of United’s stature to have a transformatory effect on the women’s side, these goals become shackles.

There is some irony in Olid leaving Hearts and coming to United. She arrived in Scotland to take charge of an amateur team that had avoided relegation only owing to the expansion of the top division and within five years had taken them to professionalism and a Scottish Women’s Premier League title. She felt the level of investment then needed to make Hearts competitive in Europe was lacking and it was announced that she would depart at the end of the season. The WSL and its teams are miles ahead, developmentally, of the SWPL and its sides but Olid has landed at a club that have repeatedly failed to invest substantially enough to make them league or European title challengers.

Olid told the Catalan newspaper Ara that she would have stayed at Hearts “if my project continued”. She said: “I wanted to coach in Europe, but it was a preliminary round and perhaps we would be there for a week and get eliminated. I don’t want to go backwards, I preferred to leave after winning everything because otherwise I would feel frustrated.”

View image in fullscreen Manchester United only lost 2-1 at London City Lionesses last Friday but were outclassed throughout the game. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Frustration was the name of the game at United under Skinner. The former head coach was frustrated with what he regarded as a lack of support in transfer windows and fans grew increasingly frustrated with a lack of sustained progress. United would take a step forward, such as winning the FA Cup in 2024 or reaching the Champions League quarter-finals last season, then fail to push on.

Patience is thin and Olid’s task has been made a lot harder by seven departures and only four additions to what many viewed as an already light squad. Olid has said she has had assurances that United will be active in the winter window. “We have some plans in January about signing players that I really need for my style of play and game model,” she said in her first press conference.

However, United have 12 WSL games before January, plus cup games, and with Chelsea visiting on Sunday and a trip to Arsenal next Saturday, they have an extremely unforgiving start.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Olid deserves time and patience. She is well respected and comes with a wealth of experience in her native Spain across boys’ academy football and women’s football and spent time at Houston Dynamo in the US.

Alongside battling critics unimpressed with the state of the team in their opening WSL game or questioning her managerial pedigree, she must contend with wave after wave of appalling sexist comments on social media that greet her every appearance. That surely will take a toll.

If Olid is able to weather the storm of frustration – which will grow if the team falter while players get used to her philosophy – and to force United to loosen the purse strings, they will be huge accomplishments.

Unfortunately, even success on the pitch is unlikely to end the online comments; it will probably just shift their tone. She deserves better in so many ways. The hope will be that she can build a connection with the playing group that enables them to punch above their weight until reinforcements potentially appear in January.

Their first opportunity to fend off the vultures is when they welcome Chelsea to Leigh and, with the Blues unconvincing in the final third against Aston Villa last Saturday, they can have a little hope.

Sports.title: Pochettino’s ‘different’ vow to the US invites unwelcome speculation
Sports.content:
I hope, in this lifetime, you find someone who loves you the way Mauricio Pochettino loves Tottenham Hotspur. The grip Spurs have on his heart seems the stuff of a literary classic: his imperfect partner who called things off at the first sign of trouble must merely check in on him occasionally to rekindle hopes of a reunion.

Perhaps a bit extreme, but this week’s revelation – that he’d return to Tottenham even if they were relegated and chalking his absence up to imperfect timing, not the part about handing the club a decade-old title – has implicity laid out the terms of his return as United States manager. Others may always have interest in his services, and a certain North London suitor will never get the door slammed in their face outright.

“Now it’s a four-year contract, it’s different,” Pochettino said this week. “We can next season lose the Copa América or the Gold Cup, they’re not happy with us and they can sack us. Or we can say: ‘OK. It’s not in the way that we think.’ Four years is different. Maybe now if someone calls in the future, it’s a different, different type [of thing]. We are excited, we are thinking to spend four years to the next World Cup. But now it’s a long period.”

If you’re a Spurs fan, it warms the heart to revisit last decade’s glory days. If you’re a US fan, you’re quite sick of hearing so much about a team besides the one he’s managing. If you’ve been cursed to support both, this must be a very confusing time. And if you’re US Soccer, you know that you no longer have an ace in the hole to outflank any outside interest.

One can’t undersell the appeal of coaching a World Cup host team, with a direct path to Pot One and raucous support for every match. Already a familiar face to Americans who follow the sport, Pochettino became a genuine sensation in the broader sports landscape. Millions of Americans had parallel thoughts that he, clad handsomely in a $500 safari shirt, resembled Russell Crowe – perhaps tacitly revealing that millions of Americans have long undersold the appeal of Russell Crowe.

Compared to his previous post at Chelsea, the US job offered relative reprieve. Never before has Pochettino been such a prolific fixture on hours-long podcasts. The stop/start cadence of international management is appealing for the football men who have grown weary of the meticulous corporatization of the club game. In that sense, Pochettino is among esteemed company.

Two years after Jürgen Klopp left Liverpool citing mental exhaustion, he has refreshed his tracksuit collection with fresh duds from Die Mannschaft. In his opening press conference, he read aloud to the press his terms of service – and was celebrated for it. Carlo Ancelotti was in no rush to abandon Brazil after a middling tournament, despite real questions about the pool’s depth and quality in midfield. Even Pep Guardiola held talks with Italy immediately after his decade in Manchester.

What’s different about Pochettino from, say, Klopp is his perceived eagerness to return to the club grind. Even atop the Red Bull Football conglomerate, Klopp was quick to brush aside any insinuations about returning to management. Pochettino, by contrast, held talks with Milan about their coaching vacancy immediately before the 2026 World Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There may be a simple answer. Each of Ancelotti, Guardiola, and Klopp – company with which Pochettino is regularly associated – has been the champion of England and Europe. Pochettino, at this stage, has not reached those summits.

Is aiming for a Copa América semi-final more enticing than restoring Tottenham to previous heights? What about reaching a World Cup quarter-final an ocean away from the tens of thousands who soundtracked the previous one? What can US Soccer offer that his caliber of clubs – Tottenham and beyond – can’t exceed?

While Pochettino and his charges have something resembling an excuse for their lack of execution against Belgium, the fact remains that the USMNT were once again eliminated in the last-16. Just like they were under Bob Bradley in 2010. And Jürgen Klinsmann in 2014. And Gregg Berhalter in 2022.

In theory, Pochettino will enter his second cycle in a position of strength having undertaken a thorough examination of the player pool. The fresh faces are no longer MLS journeymen or players in Europe’s lesser divisions. Instead, they’re promising prospects: 16-year-old wonderkid Cavan Sullivan, new Crystal Palace showman Zavier Gozo, highly anticipated La Masia netminder Diego Kochen.

If anything, working the up-and-comers into the established core and identifying sturdier central defenders to partner with Chris Richards should be an incredibly exciting project. The core is in great shape, with this summer’s headliners – Folarin Balogun, Alex Freeman, Richards, and Malik Tillman – all aged 30 or younger in the summer of 2030. There’s plenty of reason to think that the program is better positioned for a deep run at the next World Cup than the 2026.

Actualizing that potential will require a clear vision and a dedicated effort to raise this team’s standard throughout every window of the next four years. Batting eyelashes at past employers hardly projects that level of dedication. And so, for the next four years just like the past one, the biggest question surrounding the USMNT won’t be how far they can go in 2030. It’ll be whether Pochettino will still be the man leading them there.

Sports.title: Fenerbahce coach resigns after draw with Roma – but president insists he will stay
Sports.content:
The Fenerbahce head coach, Ismail Kartal, announced his resignation on Thursday after ⁠his team drew 1-1 at home to Roma in the Champions League – but minutes ⁠later, the club ⁠president ​said Kartal would stay in the job.

Kartal shocked the post-match press conference by claiming he was ⁠leaving Fenerbahce “never to return”. The 65-year-old added that he was taking the drastic decision “to clear the way for the club” – but the Fenerbahce president, Aziz Yildrim, quickly moved to play down his manager’s remarks.

Minutes after ⁠the press conference, Yildirim told reporters that ​Kartal “continues in his role” with the Turkish side. “Some ‌fans threw a bottle ‌at the coach’s head this evening during the game. He ‌is upset about it,” the club president added.

“I just spoke to Ismail Kartal. He mentioned the bottle incident and he also complained about being under pressure,” he said. Asked whether the manager had told him he would stay, Yildirim said: “There’s no need for him ‌to say that he’d continue. I am his senior, I told him to continue and that’s ​it. We are a family.”

Kartal, who spent a decade at Fenerbahce as a player, coached the club in 2014-15, then on an interim basis in 2021-22 before returning for a full ⁠campaign in 2023-24. He was the assistant manager at Fenerbahce the ​past two ​times the club won ​the Turkish title, and returned for a fourth ​managerial spell in ‌June.

View image in fullscreen Archie Brown celebrates his equaliser for Fenerbahce. The English full-back was left dumbfounded when learning of his coach’s resignation after the final whistle. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

Fenerbahce have ​finished second ​in the Turkish Super Lig in each of the past five seasons, and reached the Champions League’s league phase this season for the first time in 18 years. The team sit ninth in the Turkish top-flight, having lost twice in their opening four games, including Saturday’s 2-1 home defeat to Besiktas.

Roma took the lead in the 39th minute when Donyell Malen rolled a pass to ​Bryan Cristante, who beat Fenerbahce keeper Ederson with a bouncing finish. The hosts levelled before half-time when Mason Greenwood slipped a ​pass through to Archie ​Brown, who clipped a finish over ​Mile Svilar.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Roma were awarded a penalty in the 68th minute when ​Kerem Akturkoglu was ‌penalised for a ​foul on Paulo ​Dybala, but a VAR check ruled that the challenge had taken place outside the area. Fenerbahce came closest to grabbing a winner late on when Nathan Aké headed against the Roma crossbar.

Fenerbahce will travel to Aston Villa and host Liverpool in two of their remaining league phase games – whether Kartal will be in charge or not remains to be seen.

Sports.title: Champions League opening data shows English dominance and too few shocks
Sports.content:
The 2026-27 Champions League is under way. There are still 126 matches to play until we know which 24 teams will feature in the knockout phase but that doesn’t mean we haven’t learned anything yet. Here are the key data talking points from week one.

England good, Italy bad?

Premier League teams took five of the eight automatic qualification spots in 2025-26. England’s representatives all won this week to take a step toward repeating that feat. Arguably the biggest winners were Liverpool, as they were the only English team to play an opponent drawn from pot one.

They were at home, though, so perhaps the away victories for Arsenal, Aston Villa and Manchester City were more impressive. Regardless of which club can be most pleased, the Premier League’s dominance was absolute. English teams collectively out-shot their opponents 102-44, put 28 more efforts on target and had 24 shots deemed by Opta to be big chances while conceding only five.

They topped the expected goal difference by country too, a chart that has Italy at the bottom. Como won, Roma drew at Fenerbahce while Napoli and Inter faced Arsenal and Real Madrid respectively. All is far from lost, but Serie A’s numbers were not pretty.

Inter dominated Real Madrid

It wasn’t all bad for Inter. They were one of two teams who had at least 57 touches in the opposition penalty area this week. It’s an incredibly high tally – one that has only been topped once in the Premier League this season, where the average is 24.6 per team per game. For Paris Saint-Germain to be so strongly camped in the Slovan Bratislava box was hardly a surprise. For Inter to be so busy in the Real Madrid penalty area at the Santiago Bernabéu was more worthy of comment.

It would be easy to dismiss this as classic Real; they did not play well in the Champions League but won regardless. And they mustered an enormous nine big chances, missing seven of them, so might have won more comfortably with sharper finishing. But as Inter had the most shots of any visiting team in the league or Europe (in a 90-minute match) for eight years, Real might have lost too.

The only player among the back four who was there last season was 21-year-old Dean Huijsen, which may help explain how Inter were able to have so many attempts at goal. José Mourinho called it “mad, and not a madness I like”. He wasn’t wrong.

Few even games

There were no draws in the first two nights of action. Ismail Kartal resigned as Fenerbahce head coach on Thursday after his side drew 1-1 with Roma, presumably because he was so shocked that the match had finished level.

There were not even many close games on the underlying numbers, with only four of the 18 matches having an expected goal margin between the two teams that was below one. Every team that won deserved to, at least according to the xG.

With so many games still to play, a relative lack of draws this week may prove insignificant. However, it will affect the points tally required to reach the playoff round if the trend continues. There were 25 draws in the 2025-26 league phase, with the team in 24th (Benfica) finishing on nine points. But there were only 18 the season before when Club Brugge finished with 11 points when taking the final playoff spot. Fewer draws mean more teams earn three points, which lifts the bar for competitiveness. We’re currently on track for 16 draws, so keep an eye on how many matches end all square when match week two rolls around.

No surprises

Despite 16 of the 18 matches being won, there were no shocks. For the bloated league phase to generate serious excitement, it needs major upsets. Only two wins were secured by the underdog according to bookmakers, and one of those was Europa League champions Aston Villa beating Club Brugge. Hardly an upset when you compare their finances.

The surprise of the week based on pre-match prediction was Real Betis winning 3-2 at Lille. They are 49th and 52nd respectively in Opta’s Power Rankings, so Betis did not overcome an insurmountable challenge. The early weeks of last season had Qarabag winning at Benfica and Galatasaray beating Liverpool. We need more of those types of results.

Sports.title: Kylian Mbappe responds to dictator memes as Real Madrid and France star claims viral trend shows a 'lack of awareness' from fans
Sports.content:
Kylian Mbappe responds to dictator memes as Real Madrid and France star claims viral trend shows a 'lack of awareness' from fans

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Kylian Mbappe has admitted to having mixed feelings over memes depicting him as a dictator, with the star suggesting it showcases a 'lack of awareness' from people.

The Real Madrid and France star has been shown in military uniform in the meme, which was reproduced by several fans at the FIFA World Cup in the summer.

The origin of the meme is unconfirmed, but there has been speculation the trend emerged amid reports that Mbappe enjoyed significant power at PSG during his time at the French club.

It has also been suggested that it originated after Mbappe took legal action against a kebab shop owner in 2024 after they used his name in the description of a sandwich without permission.

Mbappe was asked for his response to the memes by L'Equipe in an interview in the build-up to this year's Ballon d'Or, where the 27-year-old is among the favourites.

While acknowledging it is largely 'light-hearted', Mbappe expressed a view that people were showing a lack of awareness due to the misery several dictators have caused throughout history.

Kylian Mbappe has claimed memes depicting him as a dictator are largely 'light-hearted', but show a 'lack of awareness'

Mbappe expressed a view that people were showing a lack of awareness due to the misery several dictators have caused throughout history

Some fans had displayed the memes during the World Cup, with the suggestion the trend emerged due the power Mbappe is said to have at both club and international level

'Part of it is funny because you can tell that for some people it’s all in good fun,' Mbappe told France Football.

'Part of it is a little less funny because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history.

'So being compared to people who murder people, who have made millions and millions of people miserable.

'I don’t think I’ve ever done that in my life, so there’s a mix of things where you think to yourself: “I know it’s meant in a light-hearted way”

'It doesn’t go that far but it sometimes showcases that there’s a lack of awareness, sometimes political, sometimes human among people.'

Mbappe also addressed the nickname 'Mobutu', which was given to him by his France and former PSG team-mate Ousmane Dembele.

The nickname was made in reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who was president of DR Congo, then Zaire, between 1965 and 1997.

'Ousmane, it’s something else, he took it from social media, so no, with him it’s just for fun,' Mbappe said.

Sports.title: I've seen JJ Gabriel's supreme talent develop first-hand: This is why he MUST be fast-tracked into Man United's squad for the Carabao Cup, the team-mates he's wowing at Carrington and the real reason he's deleted his United photos on Instagram
Sports.content:
I've seen JJ Gabriel's supreme talent develop first-hand: This is why he MUST be fast-tracked into Man United's squad for the Carabao Cup, the team-mates he's wowing at Carrington and the real reason he's deleted his United photos on Instagram

To watch JJ Gabriel at work inside a near-empty Leigh Sports Village each week feels akin to being given the first look at the next Oscar-winning movie from the back room of your local cinema.

There are only ever a hundred or so in attendance, half a stand is all they open these days, but all of those that go regularly know that Gabriel is destined to take his talents to the very biggest stage.

I have seen Gabriel score on his competitive debut at Old Trafford, netting in front of the Stretford End in the FA Youth Cup to become the club’s youngest scorer in that competition. I was also there when Gabriel dazzled away at Oxford United, which had my colleague Oliver Holt in awe.

I was there when Gabriel scored on his Under 21s debut earlier this season, a stunning scoop over the Ipswich Town goalkeeper from outside the box. And I was there in the rain on Thursday when Gabriel made light work of his UEFA Youth League debut, surpassing Rayan Cherki as the competition’s youngest-ever hat-trick scorer at 15 years and 339 days.

As he scooped the ball out of the net at full-time, he casually strode towards team-mate Yuel Helafu, gave it a toss into the air, and flashed a signature smile. Another record to add to his collection.

Make no mistake – Gabriel is a supreme talent. His 840,000 Instagram followers – more than, for example, the official accounts of Ipswich Town or Coventry City – suggest his ability is widely known.

Manchester United's 15-year-old JJ Gabriel completes his hat-trick for their Under 21s against Sabah in the UEFA Youth League on Thursday

Gabriel became the Youth League's youngest hat-trick scorer, surpassing Rayan Cherki, now of Manchester City

Top executives at Nike, who beat competition from adidas for Gabriel's signature, have had him on their radar as a top-tier talent since he was 10.

It was why in one key meeting they outlined why they believe he is ‘next in line to Cristiano Ronaldo’s throne’ as the face of their 'Mercurial' brand. It was, in Nike’s mind, a safe bet, even before he kicked a ball at Under-18s level.

And yet watching him up close, it really feels like the masses still don’t quite know just what a phenomenon is waiting to be unleashed. The days of watching his artistry in front of a hundred-plus crowd are undoubtedly coming to an end.

‘He’s a scary talent,’ one youth football source raved to me recently.

‘Players cannot get near him, it’s remarkable. He’s got the chance to be one of the best players this country has ever produced,’ said another after Gabriel’s Under 21s debut, where he added a pair of assists to his goal.

One recent training session had £50million summer signing Andrey Santos with hands on his head as he watched Gabriel’s technique in a small-sided drill.

Others such as Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford and Bruno Fernandes have been keen to take the 15-year-old under their wing.

‘He’s often with us in training and you can feel and see that he’s got something special,’ Mbeumo said earlier this year. ‘Everything is easy for him. He has a lot of composure in front of goal, he has a good shot, and he’s technically strong.’

But back to Leigh Sports Village and an historic afternoon which put Europe – and United’s top execs – on notice. His first goal was instinctive, the ball ricocheting off a defender after Nathanial Junior Brown’s initial effort, before Gabriel took it on his chest and volleyed in with his right foot.

Gabriel scores the first goal of his hat-trick, a right-foot volley, against Sabah

‘Players cannot get near him, it’s remarkable,' says one youth football source. 'He’s got the chance to be one of the best players this country has ever produced’

His second was even better, with some intricate footwork in the box allowing him to skip inside to pick out the bottom corner after he seemingly evaded everyone to meet Amir Ibragimov’s pass.

Then came the clincher. A ball over the top by Jim Thwaites picked out Gabriel, by now drifting in from the left, who ran clear and lifted it over the goalkeeper. Match ball secured.

It’s a modest set-up at Leigh. Team-sheets are like gold dust – we got just two between a group of seven on Thursday – and there is often a who’s who in attendance in the boxes above.

Michael Carrick is a regular, as is his assistant Steve Holland. Director of football Jason Wilcox and Matt Hargreaves, head of football negotiations, were both there on Thursday, along with recruitment chief Christopher Vivell.

It was Wilcox and Hargreaves that intervened in June 2025 to ensure United didn’t lose one of Europe’s most gifted young players. The meeting, first revealed by Daily Mail Sport, was decisive. The pathway was laid out to Gabriel and his family. The first team, by that stage, were already well aware of the teenager.

Now there are legitimate questions being asked as to whether the 15-year-old should make his first matchday squad with the first team for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup clash against Brighton. It's a must. He looks ready.

Gabriel isn’t 16 until October 6 so has ample opportunity to become the club’s youngest-ever player, breaking the record held by goalkeeper David Gaskell, who was 16 years and 19 days old when he debuted for United in 1956.

So, just how difficult, or scary, is it to have the responsibility of coaching a player many inside United believe is destined to become world class?

‘He’s often with us in training and you can feel and see that he’s got something special,’ Bryan Mbeumo (second left) has said of Gabriel

Only days ago United legend Ryan Giggs called Gabriel a ‘generational talent’

‘It’s my job not to ruin him,’ said Under 21s boss Adam Lawrence, who will also manage the Under 19s in the Youth League, on Thursday. ‘When you have a talented player like JJ and the other lads, of course, you don’t want to stifle their freedom and their creativity.

‘I try to set the team up to allow the talent to function and to play free at the right moments. It's enjoyable working with him and challenging as a coach because the best players challenge you – in a good way. Of course there’s things he can keep working on, but he's in a real good place.’

The noise around Gabriel is relentless. Overnight there were questions asked why he had wiped his Instagram account clean. Those close to him insist it’s merely to remove any distractions from his game.

Only days ago United legend Ryan Giggs called Gabriel a ‘generational talent’. Rio Ferdinand simply called Gabriel’s talent ‘ridiculous’ to comprehend.

Others, who don’t speak to those he works with each day, sometimes bring up attitude as a negative. But having spoken to coaches right through the academy, a set-up Gabriel joined at the age of nine, they are effusive in their praise. The criticism couldn’t be further from the truth.

'JJ's an amazing talent and his enthusiasm for football, that he brings to the pitch every day to learn, want to play, be on the ball, he's been a pleasure to work with,’ Under 18s boss Darren Fletcher told me last season.

‘He’s a fantastic kid. He's desperate to do better, to improve, to learn. He takes constructive criticism fantastically and I've got a great relationship with him.'

Carrick, too, has a pep in his step when it comes to Gabriel, describing the young teen as ‘one of the boys’.

‘It’s my job not to ruin him,’ Under 21s boss Adam Lawrence says. ‘When you have a talented player like JJ, you don’t want to stifle their freedom and their creativity'

‘He’s a fantastic kid,' says Under 18s boss Darren Fletcher. 'He's desperate to do better, to improve, to learn. He takes constructive criticism fantastically'

Sir Jim Ratcliffe even made sure to see this burgeoning superstar for himself in a Premier League Cup match at Carrington last season. Naturally, Gabriel scored that day, too.

It was Ratcliffe that once said he wants United to produce their own superstars, their own Kylian Mbappe, rather than going out to sign the finished article. There is no doubt in my mind they’ve got one in the building.

'It's not for us to create robots here,' academy director Stephen Torpey told me in a chat at Carrington back in March. 'It's for us to allow individuals to flourish and express themselves.'

The joy of watching Gabriel is that he tries things, and can do things with the ball, that others cannot. A refreshing antidote to the ‘robots’ we can often see in the Premier League. It feels inevitable that Gaskell’s record will be shattered in the weeks ahead.

Sports.title: How Ben Shelton became US tennis' new superstar: Big-hitting American downed Carlos Alcaraz, is dating NBA legend Dennis Rodman's daughter and is now on the cusp of a $10MILLION brand deal after New York exploits
Sports.content:
How Ben Shelton became US tennis' new superstar: Big-hitting American downed Carlos Alcaraz, is dating NBA legend Dennis Rodman's daughter and is now on the cusp of a $10MILLION brand deal after New York exploits

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

If you had told Ben Shelton he would play the second US Open semi-final of his career tonight in July, he might not have believed you. The 23-year-old had endured a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it first-round exit at Wimbledon and he was frustrated.

‘It's been a weird season for me this year,’ Shelton admitted. He had three titles under his belt, but a string of early exits where it mattered - the majors and Masters. There were so many things that disappointed him in his game.

But two months is a long time in tennis. Shelton started August by defending his Canadian Open title, before taking his form to New York and beating Carlos Alcaraz in a late-night instant classic.

His meeting on Friday evening with fellow American Frances Tiafoe is not the first time he’s been at this stage. In 2023, he was a gregarious upstart one year into his career, with the unvarnished gifts, and ego, of a champion-in-waiting.

He had a controversial celebration: hanging up the phone on his opponents. He had hyped himself before the tournament saying he was looking to become someone players feared in the draw. And Shelton was, until Novak Djokovic hung up on him, winning in straight sets.

At 20 years old, Shelton had become box office. A tennis nepo-baby, Shelton is the son of former tour journeyman Bryan Shelton, but as a child, saw the family business as ‘boring’, preferring American football or basketball. It’s no stretch to imagine the left arm that provides his 146mph serve attached to an NFL quarterback. After he switched full focus to tennis at 13 however, Bryan now sits in his box as coach.

Add to family lore the draw of Shelton being one-half of one of America's sportiest power couples. Since sliding into his Instagram DMs in early 2025, USWNT star Trinity Rodman - daughter of NBA legend Dennis - is a frequent fixture on tour, with Shelton pitchside for her Washington Spirit matches when the ATP’s gruelling schedule allows.

Ben Shelton's courageous showing in his US Open quarter-final against Alcaraz has given him a shot at the final

The 23-year-old has reached this stage before in 2023 (left) - before Novak Djokovic hung up on him to win his 24th Grand Slam

Shelton is now frequently accompanied by his girlfriend Trinity Rodman - a blockbuster USA athlete in her own right

All this has brought Shelton attention, celebrity and riches - after three years wearing Roger Federer’s ON brand, he is reportedly set to ink a $10million deal with New Balance - but results? That’s where things get more complicated.

Shelton has been dogged by inconsistencies, particularly at the Grand Slams. In Paris, he has never made it past the fourth round, and Wimbledon’s 2025 quarter-final is an outlier amid early exits. Never mind that he has titles on both of the natural surfaces. When asked to perform on the biggest stages, his standout attributes can turn into fatal flaws.

‘That’s the challenge, working with a guy like Ben, who is very aggressive,’ his father said in July. ‘There are times when he crosses that line and sabotages himself, and doesn’t make it to the second or third round of the tournament.’

But the win against Alcaraz showed the soaring height of his ceiling. The biggest weapon is his serve. Keeping himself in top condition to deploy it leaves him covered in cupping marks. Shelton is devoted to the traditional Chinese medicine technique for recovery and would sooner skip tending to his arm than Samson would book in for a buzzcut.

Shelton is also a superior athlete, and proved he was able to match Alcaraz’s lightning-quick movement with his own work-rate, chasing down shots which should have been impossible, and getting them back over the net with flair.

If Shelton can play like he did against the Spaniard twice more, he could end America’s 23-year wait for a home men’s Grand Slam winner. But to do that, he has to pass another psychological test by defeating his close friend Tiafoe. Tiafoe is a three-time finalist and a fellow showman who saves his very best for his home Slam.

Like Shelton, Tiafoe saw out his own five-set comeback epic to reach the semi-finals, and having met twice before, their head-to-head at the tournament sits tantalisingly at one win apiece.

He has met US Open semi-final rival - and fellow American - Frances Tiafoe twice before at their home Grand Slam (pictured in 2023)

After beating Alcaraz, Rodman prompted Shelton to bring back his once-iconic celebration - his confidence has hit new heights at just the right time

The final series of their trilogy has added potency, their clash guaranteeing a Black US Open men’s finalist for the first time on Arthur Ashe since, well, Arthur Ashe in 1972. History is on the line.

But Shelton’s form has been cresting, and he will come into their contest buoyed up by his meeting with Alcaraz with lethal confidence.

At 3.34am on Wednesday morning, Shelton looked up to his player’s box. There, Rodman cheekily picked up the phone, like it was 2023 again. Shelton has learned a lot in three years. But he still answered.

Sports.title: Angry Arsenal staff fear job cuts as Premier League champions call in US consultants to lead review despite team lifting first title in 22 years
Sports.content:
Arsenal staff are fearing job losses – after the side won the Premier League title for the first time in 22 years.

Daily Mail Sport understands that US consultants BCG have been carrying out a review at the champions for the last three months.

It is believed that BCG managing director Jean-Paul Petranca is leading the review, which some claim has created a split within the offices of the club despite a stunning season in north London in which the Gunners also reached the Champions League final.

Arsenal insiders insist that BCG are there to help the club grow the business, capitalise on their success and ensure a sustained period of high performance.

However, sources have disclosed that many staff members believe job cuts are inevitable and that there is a perception – and an anger – that the football side of the business will not be impacted.

Petranca, who has been reporting to chief executive Richard Garlick, has ‘more than 20 years' experience advising senior leaders in the UK and internationally on strategy, transformation, and organizational performance’ according to BCG’s website.

Arsenal are thriving on the pitch but staff behind the scenes are fearing job losses

Arsenal have refused to comment but it is thought that making efficiencies is part of Petranca’s remit.

There is thought to be a particular nervousness within the commercial department, with some staff struggling to see the logic behind any cuts, should they take place.

In the summer, that side of the business lost its boss, Juliet Slot, who departed after almost five years with the club which saw record-breaking revenues.

There is a view that any restructuring in that area would be incredibly short-sighted given Arsenal, like many others, rely on driving income to ensure they comply with the Premier League and UEFA’s spending rules. The emphasis, many believe, should be on servicing relationships with existing partners, while searching for new sponsorships.

One member of staff, speaking anonymously, explained: ‘Obviously everyone was delighted at the success of the team last year. But it has not gone unnoticed that the football department, which has extended recently, appears immune to any changes.

'It doesn’t feel right that, given the amount of money spent there, normal people with bills and mortgages to pay feel under threat.

'You would think that it’s a great place to be at the moment but that’s just not the case. There’s also an anger that, should there be cuts, they will be made by someone from outside the business rather than your own boss.’

Sports.title: Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival
Sports.content:
Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

‘Who ya like buddy?’ It’s the most asked question in casino-ville as the hours tick down to this Saturday’s world title fight between two angry young men.

One, America’s extravagantly gifted but troubled world welterweight champion. The other, the ever-persistent English challenger who never stops throwing punches whether they connect or not. As if in manic obsession with defeating not only opponents but also his demons and a sceptical outside world.

So, Ryan Garcia or Conor Benn?

When the denizens of this neon gambling Strip in the Nevada desert ask that question they don’t’ want to know which of these two combatants you like personally more than the other. It is their way of trying to find out who you might be betting on to prevail in the atmospheric T-Mobile Arena.

Their inquiries are even more numerous than usual on such occasions as this. Because neither the Americans nor the Mexicans who are thronging here in support of their blood brother by heredity know very much about Benn. Other than the fact he is the son of a fabled icon of the British ring.

On his two previous US visits Benn Jr made hard work of beating men who looked more like nightclub bouncers than professional boxers. Of his exploits back home only the pair of fights against Chris Eubank Jr evoked any interest whatsoever on either side of this border.

What they are aware of is the two positive tests for performance enhancing drugs and the protracted legal battle to technically clear his name which kept him out of the ring for months. Just as they know about Garcia’s conviction and suspension for a similar finding.

Conor Benn is locked in the battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars in Las Vegas

Benn is lining up a $10m payday after burning his bridges with promoter Eddie Hearn

So, what’s to like?

There can be no doubting Benn’s work ethic. He trains like a dervish to manufacture the maximum possible out of however much natural-born ability he inherited from Nigel the Dark Destroyer. Nor does he ever give up. Eubank Jr had to go beyond the normal limits of even this battle-hardened business to inflict the only defeat of Conor’s career thus far. A loss he avenged, albeit in partly contrived and contentious circumstances.

Eubank the Younger was perilously drained in the rematch by a clause in the contract which prevented him rehydrating fully after struggling to cut poundage to meet the agreed catchweight.

What goes around comes around. If not in a full measure of the irony. Benn has had to sweat and strain down by almost a stone from middleweight to make the welterweight championship limit of 147 lbs. As he puts it: ‘Five weeks in hell.’

To say his body looks shredded is putting it mildly. But he has not been subjected to rehydration limitations following his Friday morning visit to the scales.

Eubank was handsomely rewarded to put his health on the line, and now Benn has been lured into similar jeopardy by the fortune – some reports say ten million dollars – he is receiving from UFC boss Dana White to be one of the first poster boys for his venture into boxing.

Benn tells it otherwise: ‘I’m doing this because I relish challenges. Have always wanted to strap on the same green WBC belt my dad was so proud to wear. To start getting the world titles that will leave a legacy for my kids. And to prove wrong everyone who doesn’t give me a chance of winning. That puts all the pressure on him, not me.’

Hearn backed the British fighter during his controversial doping ban saga

Ryan Garcia stands in his way of the WBC title, who is the more talented of the fighters

Whether or not Benn can take in sufficient liquids and pasta before entering the ring, the dangers to him are greater than those with which Eubank struggled. Garcia, one year the younger at 28 but the riper in championships experience, has authentic one-hit-knockout power.

Benn goes into his first world championship fight reliant on the cumulative effect of his non-stop output. The problem with this is that King Ry is probably the best counterpuncher in the world right now and Benn’s headlong style will likely suit him nicely, thank you.

To complicate the evaluation, both have blotted their copybooks as people. Garcia, the handsome heartthrob, burnished his bad-boy rock-star image by trashing a five-star hotel room. He also needed his family’s help with overcoming mental problems aggravated by a passing fancy for social drugs and booze.

Benn invited mockery for claiming initially that he failed his drugs tests because of eating enough eggs to fill the shelves of all the Tescos in London. Then, in order to collect his bonanza from Mister UFC, he unceremoniously dumped his long-time promoter Eddie Hearn who had bankrolled his hefty legal costs and loaned him half a million quid to help sustain his flamboyant lifestyle through that crisis.

Not much to like there.

So, when it comes to the fight, who ya like? The answer is not Conor Benn’s to give. Because the real question is which Ryan Garcia turns up.

If it is the narcissist whose arrogant complacency has cost him a couple of big fights, it may not be totally beyond the bounds of possibility that Conor could pull off one of the major upsets by a British boxer abroad.

If it is King Ry fully prepared and ready to unfurl all the majesty then we can only hope the son of Nigel is not seriously hurt.

Sports.title: Man United ban 685 accounts in ticket tout crackdown - as fans claim 'a line has been crossed' ahead of derby protest
Sports.content:
Man United ban 685 accounts in ticket tout crackdown - as fans claim 'a line has been crossed' ahead of derby protest

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester United fans will go ahead with a planned protest before Sunday’s Old Trafford derby after launching another attack on the club over its clampdown on ticket touts.

United issued a statement on Friday confirming that the investigation is complete. They revealed that out of a total of 1,617 accounts identified as suspicious, 685 have been hit with a ban for breaching season-ticket rules.

Club sources denied claims that innocent fans have been accused without clear evidence, but that was dismissed by a spokesman for protest group The 1958 who will go ahead their demonstration on Sunday.

He said: ‘There is still no apology from the club at the way they’ve treated time-served, loyal fans. The stress and aggravation caused has been immense for some.

'The fans impacted by the bans have still not received clear reasoning. That is unacceptable and should be challenged. We are supporters and human beings, not cattle in a slaughterhouse!

‘We protest against being treated like this, and we protest against the owners of our club. We urge all fans to turn up and let the club know what we think.’

Fans protested against the club on the opening game of the season against Hull

United defended the investigation by saying it has broken up large-scale organised networks involved in touting based on the strongest data ever gathered.

Insiders insist that some examples of unfair treatment of fans shared on social media are untrue and don’t tell the full story. They acknowledge the frustration among supporters over the crackdown, but say a total of 468 cases have been resolved without any further action.

A statement read: ‘Where satisfactory explanations were provided, restrictions were removed and no further action was taken. In many of those cases, the cause was sharing of account details and passwords, which is in breach of our terms and conditions.

‘We recognise that many supporters have shared account login details in circumstances they regarded as legitimate, and we did not anticipate the extent to which this was occurring. In those cases, where there was no additional evidence of misuse, no sanction was imposed.’

As a result of the investigation, United maintain that more tickets will now be available to genuine supporters rather than touts who they say were exploiting fans.

Out of the 685 accounts that have been banned, there were 499 cases in which fans lost an appeal, 73 cases where there was no appeal, and 113 where there was no response despite requests for information. A further 464 supporters received a reduced sanction or final warning.

The statement added: ‘Over the course of the summer, Manchester United undertook an operation to review accounts that showed irregular activity resembling ticket misuse. We committed to providing a further update once our investigation had concluded.

‘The club's guiding principle around ticketing is simple: to keep our fans safe and secure, to protect fair access to tickets for genuine Manchester United supporters and to tackle ticket touting, misuse and activity for financial gain.

‘Bans were issued where there was significant misuse of the ticketing system. This included the operation of organised ticketing networks, which were controlling, selling and distributing tickets from hundreds of accounts. These actions undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United.

‘Our focus now turns to ensuring these tickets are returned to our supporters. All season tickets released through this process will be offered to supporters on the season ticket waiting list. Refunds have been or will be issued to each of the season ticket holders who have been banned.

‘We want to allow any sanctioned ticket holder the opportunity to refer their case to the Independent Football Ombudsman. Therefore, we will wait until after the international break before reallocating season tickets. Any seats used on a match-by-match basis before then will be sold at season ticket prices, not matchday prices. The club is not profiting from this process.’

Sports.title: Revealed: How Enzo Fernandez fell out with Chelsea team-mates in a 'broken beyond repair' relationship breakdown - Insiders reveal details of star's two transfer requests before £125m deal
Sports.content:
Revealed: How Enzo Fernandez fell out with Chelsea team-mates in a 'broken beyond repair' relationship breakdown - Insiders reveal details of star's two transfer requests before £125m deal

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Enzo Fernandez told Chelsea that his relationship with the changing room was broken and beyond repair as he pushed for his Manchester City move, Stamford Bridge insiders have claimed.

In further revelations, it is also said the 25-year-old Argentine communicated with his club how he had been speaking privately with his former head coach, Enzo Maresca, and that he submitted two written transfer requests before finally securing his £125million switch on deadline day.

Daily Mail Sport attempted to contact Fernandez's representative, Javier Pastore, for a response to these claims concerning his client on Friday afternoon.

The news came as Chelsea announced a new deal for Pedro Neto, partially as a reward for his loyalty with City having also shown interest in the 26-year-old Portuguese over the summer.

Unlike Fernandez, who failed to agree an extension with Chelsea despite engaging in talks previously, Neto showed a willingness to stay. The winger has now been handed a six-year contract, which involves five years with the option of the sixth, and a pay rise.

Neto follows Joao Pedro, Reece James, Moises Caicedo and Cole Palmer in likewise securing improved terms. Others are expected to follow in the coming weeks and months, with Levi Colwill among those in line for a bump.

Enzo Fernandez 'told Chelsea his relationship with team-mates was broken' before leaving

Fernandez left Chelsea for Manchester City in a £125million deadline day transfer

Neto has impressed under new manager Xabi Alonso this season, having primarily been used as a wing back and scoring two goals in five games across all competitions.

Alonso spoke highly of him at his pre-Hull press conference on Friday, describing him as having multiple 'qualities' and that he 'connects well' with his team-mates.

Chelsea previously held talks with Fernandez and his camp about his own contract boost, but unlike his peers, an agreement was never able to be reached.

Fernandez's relationship with Chelsea became particularly strained last season when he openly flirted with Real Madrid – with the vice-captain suspended by his own club for two games for those comments.

Real went on to release a statement insisting they were not interested in Fernandez.

However, City never gave up on securing him in the summer despite it being left until the final two days of the window, when the £125m deal was done in order for Maresca to land his top target.

The Argentina international is now set to take part in his first Manchester derby this Sunday.

Sports.title: Ricky Hatton's mother recalls last hug with boxing champion three days before he took his own life a year ago as parents speak out for first time
Sports.content:
Ricky Hatton's mother recalls last hug with boxing champion three days before he took his own life a year ago as parents speak out for first time

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Ricky Hatton's mother has recalled her last hug with him three days before he took his own life one year ago as his parents speak out for the first time.

Carol and Ray Hatton have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late after the boxing champion hanged himself on September 14 last year.

One year on from Ricky's death, aged 46, his mother has revealed the last time she embraced her son.

Just days before he took his own life, the boxing champion had been in an argument with his parents but the family were 'building bridges'.

Carol decided to make an unplanned visit to his gym in Hyde and gave him a 'real proper hug'.

She told ITV News: 'I pulled up on the car park because I saw his car. He asked if everything was okay.

'I said "yeah, everything's fine". I said I'd like to see a bit more of him.'

Ricky's mother said he told her he wanted to see his father Ray the next week. However Ricky died three days later.

Former world boxing champion Ricky Hatton died by suicide in September last year aged 46

Ray and Carol Hatton (pictured at their son's funeral) have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late

Ricky had previously opened up about his struggle with drug and alcohol addiction and had become estranged from his parents before the reconciled

She added: 'I'm so glad (I got to see him) because nobody knows when it's the last time you're going to see somebody.'

Ray, the boxer's father, said: 'You tell your grandkids how much you love them, you tell your wife how much you love them but I think, especially with men, don't ever be afraid of getting hold of your son and telling him you love him.'

Ricky had become estranged from his parents for around a decade before he reached out to patch up their relationship several years before his death.

He had survived previous suicide attempts and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.

Ricky fell out with his parents over money and despite the dispute he still allowed Carol and Ray to see his newborn daughter Millie.

However the boxer became upset when his girlfriend Jennifer was not invited to a Christmas Day party.

Months later he received letters from his parents' lawyers saying they wanted to see their granddaughter.

But he told Manchester Evening News in 2013 that he responded by saying: 'I replied to my parents, through solicitors, and said we did not want them to have contact with Millie.'

Carol Hatton wipes a tear from her eye while reading a statement at her home after Ricky's death

Ricky had survived previous suicide attempts before he died in September last year

'We have never stopped them seeing her, as far as I was concerned they had just not been ******.

'I know that sounds harsh and I am sure they see it differently, but it is how I feel.'

He added that the situation 'was a mess', describing the family feud as 'bitter and horrible', referring to back-and-forth letters between his and his parents' lawyers.

This culminated in his father attacking him in a car park fist fight.

Angry about 'all that stuff you've written about your mum in that solicitor's letter', Ray then punched his boxing champion son in the face before Ricky hit back and his father then drove off.

But Ricky's parents are still struggling to come to terms with his death and Carol said the couple 'have to move forward' but will continue 'remembering him and loving him'.

Carol and Ray have now called for a statue of Ricky to be erected in Manchester, saying it would be a 'fitting tribute' to their son who 'brought a lot of pride' to the city.

Sports.title: BBC football pundit breached editorial standards as he apologises after investigation launches
Sports.content:
BBC football pundit breached editorial standards as he apologises after investigation launches

This BBC pundit offered an apology following the controversy that ensued at Celtic Park

View 2 Images Pat Nevin issued an apology (Image: BBC)

BBC football pundit Pat Nevin has been found to have breached the broadcaster's editorial standards following his remarks on Celtic's pitch invasion last season. The former Scotland international was part of the BBC Radio 5 Live commentary team for Celtic's league title decider against Hearts, which Martin O'Neill's side won 3-1.

‌



The Parkhead side clinched the Scottish Premiership with the victory, prompting supporters to invade the pitch. Nevin claimed he saw "two or three" fans attack then-Hearts captain Lawrence Shankland and described the post-match scenes as "sickening" and "unacceptable".

‌



The BBC's Executive Complaints Unit (ECU) launched an investigation into Nevin's comments after viewers complained that the 63-year-old's remarks were false. The inquiry found that Nevin's claims breached the corporation's accuracy standards, but did say he made an "honest error".

‌



Nevin later took to his BBC sports column and issued an apology. He wrote: "I made a mistake in a commentary at the end of the last game of the Scottish season. From my angle in the gantry I thought I saw a punch thrown, but it appears it was a confrontation or maybe just goading from one of the hundreds of Celtic fans who invaded the pitch just before the end of the game.

"Goading is not physical violence and I will take it on the chin, the way the Hearts player probably didn’t. My apologies to those offended." The BBC ECU released a statement on their ruling, which read: "During a pitch invasion towards the end of the Hearts v Celtic match, the commentator Pat Nevin said two or three Celtic fans had punched the Hearts captain."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Celtic and Rangers hit with stadium bans after ugly scenes in Old Firm clash READ MORE :

Celtic VAR decision that rocked Scottish title race deemed wrong by SFA panel READ MORE :

It was revealed that two listeners had complained that Nevin's claims were untrue. The outcome read: "The scenes at the end of the match were chaotic, and Mr Nevin and his co-commentators were trying to give listeners an impression of events as they unfolded, with no opportunity for verification before speaking.

"Mr Nevin subsequently acknowledged that he should not have stated definitively that the Hearts captain had been punched by Celtic fans. The ECU accepted that this was an honest error made in the heat of the moment, but concluded that it fell below the BBC’s editorial standards of accuracy."

View 2 Images Pat Nevin falsely claimed that Lawrence Shankland had been punched by fans (Image: Sky Sports)

Article continues below

The broadcaster's report added: "The finding was reported to the management of BBC Sport. On his own initiative, Mr Nevin apologised for the error on air on two occasions, and again in his BBC Sport newsletter."

The triumph marked Celtic's fifth consecutive league triumph and their 14th in the last 15 years. It was their 56th league title as they pipped Rangers (55) to the most championships in Scottish football history.

Sports.title: Hull City were warned about road before Sorba Thomas overturned car outside training ground
Sports.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Hull City were warned about road before Sorba Thomas overturned car outside training ground

Hull City's £10.5million summer signing Sorba Thomas was involved in a collision outside the club's training ground, five days after the club were urged to warn new players about the road

View 4 Images Sorba Thomas' car overturned in the crash (Image: Cllr Phil Redshaw)

A local councillor says he asked Hull City to warn their new players of the dangers of the road outside their training ground just days before Sorba Thomas' crash.

‌



Thomas, who joined Hull from Stoke on transfer deadline day in a £10.5million deal, was involved in a collision on Millhouse Woods Lane on Friday morning, remarkably escaping the scene "completely unscathed".

‌



The residential road is just a stone's throw from Hull's training ground. Two other cars were damaged in the incident. Hull issued a statement to "reassure supporters that he has sustained no injuries and emerged from his vehicle completely unscathed."

‌



Meanwhile, Humberside Police confirmed they were "in attendance following reports of a road traffic collision" and advised motorists to avoid the area. The incident comes the day before Hull face Chelsea in the Premier League at Stamford Bridge and the proximity of the crash to the training ground meant their team coach was delayed in leaving for London.

4 View 4 Images Two other cars were damaged in the incident (Image: Cllr Phil Redshaw) 4 View 4 Images Sorba Thomas car was towed away after the crash (Image: Cllr Phil Redshaw)

‌



Local councillor Phil Redshaw visited the scene of the crash on Friday. He told The Mirror there have been “a few near misses” recently down the road in Cottingham, a suburb of Hull.

He added: “I wrote to the Hull City club secretary on Sunday asking them to remind players to be careful driving down the road because of the residents’ concerns. I wanted them to remind their staff to drive with extra care, because they get new players in every season.”

Hull City referred to their statement when asked about councillor Redshaw's comments.

‌



Redshaw says he visited residents of Millhouse Woods Lane on Friday to warn them about the dangers of the road, with gardens backing directly onto the pavement where “lorries have no option but to go" in order to get past.

View 4 Images The £10.5m winger escaped the wreckage unhurt (Image: Cllr Phil Redshaw)

Thomas was one of 17 new players to sign for Hull this summer following their promotion to the Premier League via the Championship play-offs. The Tigers were the busiest club in the Premier League this summer, with their 17 incomings the most of any side, while their net spend of £160m put them fourth in the division.

‌



The 27-year-old Wales international has made two appearances for The Tigers so far, making his Premier League debut in the goalless draw with Aston Villa on the weekend before starting in the 1-0 defeat by Sunderland in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday night.

Hull have made a brilliant start to the top-flight campaign, keeping three successive clean sheets to beat Manchester United and Coventry and draw with Villa. Sergej Jakirovic's side sit third in the Premier League table ahead of their trip to Stamford Bridge for Saturday's 3pm kick-off.

Sports.title: Jake Wightman looks for redemption at World Athletics Ultimate Championship
Sports.content:
Jake Wightman looks for redemption at World Athletics Ultimate Championship

Jake Wightman has arrived in Budapest for the inaugural edition of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship, competing in Sunday’s 1500m as he looks to make up for lost time after a challenging spell.

View Image Jake Wightman running at the European Athletics Championships (Image: Matt Dickens/Novuna)

Jake Wightman is only too happy to fly under the radar in ‘the toughest 1500m field’ ever assembled after another season marred by injury. Wightman has arrived in Budapest for the inaugural edition of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship, competing in Sunday’s 1500m as he looks to make up for lost time after a challenging spell.

‌



It is far from the first time that the 2022 world champion has had to deal with the injury bug. But having spent the best part of the two years following his global crown in Eugene, Oregon, missing out on major events, Wightman returned to the World Championship podium last year with silver in Tokyo. However, after a strong start to the outdoor season, he suffered calf tightness and then a back issue that required an epidural 10 days before the Commonwealth Games.

‌



As compatriot Josh Kerr streaked clear to the acclaim of the Scotstoun crown for mile glory, a matter of weeks after breaking the 27-year-old world record in the event, Wightman was run down on the final straight – usually his strength – finishing sixth. A week later, it was a similar story at the Europeans in Birmingham, finishing in the same position over 1500m.

‌



And after the frustrations over those two races, the 32-year-old Wightman is not lacking for motivation in an elite field that features Kerr, his great Norwegian rival Jakob Ingebrigtsen, Olympic champion Cole Hocker, and world champion Isaac Nader, who edged out Wightman last year in Japan. Wightman said: “If my champs had gone the way I wanted, I think I would be feeling a lot less motivated towards this but because I don’t feel I’ve proved myself at all this year, this is my chance to do that. I’m excited to get a bit of redemption.

“I’m hoping I can come in under the radar, I think that is when I run my best. There is no talk about me which for better or worse, I’m going to try and go out there and do as well as I can. I hope it can be my best run of the year. But you are racing against perhaps the best field it’s ever been for the 1500m. The ‘ultimate’ test! Even without Jakob and Josh being added, it was tough, but with them it becomes the toughest field there has ever been. I think more than anything, if you go well here and manage to win it, it makes it an even more incredible achievement.”

‌



While Wightman is now fully fit, it follows a summer of frustration as his body betrayed him once again. That disappointment was exacerbated by the fact that he had started the season like a house on fire.

He said: “My May and June was the best it’s ever been, I went to Monaco and ran the fastest 1k I think I could have done on the day. Three days later, I was on a run and my calf felt tight. I had a nerve in my back that was not very happy, it took two weeks where I could get to a point where I could run again with no pain. I got to Commies and was managing it. After Commies it disappeared and I had a week between them and Europeans, I thought I had done enough work but by that point it had been three weeks of disrupted training.

“It’s a shame because I don’t think I ran the races badly, I think I ran them the way I believed I should to be able to win but I just didn’t have the edge I needed. There was nothing I could have done, that is the most gutting thing. It’s the nature of how your body reacts to stuff at times.”

Article continues below

The three-day event in Budapest marks a new era for athletics, with World Athletics president Seb Coe hoping that some of the innovations that will be on show – including a live draft for the 200m lanes, a new format for field events and the elimination of ties in vertical jumps – will be adopted at World Championships and Olympics in the future.

He said: “We want this championship to be an incubator for change. As a proud Sheffielder, I would call this a blast furnace, ultimately casting what our sport can look like going forward. We want to take some of those innovations into the World Championships and the Olympic Games.”

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
