World.title: Kenya: Kenya Rebuilds The Cotton Chain From Field To Fabric
World.content:
Joyce Njogu, head of Consulting and Business Development at the Kenya Association of Manufacturers (KAM)

Farmers are returning to cotton in coastal Kenya, while a new ginnery and one of the country’s few surviving integrated textile mills are rebuilding links from field to factory.

In the small coastal town of Mpeketoni in Lamu County, cotton is once again becoming a crop worth growing.

Farmers are returning to their fields, Bt cotton seed is being distributed and a new ginnery is bringing processing closer to where the crop is grown. The cotton produced here is transported to Thika Cloth Mills (TCM), one of Kenya’s few surviving integrated textile manufacturers.

The revival aims to create jobs, strengthen manufacturing, reduce dependence on imports and enable Kenya to capture more value from its own raw materials. Cotton and textiles are identified as a strategic value chain under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda and the Fourth Medium Term Plan , which runs from 2023 to 2027.

The government’s Draft National Cotton, Textile and Apparel Policy of 2024 seeks to increase cotton production, local value addition, employment, skills and market access.

Interviews with people across the value chain suggest that the revival is showing progress as Kenya rebuilds a system weakened over decades.

Kenya was once a major player in cotton and textiles. The draft Cotton, Textile and Apparel (CTA) policy says the sector declined following trade liberalisation and the introduction of second-hand clothing, which weakened local manufacturing and demand.

Dr Concepta Sitati, a lecturer at Mount Kenya University who grew up in western Kenya when cotton was an important cash crop, remembers a more connected system.

Cotton was collected through cooperatives and moved from farms to processing industries, she says. When factories closed, farmers lost reliable markets and stopped growing cotton.

The result was a cycle of decline. Fewer farmers meant less cotton for ginneries and less raw material for textile mills. As factories shut down, workers also lost jobs and technical expertise.

The government hopes to reverse that cycle by rebuilding the value chain from farm to fashion. The CTA policy identifies production, ginning, manufacturing, employment, market access, sustainability and innovation as areas requiring coordinated intervention.

Rebuilding the value chain

For Dominic Ngugi, operations manager of Thika Cloth Mills, Mpeketoni Ginnery, the change is visible in the fields.

The ginnery works through four cotton cooperatives in Lamu: Lake Kenyatta, Hindi, Witu and Lamu Cotton. Ngugi says Lake Kenyatta alone has more than 7,000 farmers.

Last season, the area produced about 3.5 million kilogrammes of seed cotton, with a current target of 5 million kilogrammes.

The arrangement links farmers directly to Thika Cloth Mills. Ngugi says TCM provides funding to the cooperatives, which then buy cotton from farmers. The ginnery processes the crop, separating the seed from the lint, with the lint ultimately going to TCM.

The model is intended to restore a reliable connection between farmers and processors.

But challenges remain. Ngugi identifies seed availability, pests, transport costs and cash-flow delays. The Ministry of Industry and the Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) help provide seed and other inputs, but farmers still need to produce enough cotton at the right quality, and manufacturers must be able to absorb it.

Joyce Njogu, head of Consulting and Business Development at the Kenya Association of Manufacturers (KAM), says the revival is already producing results.

She says cotton production has risen from about 1,300 tonnes in 2021 to roughly 8,800 tonnes in 2025.

But that remains far below manufacturers’ needs.

Njogu estimates that Kenya currently produces about 25,000 bales of cotton against demand of roughly 200,000 bales. She says the country therefore continues to import cotton from countries including Tanzania and Uganda.

Official figures also show how much manufacturing capacity remains underused. The 2024 draft CTA policy says Kenya had 52 textile mills, but only 15 were operational, with mills working at about 45% capacity. Sitati argues that restarting factories will also require rebuilding the technical workforce that disappeared when many mills closed.

AFA figures provide a clearer measure of the raw-material gap facing textile manufacturers. In 2024, Kenya produced 11,268 bales of cotton lint from 16,477 hectares, up from 7,006 bales in 2023. This was well below AFA’s estimated national demand of 48,000 bales and even further below Njogu’s estimate of 200,000 bales. AFA reported that seven ginneries were operating during the year.

An integrated approach

At the centre of that effort is Thika Cloth Mills (TCM).

Tejal Dodhia, the company’s managing director, describes TCM as a fully integrated textile manufacturer, taking cotton through spinning, weaving and processing to produce fabric. The factory employs about 650 people.

Bird Story Agency Tejal Dodhia, TCMâs Managing Director

For James Njagi, who joined the company in 2001 and now heads the spinning department, the industry is personal.

“Cotton means everything to me,” he says. His work has enabled him to educate his children and meet his household’s needs.

When he joined, the factory was struggling. Njagi says production has since risen from less than 50 tonnes of yarn a month to about 100 tonnes. The factory has also moved from periods of operating one shift to running two or three shifts, while its machinery and technology have been modernised.

Dodhia says TCM has invested in green energy. Its one-megawatt solar installation, she says, has reduced electricity costs by about 25%. Biomass boilers using materials such as coffee husks and nut shells have also reduced the cost of generating steam.

The company supplies fabric to government institutions, the disciplined forces, shoe manufacturers and smaller garment producers.

Dodhia says TCM has increasingly been able to source cotton locally and did not import cotton last year, after previously relying on supplies from Uganda and Tanzania.

But, she says, the next challenge is finding enough markets to sustain further expansion.

That challenge is visible at the other end of the chain.

Jamin Sitandi Mwenje, a tailor and fashion designer at Thika Market, says imported fabric still dominates his work.

Some of the materials he needs are unavailable from Kenyan manufacturers, he says. Other fabrics imported from abroad offer qualities that he believes local producers do not consistently match.

Kenyan fabric can be cheaper, making it useful for uniforms and other garments where affordability matters. But Sitandi says quality remains a concern.

He also points to a practical issue. Some Kenyan manufacturers require minimum orders of about 30 metres, he says, which can be difficult for small tailors who need much smaller quantities.

His message to manufacturers is simple: talk to the people who use the fabric.

If producers understood the materials, quantities, quality and prices that designers and tailors need, Sitandi believes more buyers would choose Kenyan products.

That exposes one of the biggest challenges in rebuilding the sector. Growing cotton is only the beginning. Kenya must also produce fabric that businesses and consumers want to buy.

Rebuilding more than factories

For Sitati, restarting the sector requires more than factories.

The industry also lost skilled workers and technical expertise when factories closed, she says. Machinery that remained idle deteriorated, while training systems for textile technology weakened.

She argues that farmers, cooperatives, ginneries, manufacturers and skilled workers must be rebuilt together.

The government’s strategy recognises many of the same problems. The CTA policy calls for increased cotton production, modernised ginneries and textile mills, skills development, greater value addition and improved market access.

The policy also places cotton within the wider economic transformation agenda. Under the Fourth Medium Term Plan, the government aims to strengthen productivity, create 1.2 million jobs annually, expand markets and improve Kenya’s competitiveness.

There are encouraging signs. Cotton production has risen from the low recorded in 2021. Farmers in areas such as Lamu are returning to the crop, a local ginnery is strengthening the connection with processors, and TCM says its use of Kenyan cotton has expanded.

KAM also sees traction in the revival. Njogu says the combination of seed distribution, support for processors and stronger value-chain linkages is beginning to show results.

But the recovery remains incomplete.

Kenya still produces far less cotton than manufacturers require. Buyers continue to cite gaps in quality, product variety and pricing. Much of the country’s manufacturing capacity remains unused, while local producers face competition from imports and international manufacturers.

The real test, therefore, is not simply whether Kenya can grow more cotton. It is whether the country can make the entire chain work: from the farmer planting cotton in Mpeketoni, to the ginnery separating seed from lint, to the spinner turning fibre into yarn, the weaver producing fabric and, finally, the tailor deciding whether that fabric is good enough to sell.

Kenya is reconnecting some of those links. The bigger question is whether it can reconnect all of them and turn a promising revival into a sustainable cotton and textile industry.

World.title: Ethiopia: Fano Claims Capture of More Than 150 Ethiopian Soldiers in Amhara Clashes
World.content:
A map showing the location of the Amhara region in Ethiopia.

Amhara — Ethiopia's Fano militia has claimed it captured more than 150 soldiers from the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) following heavy fighting in the Wadla-Delanta-Dawunt area of the Amhara region on September 8.

Fano fighters launched attacks on government positions during the clashes, according to pro-Fano sources, which said the militia inflicted heavy losses on the federal forces and destroyed a military brigade.

The sources also claimed that more than 150 ENDF soldiers were taken prisoner after the fighting, while other government forces were alleged to have withdrawn from parts of the battlefield.

The reported clashes come as fighting continues between Fano fighters and Ethiopian government forces in Amhara, where armed violence has persisted despite repeated government efforts to restore security in the region.

The Fano claims could not be independently verified.

There was no immediate statement from the Ethiopian government or the ENDF confirming the reported casualties, destruction of the military brigade or capture of the soldiers.

World.title: Kenya: Finance Should Work Around How Customers Actually Earn, says Watu Kenya's Damien Gueroult
World.content:
Watu Kenya Country Manager Damien Gueroult says serving customers outside traditional banking starts with understanding how they earn, what they use financing for and what it takes to lend sustainably.

When Damien Gueroult talks about boda boda riders, he describes them first as entrepreneurs.

"Our clients are effectively entrepreneurs. It's not a consumption loan," says Gueroult, Watu Kenya's Country Manager. "When you speak to a boda client, it's very clear: this is their tool of trade, this is how they generate income."

This distinction shapes how he thinks about asset finance more broadly. Many of Watu's customers earn daily rather than receiving a fixed salary at the end of each month. Their income can shift depending on demand, weather and how much they are able to work. Many are also accessing formal credit for the first time.

"You can't expect clients in the informal sector to behave like clients in the traditional banking sector," Gueroult says. "Income is erratic, most don't have medical insurance, and many earn daily. Our practices have to reflect that."

Gueroult took over Watu's Kenya business this year after previously leading its operations in Uganda. Across both markets, he says one of the most important lessons has been to start with how the customer actually earns and uses the asset, rather than expecting them to fit a financing model designed around a salaried borrower.

That affects repayment structures and customer support. It also changes how the asset itself is understood.

Smartphones are one area where Gueroult says his own thinking shifted.

"I may see it that way because I've personally used smartphones for the last 20 years, so I've forgotten what it's like to move from no smartphone to having one," he says. "But about 80 per cent of our clients in East Africa are people moving from a button phone to a smartphone, and for them too, it's a tool of trade. It makes them more productive and opens up career opportunities."

Watu has sought to understand those outcomes through research it commissions from GeoPoll across its East African markets. Close to a third of surveyed customers said access to a financed smartphone helped them secure work, while around half reported improved productivity in work they already had. Close to 80 per cent reported stronger connection to family or improved quality of life, and 44 per cent cited new access to savings products.

The research supports something Gueroult says is easy to overlook from the perspective of someone who has used a smartphone for years. The distinction between a consumer product and a productive asset can look very different for someone moving from a basic phone to their first smartphone.

For many customers, however, the challenge starts even earlier. They may have little or no formal borrowing history.

"Most of our customers have never been banked and have no credit score, so what would we do — tell them we can't lend to them?" Gueroult says. "No. We see our role as being the first ones to lend to these clients."

Watu verifies a customer's identity and personal information rather than relying solely on a conventional credit score that many first-time borrowers lack. From there, the financing relationship begins to create a record of actual repayment behaviour.

That does not mean treating access and risk as separate issues. Gueroult is clear that the ability to continue serving customers depends on getting both right.

Watu Kenya Damien Gueroult - Watu Kenya Country Manager

Watu's own experience has shaped that view. Several years ago, while the business was still largely focused on motorcycle financing, the company expanded quickly into a market already approaching saturation shortly before the COVID-19 pandemic.

"That taught us that we'd scaled too far relative to the risk we were carrying at the time," Gueroult says.

The lesson, he says, was not that lenders should retreat to serving only customers who already fit traditional measures of creditworthiness. It was that access has to be backed by strong operations and a clear understanding of risk.

"You could build a fantastic, low-risk portfolio by lending only to a small pool of very creditworthy people, but then you won't achieve scale, and you may struggle to attract investors."

That balance becomes more important as asset finance grows. Capital matters, but so do the systems around the financing: how customers are supported, how repayment behaviour is understood and how the lender responds as market conditions change.

It is also relevant as Kenya develops its first framework for asset-backed lending. Gueroult sees clear customer protections as an important part of the sector's development, while noting that the market includes many people who earn informally and may be accessing formal finance for the first time.

His approach to electric motorcycles follows much the same logic.

Watu finances electric motorcycles in Kenya, where Gueroult says the economics have become increasingly competitive with petrol alternatives. But he does not expect environmental arguments alone to determine whether riders make the switch.

"We wouldn't pursue it if the economics didn't work," he says. "For the riders themselves, it's not that they don't care about the environment, but if switching to an EV didn't make economic sense, most wouldn't do it."

For a rider whose motorcycle is a source of daily income, running costs matter. If an electric motorcycle reduces those costs sufficiently, the case for switching becomes much more practical.

The same principle can be seen in customers whose financed assets have continued to create value over time.

Elly "Kidole" Kegode, from Kibera in Nairobi, started with a Watu-financed motorcycle in 2016. Today, he operates a fleet of six and runs a mobile riding school. Two of the motorcycles transport schoolchildren, two serve commuters and two are used to train young riders in road safety and discipline.

"Mobility gave me freedom and stability," Kegode says. "Now I mentor others to achieve the same."

Gueroult is still relatively new to the Kenya role and is careful not to draw sweeping conclusions about a market he is continuing to learn. His career has taken him across Asia and Africa, including work in solar financing and microinsurance before Watu, and he says each market has required a close look at how people actually live, work and make financial decisions.

In Kenya, that has reinforced a relatively straightforward idea: financing works better when it begins with the economic reality of the person using it.

For a customer earning daily, that means understanding daily income. For someone borrowing formally for the first time, it means recognising that a credit history has to begin somewhere. And for a rider considering an electric motorcycle, it means making sure the economics work before expecting adoption to follow.

The products may change. Gueroult's starting point does not: understand how the customer earns, then design from there.

World.title: Nigeria: Academic Union Threatens Nationwide Strike
World.content:
The main thoroughfare at the University of Ibadan (file photo).

The union said its decision was prompted by the government's failure to fully implement the December 2025 agreement reached after years of negotiations.

The Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) has threatened a nationwide strike if the Nigerian government fails to address the outstanding issues affecting universities urgently.

ASUU president, Christopher Piwuna, a professor, disclosed this in a statement issued after an emergency meeting of the union's National Executive Council (NEC) on Thursday.

The union said its decision was prompted by the government's failure to fully implement the December 2025 agreement reached after years of negotiations.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The 2025 agreement followed prolonged disputes between ASUU and successive governments over the funding and conditions of service in Nigerian public universities.

The union said the non-implementation or "haphazard implementation" of the 2025 agreement, combined with the outstanding salaries and unremitted deductions, could trigger another industrial crisis in Nigeria's public universities.

The union said it may activate the suspended strike "without any further notice" if there is no satisfactory response to its demands.

"ASUU cannot guarantee an uninterrupted academic calendar at the expense of the existential needs of our members," the union said.

"ASUU-NEC resolved to notify all concerned that the Union may activate its suspended strike action without any further notice if the critical issues raised in this release are not speedily addressed."

ASUU's grievances

According to Mr Piwuna, the union remains concerned about the non-implementation of the agreement, the withholding of lecturers' outstanding salaries, unremitted third-party deductions, and what it described as violations of university laws and autonomy.

He said that apart from recent attempts by the Federal Ministry of Education to pay outstanding salaries to lecturers in federal universities of agriculture, there had been no "concerted efforts" to address the union's concerns on a sustainable basis.

"Unless immediate and concrete steps are taken to fully and comprehensively address issues bordering the welfare and well-being of Nigerian academics, ASUU-NEC will not accept any blame for calling out its members on a nationwide strike action within the shortest time possible," Mr Piwuna said.

The union said lecturers continued to face uncertainty over their monthly salaries, with some allegedly unsure of when or what portion of their salaries would be paid.

ASUU also renewed its demand for payment of the remaining three-and-a-half months' salaries withheld from lecturers in 2022 during the administration of former President Muhammadu Buhari.

The Buhari government withheld seven-and-a-half months' salaries during the 2022 industrial dispute, but the administration of President Bola Tinubu has since paid four months' salaries.

Third-party deductions

Another major concern raised by the union was the alleged failure to remit deductions made from lecturers' salaries.

ASUU said deductions for pension contributions, staff cooperative societies and union check-off dues had not been appropriately remitted for several months.

The union said the deductions run into billions of naira and accused the government of failing to resolve the matter despite previous engagements.

ASUU has historically opposed the Integrated Personnel and Payroll Information System (IPPIS), which it says does not adequately accommodate the peculiarities of university employment.

The union said it was prepared to "call out" its members if the issue of third-party deductions was not addressed.

State universities

Close 

ASUU also raised concerns about the implementation of the December 2025 agreement in state-owned universities.

The union commended Abia State Governor, Alex Otti, for adopting the agreement and apologising to ASUU over delays attributed to bureaucratic bottlenecks.

It also said implementation had commenced in Bauchi, Ekiti, Ogun, Benue, Yobe, Adamawa, Kebbi, Katsina and Borno states.

According to ASUU, Kano, Edo, Plateau, Taraba, Gombe and Bayelsa states had pledged to begin implementation in September or October.

The union, however, warned that state governments that had not started implementing the agreement could plunge their universities into an industrial crisis.

It said the authorities of the affected universities had been notified that strike action would commence at their institutions, with the backing of the union's national leadership, unless satisfactory progress were made.

World.title: Texas man remembered by Fox News hosts after repeat offender arrested in savage park bench slaying
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A 62-year-old Texas engineer with ties to multiple Fox News hosts was stabbed to death from behind in what authorities have described as a random attack on a park bench in Round Rock, Texas, and deputies have arrested a repeat offender who spent months in the local jail earlier this year.

Andrew James Wimsatt, of Austin, was killed on Sept. 7 — minutes after he sat down in the park after visiting his mother at a nursing home nearby, according to authorities.

Williamson County deputies have arrested a 26-year-old local man named Benedict Chinedu Ogbodiegwu on murder and theft charges.

GOT A TIP?

The murder was recorded on surveillance video, according to the Williamson County Sheriff's Office.

A man identified as Wimsatt sat down on a park bench at around 11 a.m., authorities said. A few minutes later, another man, alleged to be Ogbodiegwu, grabbed him from behind and repeatedly drove a knife into his neck.

The victim struggled but was unable to push his attacker away as the stabbing continued, according to a probable cause affidavit obtained by Fox 7 Austin. The suspect then wiped the blood off on his shirt and walked out of view.

REPEAT OFFENDER BUSTED AGAIN LESS THAN 24 HOURS AFTER RELEASE IN BRAZEN JEWELRY STORE THEFT CASE: POLICE

Wimsatt, who had a Ph.D. in civil engineering, is credited on IMDB as an executive producer of the Penn Jillete horror/comedy "Director's Cut." He worked for the Texas A&M Transportation Institute and had an Instagram account filled with photos of wildlife, vintage storefonts and city landscapes.

He also had ties to several Fox News personalities.

"He might be the only person on social media to never leave a bad word on a post about anyone," Greg Gutfeld wrote in an X post after news of the arrest. "He was relentless supportive and if he didn't like something, he usually kept it to himself, or found a way to engage positively."

Kat Timpf called him a "fan who became a friend" — a friend not only to her, but also to her family. They had lunch in Fort Worth in June, and she said she was expecting to see him at a show in Nevada later this month.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"He was so kind and generous it almost seems impossible," she told Fox News Digital Friday. "He always supported me... whether that was sending me clips I wanted to post or offering truly helpful words of encouragement during the times throughout my career that the internet was piling on me."

They spoke regularly — one a week or more for years — and he became known for sending TV clips to members of the "Gutfeld!" cast.

"Whenever the rest of the internet was making me feel hopeless about the state of the world, I could always count on a message from Andrew to remind me of the good that's out there, too," Timpf said.

Wimsatt attended Tyrus' standup shows as well.

"[He] took care of his mother… always positive… he was kind man, 62 years old fragile looking but had a monster laugh," Tyrus said in a statement. "I was honored to know him I was honored he cared so much and honored that my jokes and thoughts brought him joy."

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

On Labor Day, a witness called 911 after finding Wimsatt on the ground in the park, and paramedics pronounced him dead at the scene, according authorities.

Investigators were able to retrace the suspect's steps and allegedly recovered prints and other evidence, including bloody clothes and the suspected murder weapon, according to the affidavit. When confronted with video evidence, Ogbodiegwu allegedly claimed he had a twin brother but could not provide his name.

Ogbodiegwu has a criminal record in Williamson County going back to at least 2017, when he was charged with stealing. He had two prior arrests this year, on charges involving theft and carrying fake identification.

Prior to his arrest in connection with Wimsatt's murder, he was most recently released from the county jail on June 9. He had also been incarcerated between January and April.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He's being held on $1 million bond. His next court date is on Oct. 8 at 1:30 p.m., for a pre-indictment docket call.

World.title: 49ers star Christian McCaffrey recalls hilarious 'cracker' compliment with Australian barber
World.content:
For Christian McCaffrey, the San Francisco 49ers’ trip to Australia was quite the learning experience, as he found that words and sayings are a lot different Down Under.

McCaffrey, 30, revealed a hilarious interaction he had with a barber while getting a haircut.

"I was getting a haircut a few days ago and one of the barbers looks at me and says, ‘Looks cracker,'" McCaffrey said during his postgame press conference.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I said, ‘Sorry, what did you say?’"

George Kittle and Deebo Samuel, who flanked McCaffrey at the press conference, laughed at the star running backs retelling of the story. McCaffrey, accustomed to "cracker" being used as a derogatory term for White people, had no idea the barber was paying him a compliment.

"I didn’t know what it meant, I guess that means it looks good. But that was funny," McCaffrey said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

In Australia, the meaning of "cracker" is much different than in the United States, as it’s slang used to describe something as very good.

"He said (cracker) again, I said, ‘Dude, I hear that every Sunday.’ That was good, we had a good moment. I enjoy all the slang," McCaffrey said with a smile.

The 49ers had plenty of reasons to joke after their 27-7 trouncing of the Los Angeles Rams on Thursday night. McCaffrey had 10 carries for 68 yards while also catching five passes for 20 yards.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Rookie running back Kaelon Black split carries with McCaffrey, presumably in an effort to keep the four-time Pro Bowler healthy and had 14 carries for 65 yards.

McCaffrey and the 49ers will return to the United States after their win and lesson in Australian slang to play the Miami Dolphins in Week 2.

CUT OF THE DEAL: As opposition to artificial intelligence data centers spreads across rural America, one group is proposing "data center dividends" to counter the backlash by allowing residents to share directly in the wealth generated by the technology hubs.

BOLD FRONTIER: Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang declared that the era of artificial general intelligence (AGI) has arrived after OpenAI released its latest model.

AISLE BE WATCHING: Artificial intelligence is making its way into the grocery aisle, and it could have an unexpected effect on how much you spend. You grab a grocery cart, start working through your list and notice a screen on the handle offering directions, coupons and product suggestions. It can keep a running total and may even let you skip the checkout line. That sounds convenient. It also gives the store a new way to reach you while you are deciding what goes into your cart.

World.title: US warns Americans to stay vigilant as terror risk looms at major vacation hot spot
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Americans are being warned to exercise increased caution when traveling to one of Europe's most popular tourist destinations amid multiple terrorism-related arrests in recent months.

The State Department updated its "Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution" travel advisory for Italy on Thursday — keeping the country at the same advisory level while revising its summary.

Italy draws millions of visitors with its beaches, quaint villages and iconic ancient Roman landmarks.

TOURIST HOT SPOT SLAPPED WITH US TRAVEL WARNING RENEWAL DUE TO CRIME AND TERROR

But despite its appeal to tourists, the State Department is warning travelers to remain vigilant due to the threat of terrorism.

"There is risk of terrorist violence, including terrorist attacks and other activity in Italy," the advisory said.

While the threat of terrorism in Italy may receive less attention than in other parts of Europe, authorities have made several terrorism-related arrests in recent months.

In August, Italian news agency ANSA reported that a 16-year-old in northern Italy was arrested on international terrorism-related charges after investigators said he had spread jihadist and pro-ISIS material online.

SEXUAL ASSAULTS AND SCAMS PLAGUE TOP VACATION HOT SPOT, PROMPTING URGENT ADVISORY

In a separate incident in June, another 16-year-old near Bologna was arrested after authorities allegedly found jihadist material and weapons-making manuals in his possession.

The State Department advisory noted that petty crime is also a significant concern in Italy, especially "in popular tourist locations and on public transportation, including trains."

"Stay aware of your surroundings," officials said.

CLICK HERE TO 

"Most crimes against foreigners are crimes of opportunity, like purse snatching, pickpocketing, and car break-ins."

Americans who decide to travel to Italy are urged to monitor local media for breaking news and "stay alert in tourist spots."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Be prepared to adjust your plans," the advisory states. "Stay aware of your surroundings."

Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for additional comment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

World.title: Reporter's Notebook: Countdown is on as Senate races to pass crypto, college sports bills
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

It’s a twofer in the Senate.

Senators return to Washington Monday for the first time since the wee hours of Aug. 8. The Senate’s slated to meet for three weeks before heading home for the midterms — if the session even goes that long.

There are a lot of items senators want to tackle. But only two big ones are lined up for test votes right now.

The first legislative vote is locked in. It’s a procedural vote on a measure to regulate cryptocurrency. That comes Tuesday afternoon. The bill needs 60 votes to be in play.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: SUMMER ENDS, BUT THE SENATE'S FALL CRUNCH BEGINS

There’s no bigger advocate for cryptocurrency than President Trump. He’s pushing for the Senate to move legislation.

"We ended the war on crypto once and for all," said the President. "Now we need Congress to take the next step by passing the Clarity Act."

Let’s clarify what the Clarity Act does. The measure clarifies federal rules for digital currencies and tokens. The framework would divide oversight between two regulators: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CTFC). Approval of the bill would be the first step toward establishing guardrails for cryptocurrency.

"We passed the Clarity Act in the House last summer with 78 Democratic votes. It's now time for the Senate to join us," said House Financial Services Committee Chairman French Hill, R-Ark., on Fox Business.

The package has bipartisan support. But there’s a roadblock coming from the Democrats.

"The one remaining significant issue, I think, is the ethics provision," said Hill.

President Trump’s own financial disclosure report reveals he earned $1.4 billion on cryptocurrency last year alone. That’s why Democrats want specific rules for the Trump family and crypto.

"It basically exempts the President from any kind of ethical constraints. And that's just not going to fly in the Democratic caucus," said Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., says the bill is too closely aligned with what the President and his industry allies want.

"Yes. We need crypto legislation. But not this legislation that has been written by this industry," said Warren. "I just don't see how anyone, Democrat or Republican, moves forward on this bill."

That’s why many doubt the measure can score 60 votes twice to break a filibuster. The naysaying aggravates cryptocurrency advocates.

"This is the right bill at the right time, and it's time to vote," said Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wy.

She argues that crypto supporters bowed to demands to firm up ethics rules.

"In 2023, we added 100 pages with stronger consumer protection provisions. Yet we got feedback from colleagues that they wanted more. So again, we listened. Today, this bill that was under 300 pages is more than 600 pages. That's hundreds of pages built over 11 months of daily bipartisan negotiations in windowless rooms where colleagues from both parties shared their priorities, and we worked diligently to incorporate them," said an exasperated Lummis.

Warren argues that the bill makes it easier for drug runners and terrorists to fund their operations — without a literal paper trail.

TED CRUZ URGES SENATE TO STAY IN WASHINGTON UNTIL PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT PASSES THIS WEEK

Lummis says if the U.S. doesn’t establish its cryptocurrency blueprint, digital assets could flee overseas.

"These companies can go to Singapore, Switzerland, the UAE and have a well-understood clear set of regulations," said Lummis.

So that test vote is locked in. But it’s rare to pass a major financial regulatory measure this close to the midterms. And if Democrats prevail in November, that could create friction with the White House.

The Senate also expects a test vote before the end of September on a bill to regulate money in college sports. But there’s no specific agreement on a date for that roll call tally.

You know the old saying that there’s no such thing as bad publicity? Well, the "bad" publicity surrounding college football could potentially provide this legislation a boost.

President Trump implored senators to stay in Washington to finish the bill last month. But it wasn’t ready. However, controversies over former pro players heading back to college — to say nothing of clock maintenance at the University of Michigan — could prod skeptical senators to give this measure another look.

Let’s start with LSU tight end Dae’Quan Wright. If you can keep up with him.

Last year, Wright played for current LSU head coach Lane Kiffin last year at Ole Miss — before Kiffin abandoned his squad late in the season for the Tigers. Wright decided to go pro. The Philadelphia Eagles picked him up in the spring. But then waved Wright early last month. The Cleveland Browns then signed Wright. He dressed for a preseason game against the Buffalo Bills. Never played a snap. Then the Browns cut him.

So, Wright headed back to school. But this time, at LSU.

"I’m just putting on a college uniform again and going out there and having fun and embracing my opportunity," said Wright.

A judge then cleared Wright and former Ole Miss defensive lineman Zxavian Harris to play for LSU this fall. But in between, Harris appeared in preseason camp with the New Orleans Saints — before the team waived him.

Drew Rosenhaus is Wright’s agent. He believes his client had no other option after his brief cup of coffee in the pros.

"His contract with the NFL was terminated," said Rosenhaus. "If he was still able to play in the NFL, he would be there."

Chaos like this is prodding lawmakers to try to regulate intercollegiate athletics.

"It's not fair to the high school kids coming out to play college ball if you suddenly have colleges that are going and recruiting from the NFL," said Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas.

Cruz teamed up with Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the top Democrat on the Commerce panel, to craft the college athletics regulation measure.

One big restriction: the legislation limits athletes to one transfer.

"The transfer portal is out of control. You have athletes transferring two, three, four times. You have essentially no eligibility rules. So you have athletes competing six, seven, eight years. You have 28-year-olds competing against 17-year-old kids," said Cruz.

The constant darting around from school to school worries the Trump administration, too.

LAWMAKERS PRAISE BIPARTISAN EFFORTS LED BY TRUMP ADMIN TO ‘PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS’

"It's a crazy system, man," said Vice President JD Vance to colleague Lucas Tomlinson. "When I was growing up…you would get some loyalty, between the athletes and the fan bases. You would know the names of the people who played for your team because they were there for three or four years."

The Cruz/Cantwell package also caps money schools can use for name, image and likeness, or NIL. And, considering the recent contretemps, the legislation bars athletes from going pro. Then reversing field to college.

The White House tapped legendary former Alabama football coach Nick Saban to push for passage of the bill.

"Join the winning team today and help Congress protect this American tradition," says Saban in the commercial now airing around the country.

But even if the bill gets through the Senate, it faces an unclear path in the House. The House returns to session Monday, too. But it’s unclear how long its members will stick around with the midterms looming.

"I've had coach Saban in my office, and we've talked about this, and he's right," said House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. "I think Congress is ready to act. But it takes both chambers."

In other words, just like there’s a play clock in football, there’s a play clock in Congress, too.

"I appreciate the exuberance of our Senate colleagues," said House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif. "But I don't know if there's enough days to get this done."

Time may be the enemy of both the cryptocurrency bill and the college athletics bill. Lawmakers return to Capitol Hill with one foot practically out the door, headed back toward the airport.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

It’s a Senate twofer. But if things don’t sail smoothly on either or both bills, there may be little reason to anchor lawmakers to Washington. And if lawmakers don’t address these bills now, potential legislative fixes may evaporate until the new Congress begins in January.

World.title: Saudi Arabia tells Trump now is the time for military action as Iran-backed Houthis advance
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Saudi Arabia is urging Washington to take direct military action against Iran-backed Houthis, Fox News Digital learned after the terrorist group seized key positions along Yemen’s Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday.

The dramatic strengthening of Houthi's positioning along the coastline of Yemen is in one of the world's most important shipping choke points — a narrow passage that links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, which has been used as a bypass as the Iran war continues to severely disrupt shipping, especially of oil, through the Strait of Hormuz.

The rapid advance on Friday triggered urgent discussions at the highest levels in Riyadh and Washington, and a source familiar with the matter tells Fox News Digital that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis.

NEW RISK FOR U.S. CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT

The Houthis reached the strategic island of Mayyun, also known as Perim, after Yemeni government forces withdrew and also took the mainland coastal town of Dhubab, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Friday.

Fox News Digital independently confirmed key elements of an Axios report with a source familiar with the matter, who said the crown prince spoke with Trump a few times over the past 24 hours about the escalating situation in Yemen.

The U.S. does not want to take direct military action for now, but Trump told bin Salman that Washington would assist Saudi Arabia with intelligence and targeting support, according to the source.

The source also confirmed that U.S. Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper traveled to Saudi Arabia for coordination talks.

The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on the calls or whether additional U.S. military action is under consideration.

IRAN'S BIGGEST WEAPON AGAINST THE U.S. MAY BE SLIPPING AWAY, EXPERTS SAY

The convergence raises the prospect of simultaneous pressure on two of the world’s most consequential maritime arteries: Iran disrupting traffic through Hormuz while its Houthi allies strengthen their position around Bab al-Mandab.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the shift reflects Tehran’s effort to recover leverage as pressure around Hormuz changes.

"Trump’s success in pushing back on Iran’s maritime threat in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf has made the regime lose the maritime leverage it had, and now it is looking to double down on the Houthis who have proven to be able to impact Red Sea shipping and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the past," Ben Taleblu said.

"As Tehran loses leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, it is trying to wield a knife and a handshake at once: diplomacy with Arab states and a knife in the back via the Houthi offensive," he added.

IRAN CALLS ON HOUTHIS TO PREPARE TO CUT OFF RED SEA GATEWAY — CAN THE TERROR GROUP DO IT?

The latest advance follows the Houthis’ capture Thursday of the strategic Red Sea port of Mocha, which was previously held by forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

Former U.S. special envoy for Yemen Timothy Lenderking said Friday that the Houthis had spent the years since the 2022 U.N.-brokered truce rebuilding their military strength and are now exploiting the broader Iran conflict to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia.

Speaking during an on-the-record Middle East Institute virtual briefing, Lenderking said the April 2022 truce largely put Yemen’s civil war on pause but also "did allow the Houthis to regroup, retrain, refit, restock."

"They’re extremely entrepreneurial. They use every opportunity to build their capability, to test their capabilities, such that they are now the most lethal non-state actor in the entire Middle East," Lenderking said.

Lenderking traced the latest round of escalation in part to Iranian Mahan Air flights into Sanaa earlier this summer, which he said brought personnel and equipment intended to support the Houthi war effort, adding that the personnel were from Iran and were "probably IRGC members."

IRAN-BACKED HOUTHI THREAT IN RED SEA COULD LEAD TO MAJOR U.S. POLICY SHIFT, ANALYSTS SAY

Lenderking said the Houthis are now taking advantage of the wider conflict with Iran to increase their leverage over Riyadh.

"They’ve seized this opportunity, bringing these various lines of effort together, to put a great deal of pressure on the Yemen government and the Saudis specifically," he said.

On Thursday, a senior Trump administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."

The stakes extend well beyond Yemen.

The Bab al-Mandab is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and serves as the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. About 7% of global oil output passed through the strait in June, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. Disruption can force ships to reroute around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope, adding significant time and cost to voyages.

Reuters reported Friday that only seven vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, compared with a prewar daily average of 125, underscoring the pressure already facing the region’s other critical maritime choke point.

EXPERT WARNS OF 'GENERAL ESCALATION' OF FIGHTING IF HOUTHIS RESUME RED SEA CAMPAIGN

Ben Taleblu said the speed of the Houthi advance exposed vulnerabilities in the Saudi-led effort to contain the group.

"The U.S. should help the Saudis stymie the Houthi advance," he said. "The inability of the Saudis to prevent the Houthis from taking the strategic port city of Mocha, for example, does not bode well for what may come."

Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen adviser at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the danger extends beyond the territory captured. Retreating government forces, he said, left behind military equipment that could strengthen the Houthis on other fronts.

"People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The developments mark a dramatic reversal from the relative calm that followed the 2022 truce and leave Washington and its regional allies confronting a growing question: whether the Houthi advance can be contained without opening another direct U.S. military front as American forces remain focused on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: America built a fortress after 9/11. Then the threat started hiding in plain sight
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Javed Ali drove past the Pentagon on his way to work in northern Virginia.

Roughly half an hour later, American Airlines Flight 77 slammed into the building.

From his office in Falls Church, Ali could see smoke rising from the Pentagon. A year later, in a turn that captured how dramatically the country had changed, he was walking into the still-damaged building himself — now working in the Defense Intelligence Agency's counterterrorism office.

TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE

"It was a very eerie and odd and surreal moment in my career," Ali told Fox News Digital.

Ali's career would eventually take him from the DIA to the newly created Department of Homeland Security and later the FBI, giving him a front-row seat to the enormous national security architecture America constructed after the deadliest foreign attack on U.S. soil.

Twenty-five years later, that architecture presents something of a paradox.

By one of its clearest measures, the post-9/11 system appears to have made another attack on the scale of 9/11 far harder. The United States has not suffered another terrorist attack remotely approaching the scale and complexity of 9/11, which killed 2,977 people. U.S. intelligence and military operations dismantled much of the al Qaeda network that planned it, while new agencies, surveillance authorities, watchlists and intelligence-sharing systems were designed to ensure that another group could not exploit the same seams in American defenses. The 2026 U.S. intelligence community assessment said counterterrorism operations have degraded al Qaeda and ISIS's ability to quickly rebuild their leadership and plan large-scale attacks against the U.S. homeland.

But success against the threat of 2001 did not eliminate terrorism. It helped change it.

AMERICAN YOUTH RADICALIZED ONLINE, BUSTED IN SUSPECTED TERROR PLOTS AFTER HATING COUNTRY ON SOCIAL MEDIA

Today's most difficult threats increasingly involve individuals radicalized online, small cells with little warning signature, foreign terrorist organizations seeking to inspire attacks from afar, and an expanding layer of cyber and state-sponsored threats capable of reaching deep inside the United States without hijacking an airplane.

The question 25 years after 9/11, therefore, is not simply whether Americans are safer.

They are safer from one kind of attack — while increasingly exposed to others.

AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY

Building a security state after 9/11

The scale of the American response was extraordinary.

Just over two months after the attacks, President George W. Bush signed legislation creating the Transportation Security Administration. TSA says its creation amounted to the largest civilian undertaking in U.S. government history at the time, with the federal government rapidly assuming responsibility for airport passenger and baggage screening.

The following year, Congress created the Department of Homeland Security, combining all or part of 22 federal agencies and offices. DHS began operating in March 2003 and today employs more than 260,000 people across missions ranging from border and aviation security to cybersecurity, intelligence and emergency response.

The changes went far beyond new agencies.

The 9/11 Commission found that the pre-attack breakdown was deeper than the familiar failure to "connect the dots." Responsibility had been scattered across agencies, information was not consistently shared, and no single entity was empowered to integrate intelligence and drive joint action across the foreign-domestic divide. The commission concluded that "responsibility and accountability were diffuse."

Washington spent the next two decades trying to close those gaps.

Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that post-9/11 wars and related obligations have cost roughly $8 trillion. It estimates that more than $1.1 trillion has been spent on homeland security efforts to prevent and counterterrorism inside the United States since DHS was created.

Al Qaeda didn't disappear overnight

Ali said it can be easy, with 25 years of hindsight, to forget how persistent the original threat remained.

Even after the United States invaded Afghanistan, killed or captured senior al Qaeda figures and put the organization under extraordinary pressure, the group continued attempting to find ways back into the homeland.

During Ali's years at DHS, he said officials repeatedly confronted plots involving al Qaeda and its affiliates, including a 2006 plot originating in Britain to bomb transatlantic airliners traveling to North America.

The threat then evolved again.

Usama bin Laden was killed by U.S. forces in Pakistan in May 2011. But rather than marking the end of the era of jihadist terrorism, the following years produced a new and in some ways more difficult challenge.

ISIS grew out of al Qaeda in Iraq, expanded rapidly amid the wars in Iraq and Syria and declared a self-described caliphate in June 2014. At its height, the group controlled vast territory and millions of people in Iraq and Syria while encouraging or directing attacks far beyond its borders. The State Department reported that ISIS had emerged from al Qaeda in Iraq and expanded dramatically during 2013 and 2014.

For U.S. counterterrorism officials, Ali said, the center of gravity increasingly shifted from identifying trained operatives sent by an organized group to finding individuals who might be radicalizing inside Western countries.

Then came another shift: attacks by lone offenders across different ideologies, often with no direct operational relationship to an organization overseas.

"Mostly lone actors, lone offenders, not tied to groups overseas, not traveling overseas, and not being directed by people overseas," said Ali, now an associate professor of practice at the University of Michigan's Ford School of Public Policy.

DHS CHIEF ANNOUNCES CHANGES TO ITS SEAL TO REFLECT THAT DEPARTMENT IS 'AT WAR EVERY SINGLE DAY'

The terrorist organization became a phone screen

The transformation is now reflected in the government's own threat assessments.

The 2026 Annual Threat Assessment from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said setbacks to the ability of Islamist terrorist groups to conduct "large-scale complex attacks" have pushed them toward information operations and propaganda designed to inspire or enable people in or with access to Western countries.

The assessment said there were at least three Islamist terrorist attacks in the United States in 2025 and that law enforcement disrupted at least 15 U.S.-based Islamist terrorist plotters that year. Roughly half of those disrupted plotters had some online contact with Islamist terrorists or were inspired by foreign terrorist organizations, according to the assessment.

The vulnerability was demonstrated on New Year's Day 2025, when Shamsud-Din Jabbar, a U.S. citizen from Texas, drove a pickup truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street in New Orleans, killing 14 people. The FBI described the attack as an act of terrorism and said Jabbar had become increasingly isolated before adopting extremist views.

In the days after that attack, the FBI said lone actors and small cells who radicalize online had posed the greatest terrorism threat to the homeland in recent years precisely because they can be so difficult to detect and disrupt.

That presents almost the inverse of the 9/11 problem.

The 9/11 plot required 19 hijackers, overseas leadership, financing, international travel, flight training and years of planning. The challenge for investigators was collecting pieces of information held across different agencies and assembling them quickly enough.

A lone actor may offer far fewer pieces to collect in the first place.

Ali said many recent attackers or alleged plotters had not previously come onto the radar of the FBI or local law enforcement, leaving authorities with the extraordinarily difficult task of identifying people who may not commit an obvious crime until they move toward violence.

"So yes, we are safer from a certain type of threat," Ali said, "but again, we are not immune from terrorism, and other types of threats are much more difficult to identify or stop."

KASH PATEL REVEALS THE CHILLING HOLIDAY TERROR PLOTS FBI FEDERAL AGENTS QUIETLY STOPPED

A security system built for yesterday?

That changing threat has also fueled a broader debate over whether the institutions created after 9/11 became too large, too expensive or too focused on the dangers of the previous era.

Morgan Murphy, who served as press secretary to the secretary of Defense during the first Trump administration and later worked in the Trump White House, argues that Washington built too much bureaucracy around the 9/11 threat while other vulnerabilities grew.

"TSA agents still pat down grandma and gum up travel while Beijing wires our living rooms with cheap TVs and selfie sticks through the supply chain handed to them by Clinton, Bush, Obama and Biden," Murphy said. "We spent two decades frisking American passengers while our adversaries plugged themselves into our homes and businesses."

"The genius of America after Pearl Harbor was that we built to fight. After 9/11, we built to process," Murphy told Fox News Digital, "Real security means sovereignty at home and lethality abroad — a sealed border, an untangled supply chain, and enemies who fear us."

Theo Wold, who served as acting assistant attorney general in the Justice Department's Office of Legal Policy and as deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy during the first Trump administration, offered a similar critique, arguing that post-9/11 Washington relied too heavily on large bureaucracies, expansive government authorities and wars in the Middle East.

"George W. Bush and the D.C. governing elite responded to 9/11 the way their politics demanded: create large, unwieldy bureaucracy, push for special legal authorities with limited oversight and activate ground wars in the Middle East," Wold told Fox News Digital.

"Those wars didn’t make us safer, the legal authorities were wielded against Americans, and the bureaucracy is full of waste and has proven nearly unworkable," he said.

Wold argued that the lesson from the past quarter-century should be a more narrowly targeted national-security model.

"Now we know better. Americans are safest when we are nimble and focus ruthlessly on targeting real enemies," he said.

The next threat may not look like 9/11

The challenge now extends beyond terrorism.

The 2026 intelligence assessment warns that China, Russia, Iran, North Korea and non-state ransomware groups continue seeking access to U.S. government networks and private critical infrastructure for espionage, financial gain and possible future disruption. It also warns that artificial intelligence is accelerating cyber capabilities and that several state adversaries are developing missile systems capable of threatening the homeland.

The security landscape that began with al Qaeda operatives training to fly passenger jets has therefore expanded into something far less geographically defined: terrorist propaganda transmitted to an individual's phone, malicious code inserted into a computer network, attacks on critical infrastructure and state adversaries capable of reaching Americans from thousands of miles away.

For Ali, however, the evolution of the threat should not lead Washington to conclude that the original threat has vanished.

One of the central lessons of the years before Sept. 11, he said, was that emerging terrorist organizations have to be confronted before they have the time and space to develop operational capability.

"When these terrorist threats start to emerge, whether it's overseas or here, you have to put pressure on them before they gather momentum to carry out operations," Ali said.

The danger, he argued, would be allowing counterterrorism to fall so far down Washington's list of priorities that the country begins recreating the complacency that existed before 9/11.

"Terrorism as a tactic is probably never going to be defeated," Ali said.

Twenty-five years after he watched smoke rise from the Pentagon, Ali's answer to whether America is safer reflects the contradiction at the heart of the post-9/11 era.

The United States built a massive system to prevent the next 9/11.

It appears to have made another 9/11 far harder to execute.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The harder question now is whether that system can recognize the attack that doesn't look anything like it.

World.title: 25 years ago, Tom Brokaw anchors 9/11 NBC News Special Report
World.content: 25 years ago, Tom Brokaw delivered an NBC News Special Report on September 11, 2001, after terrorists hijacked four commercial planes and carried out coordinated attacks against targets in the U.S. Two were flown into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers, one into the Pentagon, and one – after the passengers and crew fought back – crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.Sept. 11, 2026

World.title: ‘Never Forget’: How Americans remember Sept. 11
World.content:
9 a.m., Brooklyn, N.Y.: I ran into a friend at the corner coffee shop. She had just dropped off her child and was waiting for her husband to celebrate their anniversary. He was an FDNY firefighter and was just getting off of his multi-day shift when the call came in. Instead of enjoying his anniversary, Dave Fontana stayed with his brothers. He was a beautiful soul, a wonderful husband and father. I only got to know him briefly at the Music Together program we brought our children to.

— Scott Groom

9 a.m., Ashtabula, Ohio: Everyone I was around, we couldn’t stop hugging each other and trying to help those of us who were taking that day harder than others.

— Trent Reinke

9 a.m., Yulee, Fla.: I was an Outward Bound instructor, getting ready to go on a 30 day canoeing expedition with “troubled” teens. We were getting life jackets and paddles ready for the students to arrive when a staff member came down to the gear locker and told us that someone had just flown a plane into the WTC. Someone actually said, “like a passenger plane?” and we all kind of laughed it off because how the hell could that happen? Well, within two minutes we were all watching the news broadcast in horror. We left on the St. Mary’s River or Suwannee the next morning and didn’t see or hear from anyone for about four days. The first time we ran into a couple of fishermen, they asked if we had heard the news. They gave us a copy of that day’s newspaper. It was kind of otherworldly to be out on a river in nature for weeks without really knowing what was happening.

— Tommy Taylor

World.title: FBI agent died of cancer after 9/11 Pentagon response. His widow tells his story.
World.content:
He died of the disease in 2023, at just 64 years old.

On Sept. 11, 2001, 2,977 people died in the collapse of the twin towers, at the Pentagon or on United Flight 93, which crashed in a Pennsylvania field. But scores of others who worked in the wreckage have died from illnesses in the years since.

At the FBI, more than 400 people have 9/11-related illnesses and at least 33 have died from 9/11-related cancers, according to the bureau.

Jack and Susan Hess with their family in New York City. Courtesy Hess family

Sandy and Jack Hess met early on in their careers at the FBI and worked together for years, with Jack focused on counterterrorism after the attacks. Jack retired from the bureau in 2009 to pursue a career in the private sector and often thought about what he saw at the Pentagon that day, according to his wife, but never worried his health might be at risk.

Susan and Jack Hess. Courtesy Hess family

In 2017, what started as a backache became an emergency trip to the hospital, where a doctor found a tumor on his kidney. Sandy was in disbelief.

“I thought, ‘Oh, my gosh, what?’ Like, this is a guy who’s never been sick a day in his life,” she said. Her sit-down with NBC News was the first time she shared their story publicly.

When the doctor asked about Jack’s work history, she recalled saying: “‘Wait, my husband responded to the Pentagon.’ And she looked at me and she said, ‘There has been a huge increase in kidney cancer since 9/11.’”

“Nobody had any kind of protection on. We didn’t even think about it. I mean, it was an emergency situation. We had a mission,” Sandy said. “And people ask all the time if Jack knew he was going to get this cancer, maybe he wouldn’t have gone that day. And I said, ‘You’re absolutely wrong. He would have done it, and he would have been proud, and we’re proud of him. He’s a hero.’”

In 2019, the FBI created a video in which first responders like Jack encouraged others to 

First responders on the scene following an attack at the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001, in Arlington, Va. FBI via Getty Images file

Jack grew increasingly concerned that the effects of that day could threaten the health of his colleagues, even many years later, his wife said.

“Don’t be afraid to go out and get screened and find that something’s wrong with you, whether it’s related to 9/11 or not. Seventeen years is not too long. Eighteen or 19 years probably won’t be too long. You can still get sick from this,” Jack said at the time.

Four years after that plea, he died, surrounded by his wife and four children, who are hoping to carry on his message to others.

“We are not being proactive enough. We just aren’t. People who have responded to 9/11, they need yearly scans,” Sandy said. “Some of this could have been avoided had a scan been done, and maybe, maybe he would have had Stage 2 cancer … but why does he have to wait for a death sentence?”

Jack Hess at the hospital. Courtesy Hess family

Specifically, Sandy said that more thorough CT scans — imaging tests that show detailed pictures of the human body — could lead to earlier diagnoses, as opposed to the yearly physicals covered by the FBI. The FBI, for its part, says it continues to encourage first responders to register for the World Trade Center benefits screening program.

As for how she would like him to be remembered, Sandy said her husband “left a legacy of courage, determination and selflessness.”

Now, a quarter of a century after the attacks, it’s not just Sept. 11 that marks a difficult date on the calendar.

“Every holiday is hard. There’s always, always an open seat everywhere you go, so it’s really hard. Father’s Day, the toughest holiday there is. But I try to tell the kids to reflect on all the good times we’ve had and appreciate the time we had with Jack. I had a great marriage for 25 years. Many people don’t have that,” she said.

“He was a father that was hands-on, involved with his kids, and many kids don’t have that, either. And so I try to teach my kids to appreciate what we have, not what we lost.”

World.title: Lutnick says Trump’s $5,000 checks for Americans wouldn’t rely on taxpayer funds
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s promised $5,000 “dividend” for all U.S. adults would not be paid for with taxpayer dollars, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Thursday.

“It’s not tax money,” Lutnick told NBC News in a wide-ranging interview at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, where he discussed the attacks and a variety of economic issues.

He claimed that the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers.”

Trump this week pledged that if Republicans held control of the House and Senate in November’s midterm elections, his administration would issue a “dividend” to all American adults as a reward.

“Together we’re going to deliver that plan and we’re going to pay that money to the Americans, and not from taxpayer money,” Lutnick said.

He referenced the Trump Platinum Card, an upcoming Commerce Department program allowing wealthy individuals to sign up to pay $5 million in order to extend their U.S. visas for an additional 270 days.

“We have a waitlist of more than 100,000 people who want to come,” Lutnick said. “That’s $500 billion.”

Lutnick also cited an investment in Intel the administration made last year. “Everybody knows we got just about 500 million shares, and the stock was $20, and now it’s $100, so we’re up $50 billion,” he said.

The administration spent $8.9 billion from appropriated CHIPS Act funds to make the investment in Intel. While the stock has appreciated from the government’s purchase price of $20.47 to $100.32 as of Thursday, the administration has not sold those shares — meaning the gain is merely on paper.

Other Trump administration officials have offered different explanations for where the promised $5,000 checks would come from.

On Friday, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told Bloomberg Television that the White House was considering a “reconciliation process” in Congress to fund the promised checks. Initial estimates put the cost of such a plan at around $1.3 trillion.

Vice President JD Vance suggested Wednesday that the promised payments could come from U.S. tariff revenues. But even before the Supreme Court ordered hundreds of billions in tariff revenues to be refunded, they would not have come close to covering this cost, according to the nonpartisan Tax Foundation.

The distinction is largely one of accounting. Every dollar sent out in checks is a dollar the government cannot use to pay down debt, fund programs or reduce taxes.

Trump announced the “dividend” idea just weeks after the U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time. The government’s budget deficit, the annual shortfall between revenues and spending, is nearing $1.8 trillion, its highest since March 2021.

In August, the U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time. Mandel Ngan / AFP via Getty Images

Lutnick said the administration planned to pay down the national debt through the pursuit of “waste, fraud and abuse.” But economists widely believe this will not make a dent.

Polling shows Americans are frustrated with the administration’s economic policies, a worrisome sign for Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections.

The president’s approval rating for his handling of the economy was just 32% in a recent Associated Press poll.

An NBC News poll released in April found 52% of Americans said they strongly disapproved of the way Trump is handling inflation and the cost of living.

Lutnick said he’d give the U.S. economy a high letter grade.

“I think it’s an A-minus,” he said. “When we get oil to $2 a barrel, it’s an A-plus, and the only way to do it is to pound away at opening the spigots of oil in the world.”

“If you break Venezuela and have them produce the gas that they used to produce — 3, 4 million barrels a day — and you break Iran’s control on the Middle East and let that oil flow, you’re going to have $2 gas for the rest of your life and the rest of our kids’ lives,” Lutnick said.

“That’s what President Trump is attacking,” he added. “He is saying, ‘I’m going to make a generational change in America. I’m going to drive the price of gas to $2 forever.’”

The average price of regular gas Friday was more than double that, at $4.29 per gallon. In parts of California, gas hit $10.

On Friday, the U.S. consumer price index for August showed inflation overall rose 0.4% from July. However, core inflation emerged as a potential problem. That reading, which excludes food and energy prices, rose more than economists had expected.

This could indicate that inflation from ongoing trade wars and the Iran and Ukraine conflicts could be spilling over into other price categories.

World.title: CIA officer charged in gold bars case working toward a plea deal
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A former CIA officer who was arrested in May after investigators found 303 gold bars worth $40 million at his home is working to finalize a plea deal with federal prosecutors that could help keep the case shrouded in mystery.

David Rush and the Justice Department have a “plea agreement in principle,” the parties said Friday, and are asking a judge to extend a forthcoming deadline for the case to be indicted.

Rush had only formally been charged with one count of theft of public funds, accused of falsifying pay records in a case that was presented by criminal complaint and has not yet been presented to a federal grand jury.

“The parties need additional time to prepare the paperwork, including an agreed upon statement of facts,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Raizza Ty and Rush’s attorney Jessica Carmichael wrote in a joint filing. “A pre-indictment resolution promotes the public interest by conserving government and judicial resources.”

They are asking for a 21-day extension, through Oct. 8. Judge Leonie Brinkema had previously said there would be no extension past her deadline of Sept. 17.

Details of the working plea agreement are not yet available.

The case against Rush has brought a spotlight to his relationship with the No. 2 official at the Defense Department, Steve Feinberg, as NBC News reported this week. The FBI reviewed video showing Rush and Feinberg at a residence in the Washington region that is linked to the federal government, according to four people familiar with the video. Feinberg has been interviewed by the FBI, according to two people familiar with the investigation, but has not been accused of any wrongdoing, and the bureau said he is not under investigation.

The CIA placed senior officials on leave after Rush’s arrest, NBC News reported. Rush allegedly lied to his employer about his background for nearly two decades. He had a high-ranking job in the spy agency, working on some of the most secret programs in the government.

Federal agents seized about 300 gold bars at Rush’s home, federal officials alleged, along with about $2 million in U.S. currency and 35 luxury watches.

Rush’s lawyer didn’t immediately return a call seeking comment. The lawyers in the case are under a protective order that bars them from sharing sensitive information in the case.

World.title: Iran-backed Houthis seize Red Sea coastline, tightening grip on vital shipping lane
World.content:
Houthi rebels effectively completed a rapid push to take control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline on Friday, tightening their grip on one of the world’s most important shipping routes and delivering a dramatic boost to their backers in Iran.

Houthi forces captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb Strait, several news agencies reported, citing multiple sources. A day earlier, the Houthis captured the historic port city of Mocha.

That was followed by an advance on the strategic coastal town of Dhubab and the apparent withdrawal of forces from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government, from Perim, also known as Mayun.

The Houthis and the opposing coalition have been fighting a civil war since 2014. The conflict has simmered for years but erupted into intense fighting again in recent weeks, raising concerns of a return to all-out war and posing a serious new threat to the global economy.

Effective Houthi control over Bab el Mandeb, a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia, could further imperil oil exports while granting Iran powerful new leverage in its war with the United States.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has had to rely on the Red Sea route given the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world’s oil used to pass, since the U.S. and Israel waged war on the Islamic Republic in late February.

If the Houthis are similarly able to threaten shipping along the Bab el Mandeb Strait, it could reduce oil supplies through another key waterway and deepen the world’s energy crisis.

Fighters loyal to the Houthi authorities shout slogans during a rally to recruit more fighters, in the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Thursday. Mohammed Huwais / AFP via Getty Images

Global oil prices appeared set to end the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May, after the dramatic developments in Yemen and new U.S.-Iran exchanges.

The Houthis have also attacked oil facilities in Saudi Arabia itself, and, in another potentially significant development, satellite imagery on Friday showed a 60-mile smoke plume along the route of the kingdom’s East-West oil pipeline. This has been a key alternative for Saudi exports that can’t transit Hormuz.

Fire detection data showed high-temperature readings at several sites where infrastructure for the underground pipeline is located, but it was unclear what transpired. Neither Saudi officials or the Houthis have commented.
