World.title: How 9/11 brought these 2 women together — over a piece of dried fish in Newfoundland
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jeanette Gutierrez grew up with one sister, but now has two.

Her sister, Gail, saved her life when Gutierrez was working across from the World Trade Center during the Sept. 11 attacks, 25 years ago.

But the New Yorker says she met her friend-turned-sister in Gander, N.L., a decade ago. She was attending a 9/11 commemoration in the small Canadian town, where dozens of flights were diverted in the hours after the attacks. With thousands stranded, Newfoundlanders stepped up to offer shelter.

Gutierrez wanted to meet the people behind that kindness, she told The Current .

“I decided to come here on a tour of gratitude to basically thank the people of Newfoundland for doing such a wonderful thing,” she said.

But once in Gander, she found herself staring down the stinky eye of a tiny fish, as she was being screeched-in .

“I don't eat seafood anyway. Not cooked and certainly not a stinky, little skinny fish. But I had to do it — I wanted so badly to be an honorary Newfoundlander,” she said.

Gutierrez and Sceviour on the night they met, when the New Yorker was being screeched-in in Gander, N.L. (Submitted by Kelly Sceviour)

Her salvation came in the form of a local woman, Kelly Sceviour, who spied her discomfort.

“She's a New Yorker so you could tell by her face what was happening … the look on her face was like, I am not [eating this!],” said Sceviour, the town’s special events co-ordinator.

Sceviour motioned to Gutierrez, indicating she should take a small bite and hand over the rest, which she promptly disposed of.

When the ceremony was over, Gutierrez approached Sceviour at the bar.

“[She] said, ‘I owe you a beer,’” Sceviour recalled. “And I was like, ‘Well, I don't drink beer, but I'll take a vodka!’”

“That's when we became friends.”

That friendship has blossomed into both women feeling as close as sisters, which Gutierrez says has helped her navigate the memories of 9/11. While she feels a kinship and comfort with other survivors, she says she finds it hard to be in New York on the anniversary, often travelling to Gander instead.

“I still get to honour and mourn and cry … everything that I do in New York. But I do it — for me — in a better place. In a place that I can also smile and laugh and be with this sister.”

My big sister saved my life

On the morning of the attacks, Gutierrez was working at Three World Financial Center, when she heard the first plane hit the North Tower at 8:46 a.m.

She called her sister Gail, who also worked downtown. Like many people, Gail initially thought there had been an accident. But when the second plane hit, Gail called back, urging Gutierrez to leave — she hesitated.

“Eventually she convinced me to leave by saying she would come to me and we would leave together,” Gutierrez said.

WATCH | 9/11 travellers recount Canadian kindness: ‘Thank God for them’: 9/11 travellers recount Canadian kindness | Duration 2:26

Gutierrez says if Gail hadn’t persuaded her to leave when she did, she might have been caught in the towers’ collapse.

“My big sister Gail saved my life that day.”

In Gander, Sceviour was working for the municipal government when she heard something had happened. She was sent home, but told she might be needed later.

Sceviour went to her mother’s house, which was right on the flight path for Gander International Airport.

“I watched as plane after plane descended. And I thought, 'Oh dear, what are we going to do with all these people?'”

Sceviour was called back into work at midnight, where she spent the night taking phone calls from people looking for loved ones on redirected flights. Working off a passenger list, she was able to reassure them that their family members were OK.

“To hear that relief in their voice … it felt really good to be able to help,” she said.

Gutierrez and Sceviour have spent a lot of time travelling together. Left to right: the friends at Come From Away in New York City; visiting Bonavista, N.L.; and waiting for the sunrise in Greenspond, N.L. (Submitted by Kelly Sceviour)

An unbreakable bond

Dozens of planes were redirected to airports in Newfoundland and Labrador that day. Gander took in nearly 7,000 stranded passengers, hosting them for several days as the community stepped up with food, accommodation and whatever assistance they could provide.

“We're born and raised in Newfoundland to be those kind and helpful and compassionate people,” she said.

Canada’s relationship with the U.S. has grown tense in recent years, as U.S. President Donald Trump launched a trade war and repeatedly threatened to use economic force to make Canada the 51st state.

But Gutierrez said politics can’t break her bond with Sceviour, and nothing can ever erase what the people of Newfoundland and Labrador did 25 years ago.

“Nobody sitting anywhere in any office can change who Canadians are,” Gutierrez said.

“It might change some relationships. It will never change ours.”

World.title: Republican congressman wants to rename Lake Erie to Lake Pennsylvania
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

First Lake Ontario.

Now … Lake Erie?

A republican congressman from Pennsylvania wants to change the name of another Great Lake.

On the heels of U.S. President Donald Trump signing an order to rename Lake Ontario, Lake America, Rep. Congressman David Maloney of Pennsylvania wants to change the name of Lake Erie to Lake Pennsylvania.

A gaggle of Canadian Geese enjoy the open Lake Erie water near the U.S. and Canadian border in a file photo. (Joe Traver/Reuters)

In a statement put forward earlier this week, Maloney said it’s about the lake’s “modern identity,” and that he’s preparing a resolution to put before the U.S. House of Representatives — urging the president, Congress and the U.S. Secretary of the Interior to invoke the change.

“Pennsylvania has only one Great Lake and maybe it is time we put our name on it,” it read, stressing the importance of fishing and tourism the watercourse has on how people move around the lake and rely on it.

Rep. Congressman David Maloney is from Pennsylvania. (Republican Congressman David Maloney)

Trevor Jones is the MPP for Chatham-Kent—Leamington in Ontario. A portion of his riding stretches along the Lake Erie shoreline. When contacted by CBC News, his office said he would not be providing any comment about the proposal at this time.

The office for the same riding’s federal representative, MP Dave Epp, said he was unable to provide a comment or an interview due to prior commitments.

Maloney says Ohio already has plenty of shoreline, while New York has two Great Lakes — with Canada having four others. Michigan is the fourth state that touches Lake Erie.

“Pennsylvania has one. Let’s call it Lake Pennsylvania!”

'We ultimately become poorer for this loss'

Ken Drouillard is a University of Windsor professor who teaches a course on the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement .

He says renaming places with strong historical significance, such as the Great Lakes, serves to break those connections.

“We ultimately become poorer for this loss,” he told CBC News.

“Names are more than just labels on a map, they connect us to place and history,” added Drouillard, who’s also with the university’s Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Research (GLIER).

A boat enters Lock 4 of the Erie Canal in Waterford, N.Y., in 2015. The Erie Canal was an engineering marvel when it opened in 1825. (Mike Groll/The Associated Press)

He says similar to Lake Ontario, Lake Erie’s name has its roots in First Nation naming conventions that predates both the U.S. and Canada.

“Beyond this, renaming Lake Erie undermines the rich historical context that Lake Erie has played, particularly in the early westward migration and settlement of the U.S. Midwest."

"The Lake Erie Canal was the first major inter-basin diversion connecting Lake Erie to the Hudson River and the New York City Port on the Atlantic Ocean. Would renaming Lake Erie necessitate renaming this historical canal entirely enclosed in a different state?”

The name Erie is a short form of the Indigenous word erielhonan, which translates to “long tail.”

World.title: Why Trump likely won't have to fulfil his $5,000 'dividend' promise
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The long-standing trend of the incumbent U.S. president's party getting thumped in the midterms strongly suggests Donald Trump won't need to make good on his new promise to send every American citizen a $5,000 US cheque.

The president is pledging what he calls the "Trump dividend," but says the money will come only if the Republican Party wins control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

While the Democrats face a tough challenge to take the Senate away from Trump's party, the House is well within reach. The Republicans currently hold the slimmest possible majority in the House, with 218 of its 435 seats.

Michele Swers, professor of American Government at Georgetown University, told CBC News it will be very difficult for the Republicans to hang on to such a small majority.

"As a practical matter it's probably unlikely that they maintain control of the House, so it's not likely that this comes about," she said of the promised dividend.

The incumbent president's party has lost House seats in all but three of the 41 midterm elections dating back to the Civil War.

WATCH | Critics slam Trump's promised dividend: Trump's $5K dividend promise slammed as desperate attempt to buy votes | Duration 2:34 Critics slammed U.S. President Donald Trump's promise to give out $5,000 cheques for voting Republican in the upcoming midterm elections as a desperate attempt to bribe voters. But some lawyers say that while the move is probably unethical, it may not be illegal.

Since the 1960s, when a president's approval rating has been below 50 per cent, his party has lost an average of 32 House seats and has never lost fewer than nine, according to an analysis by North Star Opinion Research, a U.S. polling and strategy firm.

Trump's approval rating is currently averaging 38.5 per cent, according to the Silver Bulletin polling aggregator.

Republicans lost 40 seats in Trump's first midterm

In the 2018 midterms, during Trump's first stint in office, his approval rating sat at 44 per cent heading into election day and his party lost 40 seats in the House.

This all makes Trump's promise a little bit like a Canadian party leader vowing to send every adult $5,000 if the Toronto Blue Jays win the World Series this year: contingent on an outcome that is not within his control, possible in theory, yet in reality pretty unlikely.

If the Republicans somehow overcome Trump's low approval ratings, buck the historical trend and hang on to both chambers of Congress, the question will quickly turn to how the Treasury pays for Trump's promised dividend.

Sending $5,000 to every adult American citizen would cost more than $1.2 trillion US, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a non-partisan advocacy group in Washington, D.C.

WATCH | Trump all but ignores Canada during lengthy midterm convention speech: Trump mostly avoids trade war with Canada at GOP convention | Duration 3:51 U.S. President Trump mostly avoided the Canada-U.S. trade war during his speech at the Republican convention, in a possible sign that he's aware how unpopular it's becoming before the midterms, even among Republicans.

"This proposal is fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious," said the group's president Maya MacGuineas in a news release.

"It’s hard to understand how anyone could look at our current fiscal and economic situation and think we need to borrow another $1.2 trillion to send everyone cash," MacGuineas said.

The total is approximately nine times the net revenue from Trump's tariffs since they began in March 2025.

Yet Trump is saying tariffs will pay for the dividend, and that's part of his rationale for making it contingent on Republican control of Congress.

"If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000," Trump said in his speech at the GOP convention in Dallas on Wednesday night.

"The reason the Democrats can’t do that is because they don’t do tariffs," he said.

Also far from clear is how the government could possibly enforce the caveat that Trump added about how people can spend the $5,000.

"The dividend that we're making must be spent in the United States of America," he said. "We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money. We don't want you going to China, to Germany."

'Socialist vote-buying scheme'

The reaction from Democrats was unsurprisingly scathing, but even some Republicans were skeptical of Trump's floated $5,000 dividend.

"Some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms," said Texas Republican Congressman Chip Roy in a post on X.

Bob Good, a Republican who served two terms in the House representing Virginia, slammed it as a "socialist vote-buying scheme."

Trump's promise is "pathetic and sad at the same time," said California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat.

"Pathetic because it's just bullshit, and sad that he had to go in front of people and basically bribe them," Newsom told The Associated Press.

The political strategy behind Trump's promise appears to be aimed at giving his supporters some motivation to get out and vote in the midterms.

WATCH | Why tariffs on Canada could be a factor in some U.S. midterm races: Could Canadian tariffs swing votes in U.S. midterm elections? | Duration 7:48 While Democratic governors warn of the 'catastrophic' economic impacts of U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada, Trump promises each voting-age American a $5,000 US 'dividend' if Republicans retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections. Power & Politics hears from Chuck Todd, former host of NBC's Meet the Press and current host of the Chuck ToddCast, on what it could all mean as Americans head to the polls in November.

Trump said in his convention speech that his supporters should "pretend that I'm on the ballot" in the upcoming midterms.

His message suggested that he believes he can be the exception to the historical rule that midterms are not kind to the president's party.

"For some reason, even if he's really a good president or a great president — there aren't too many of them — they don't win the midterms, and nobody quite knows why," Trump said.

"We're going to change that."

Trump is battling a tough political environment heading into the midterms.

Poll after poll suggests the cost of living is the top concern among voters right now, whether it's from the war against Iran pushing up the price of gas or Trump's tariffs boosting the cost of consumer goods.

While Trump didn't admit it in his speech, his offer to send U.S. citizens $5,000 implicitly acknowledges that voters are feeling the economic pinch.

World.title: How big and small grocery stores are preparing for tariffs to hit shelves
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian grocery aisles will change in the coming weeks as the impacts of tariffs on some American goods take effect.

Stores across Canada will manage tariff price increases differently, with factors like supplier contracts, wholesale capacity and consumer preferences impacting what will be stocked.

Some major retailers, like Loblaw, will denote tariffed products with a "T" sign. Others, like the Salmon Arm, B.C.-based Askews, are choosing to offer even more Canadian-made or internationally-imported alternatives to American goods.

"We have the flexibility to purchase from whomever we want, basically," said Heather Turner, a store manager at Askews in Salmon Arm. The grocery store is locally owned and operated, with five locations spread across the Shuswap region.

"We're not, limited to dealing with one large wholesaler," she said.

Askews in Salmon Arm is a locally owned grocery store with five locations across the Shuswap region. (Jacqueline Gelineau/ CBC)

She said customers began asking for Canadian-made alternatives for everything, from shampoo to toilet paper last year, and the store listened.

"If our customers request a product and we have access to that product, we can source it and get it on our shelves," said Turner.

This round of counter-tariffs on American goods was imposed by the Canadian government as part of the ongoing trade war. It will impact items like U.S. dairy, paper products like toilet paper, make-up and hair care products.

Turner said as a result of customer demands, Askews already stocks Canadian or internationally-made alternatives for nearly every American product that will be impacted by counter-tariffs. She said if there is anything missing, the store will find an alternative as soon as possible.

Turner said in times like these, being independently-owned and able to quickly adjust to customer needs is beneficial. She added the store can work with small suppliers across Canada to bring in products that large corporations can't.

Turner noted that some items, while manufactured in Canada, may contain tariffed products from the USA, and could still see a price increase. Turner said a key product that may increase in price is protein powder, as many Canadian brands source whey from the USA.

Loblaw says it is bringing back the “T” symbol on shelf labels so customers can easily identify products coming directly from the U.S. that are affected by tariffs. (Chris Wattie/Reuters)

In an emailed statement, the Canadian-owned grocery conglomerate Loblaw said the impact of tariffs may not be felt for weeks, as items already purchased and currently on shelves pre-date the tariffs.

"Wh en tariffs drive up our costs, our price will reflect that increase only, " said Youmna Rab, a Loblaw retail communications manager. "N othing more."

She said Loblaw — including its brands such as Shoppers Drug Mart, Superstore, No Frills, Presidents Choice and No Name — will not benefit from tariffs.

Rab said Loblaw is pushing back on suppliers when it believes cost increases aren’t justified, and will do everything it can to keep prices down.

"We are working with our vendor to find alternatives to help keep costs as low as possible," said Rab.

Kara Stokes is the general manager of the Sweláps Market located on Tḱemlúps te Secwépemc land, in the Kamloops, B.C., area. The market is owned and operated by the Tḱemlúps te Secwépemc Nation.

Kara Stokes is the general manager of the Sweláps Market , run by the Tḱemlúps te Secwépemc Nation near Kamloops. (Jenifer Norwell / CBC)

Stokes said, like Askews, Sweláps Market has been able to tailor its inventory over the last year to meet customer preference for Canadian goods. These tariffs are only accelerating that momentum.

"We have options to look for other local or Canadian suppliers," said Stokes.

She said customers should not expect to see large increases in cost in the store. Where costs may rise when switching vendors to avoid tariffs, she said quality will not waiver.

"Together, we're going to find the best solution."

World.title: Why isn't Canada blocking the Welland Canal? Other trade war questions answered
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

How can Canada win a trade war with the U.S. when leverage isn't equal? Andrew Chang explains how Canada is retaliating against massive tariffs levied by a neighbour 13 times its economic size. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That

Reading through the emails that readers send to CBC News, one gets the impression they don't want just "elbows up" in the Canada-U.S. trade war, but also sticks, knees, skates and whatever else might be lying around.

One of the most common questions is some variation of, "Why isn't Canada doing X?" — where X is a tactic or tariff the reader supposes will hit the U.S. where it hurts.

Here's a look at some of those suggestions and what key players or observers have had to say about them.

Why doesn't Canada put export duties on energy as the cost is borne by Americans not Canadians?

Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, told CBC News late last month that export taxes are an option. Former prime minister Jean Chrétien said this week that an export tax on oil, gas, electricity and potash might be needed.

In 2025 , Canadian commodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81 per cent of imported electricity, 99 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.

However, Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa, warned that the long-term effects of such a move could be severe for Canada, both through lost revenue and damage to the relationship with its biggest customer. The U.S. could respond much as Canada has to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs: by trying to diversify away from a partner it can no longer count on and finding new suppliers.

University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe and Christopher Ragan, founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy, made the same point separately: targeting U.S. energy could play into the hands of the U.S. administration and unite Americans against Canada.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in July he doesn't "see the value" in using energy exports as a bargaining chip. Carney said being a reliable supplier is important.

"Canadians are reliable. Canadians can be trusted," he said.

Why not ban sales of certain goods in Canada?

This has mostly already happened at a provincial level with alcohol, in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan this week added a retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has shown no interest in that sort of approach, stressing that Canada's response will be proportionate, strategic and targeted.

The U.S. may, of course, reply in kind to any ban, as it has with alcohol: Most imports of Canadian-made alcohol will be banned from the United States on Sept. 29.

Tombe, discussing tariffs, told CBC News late last month that Canada has to be careful when selecting products to target because they need to be items Canadians can replace relatively easily but Americans cannot.

If tariffs are applied to harder-to-replace items — "a particular type of circuit board, say, or piece of machinery," that merely complicates life and increases costs for the Canadian importer, Tombe said.

WATCH | CBC's Linda Ward answers a reader question about toilet paper: Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war? | Duration 2:28 U.S. President Donald Trump dropped tariffs on certain Canadian products, including toilet paper, cement and salt. In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million worth of the product, making it the largest international provider of toilet paper to the U.S.

Can Canada stop U.S. ships using the Welland Canal?

The Welland Canal is on the western half of the St. Lawrence Seaway, which connects the St. Lawrence River to the Great Lakes. The canal links Lake Ontario to Lake Erie using eight locks, all in Ontario, that can be filled with water or drained to move vessels between different water levels.

But the seaway is overseen by both the U.S. and Canada.

The Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation administers the seaway on the American side as a federal agency within the U.S. Department of Transportation.

Boats sit idle in Lake Ontario close to the Welland Canal on Oct. 26, 2023. (Tara Walton/The Canadian Press)

In Canada, the federal government owns the Canadian portion of the seaway, but it is managed by the non-profit St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation.

The U.S. also controls several important locks, including ones in New York state between Lake Ontario and Montreal and others in Michigan that connect Lake Superior and Lake Huron.

John Boscariol, a Toronto-based co-head of international trade and investment law at the Canadian law firm McCarthy Tétrault, told CHCH News in Hamilton that closing the canal would be "shooting ourselves in the foot" and would hurt Canadian businesses just as much as U.S. businesses.

Trump critic Jennifer Hillman, formerly general counsel at the Office of the United States Trade Representative under then-president Bill Clinton, told CBC News Network it would "absolutely be a total violation of international law, and I think not really a good idea because you're blocking both sides' goods.

"I would hope that's not a road anybody would go down."

What questions do you have about the latest tariffs? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.

World.title: U.S. federal officials declare end to cyclospora outbreak that sickened thousands in 21 states
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The largest cyclospora food poisoning outbreak in U.S. history is over, U.S. health officials said Friday.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration officials said they are confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce related to this specific outbreak is off the market.

Nearly 13,000 reported cyclospora cases were tied to the multistate outbreak, federal officials say. While Canada has seen small, sporadic clusters of cyclospora cases in recent years, there were no known Canadian cases related to this specific outbreak.

Even with the outbreak deemed over, several questions remain, including about its origin. The parasite is spread through human feces, and it still isn't clear how sewage could have contaminated enough food to sicken so many people.

"This contamination can happen if produce is grown in soil or comes into contact with water that has been contaminated," said Ellen Shumaker, director of outreach for a North Carolina State University food safety program, Safe Plates.

Since May 1, the government has received reports of nearly 20,000 lab-confirmed cases, or more than 16 times the number reported during the same period last year. More than 6,100 suspected cases also have been reported.

The worst previous year in the U.S. for infections was 2019, when about 4,700 illnesses were reported nationally.

What is cyclospora? A diarrhea-causing parasite | Duration 2:37 A diarrhea-causing parasite has led to a growing outbreak in the United States that has sickened more than 1,000 people and sent dozens to hospital. As of Wednesday, multiple states had reported cyclospora infections, which can cause watery diarrhea, bloating, fever and nausea. While cases are common in the spring and summer, the current outbreak has led to an unusually high number, making it one of the largest the country has seen. No deaths have been reported.

Cyclospora is a microscopic, spherical parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhea "with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements," according to the CDC. Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer.

The illness, called cyclosporiasis, is less common than foodborne illnesses caused by other germs, including salmonella and E. coli. Many cases are never linked to a specific food or other source.

This year's surge in cases was dominated by an outbreak in 21 states linked to iceberg lettuce. But there are thousands of other cases that have not been linked to that outbreak.

Michigan was the hardest hit state, with the most reported cases and the two U.S. deaths tied to the outbreak.

In this outbreak, investigators initially zeroed in on lettuce served at Taco Bell. Federal officials subsequently focused on Taylor Farms as the source of the lettuce, and the company recalled iceberg lettuce grown in central Mexico.

The Taylor Farms recall involved thousands of packaged salad products combining iceberg lettuce with other vegetables. The products were shipped to major U.S. restaurant chains, including Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, Pizza Hut and KFC.

The FDA has ended its on-site inspections and sample collection at iceberg lettuce growers and the processing facility in Mexico, the agency said Friday. Samples from the on-site inspections are pending analysis, the FDA said.

The outbreak cast a spotlight on a worsening problem: U.S. regulators are conducting fewer international inspections to catch contaminated produce before it lands on American plates.

World.title: As Dean Penney gets life sentence for killing estranged wife, sister says she's 'lost' without Jennifer Hillier-Penney
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Gary Hillier's voice broke as he sat in the witness box and tried to describe the agonizing grief he's felt since his sister disappeared 10 years ago.

The man who murdered her sat a few feet away. Dean Penney was expressionless, staring into space as Hillier spoke of everything Penney had taken from him and his family.

Ten years of an empty seat at the table during family gatherings. Ten years of a torturous mystery. Ten years of sadness and rage.

"The silver lining in this is that while her murderer physically took her from us, he can never take her spirit," Hillier told the court. "It's 10 years since I gained the most beautiful guardian angel."

Penney was condemned to life in prison on Friday, without the possibility of parole for 25 years. He was found guilty of first-degree murder by a jury in May, bringing a close to a case that captured the country's attention.

Jennifer Hillier-Penney was last seen on Nov. 30, 2016, in the rural community of St. Anthony, on the northern tip of Newfoundland. While St. Anthony is named for the patron saint of the lost, there was no reprieve for the Hillier family. Her body has never been found.

Dean Penney was led away in handcuffs, facing life in prison without parole eligibility for 25 years. (Ryan Cooke/CBC)

Police long suspected Dean Penney, her estranged husband, played a direct role in her disappearance. Unable to gather damning evidence through conventional means, the RCMP turned to a rare and controversial tactic.

Penney was ensnared in a Mr. Big sting for more than four years, believing he was part of a criminal organization that transported illegal items across the country. In reality, he was surrounded by undercover police officers, including one who became as close as family.

The mission reached its main event in 2023, when Penney confessed to an undercover officer posing as a crime boss during a job interview on a yacht in Vancouver. He would add further details in a second interview weeks later. Both conversations were captured on camera and played for the jury at trial.

Penney told the officer he pushed his wife over the stairs in their garage. He said she hit her head off the corner of his gun safe. In the second interview, he said he repeatedly struck her head with a mallet while she lay unconscious on the floor.

'I maintain my innocence'

The court heard victim impact statements from Hillier-Penney's siblings, Gary Hillier and Yvonne Decker.

Decker spoke of the time she spent with her sister, and how she longed for those days again.

"That part of my life is gone. It will never be the same. I miss our phone calls so much. My life will never be the same again with her gone," she wrote. "I am lost without my beautiful sister, Jennifer. I am scarred for the rest of my life."

Jennifer Hillier-Penney went missing in November 2016. (CBC)

Justice Vikas Khaladkar then heard brief statements from the Crown and defence, before turning to Penney in the prisoner's box. He asked Penney if he had anything he wanted to say.

"No, not really, your honour," Penney replied. "Just that I maintain my innocence and I hope to be vindicated soon."

In a pre-sentence report (PSR) prepared by a probation officer, Penney also denied killing Hillier-Penney.

"Mr. Penney did not take responsibility, denying the incident took place and he maintained his innocence throughout the PSR interview process. He noted that he believed the situation was a 'farce' and that there was 'no evidence' and he reported losing faith and being frustrated with the whole situation and having no hope."

Brother says Penney told him 'good job'

Gary Hillier spoke to CBC News following the sentencing, and said Penney made a remark as he passed by him in the courtroom.

Hillier looked at Penney as he walked to the witness box to give his victim impact statement. Penney didn't look up. However, when Hillier walked past him again to return to his seat, he said Penney looked at him and said "good job."

“For a second I [thought] there might be some change in his mentality," Hillier told CBC News. "He might be taking some accountability for what he done. But then after he gets up and [says] he wants to fight for his innocence. So it was all bullshit.”

Gary Hillier is the brother of Jennifer Hillier-Penney. He attended every day of proceedings in the two-month-long trial in Corner Brook. (Ryan Cooke/CBC)

Penney has 30 days from the date of his sentencing to file an appeal. He's been represented by Jeff Brace and Mark Gruchy of Legal Aid's special defence unit in St. John's.

Hillier said he's not worried about Penney seeking vindication.

“The man is delusional. He don’t want to take no accountability. He was a spoiled brat from Day 1. He thinks he can fool everybody. He thinks he’s smarter than everybody … but he showed his true colours.”

Members of Hillier-Penney's family, including Gary Hillier, have been added to a no-contact order — meaning Penney cannot speak to them throughout the duration of his sentence.

Hillier said that was important to him, since he wants to move on from the pain and anger he's felt since his sister was murdered.

“Throughout these last 10 years, I’ve had a lot of contact with Dean Penney," Hillier said. "We had a lot of exchanges. Not always legal. I’ve done a lot of things that I wouldn’t change. I fought hard, broke a lot of rules, but I’m done with it. I’m at peace with what happened and the judgment.”

Penney's parole eligibility will take into consideration the date he was arrested in December of 2023, putting him in his late 70s before he's up for release.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with ombudsman over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.

World.title: Far-right political marketing in Colombia
World.content:
A deep dive into the murky world of far-right propaganda and political marketing in Colombia and Latin America.

The surge of the peso, which went up roughly 25% over the past year, put Colombia Reports in acute financial trouble. If you can, please donate or become a patron.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.

If there was a method to Steve’s madcap approach, it was that with each new idea he had for the Santiago Times, with each new push to improve or revive it, he bought the business a little more time. Months turned into years and then decades. And all the while, people like myself were given an opportunity to work and learn—in large part through trial and error, because although Steve had things to teach, he also gave us space to teach ourselves.

It was his special tenacity, though, that kept the whole thing going, that gave so many people the chance, year after year, to develop their skills. We had fun too. So much fun. The office on Av. Santa María produced lasting, globe-spanning friendships, even love stories. And that was also part of Steve’s gift to us all.

He was an unabashed eccentric. Smart. Complicated. He had an entrepreneurial spirit but no real nose for business. Steve was a lawyer who wrote about politics and fruit exports. An editor with a penchant for typos. Part idealist, part cynic. A campaigner with no patience for diplomacy. He was perpetually cash-strapped, but generous. He was impulsive and impatient at times, but also deeply committed—to his various projects and causes, and to his family and colleagues. He was a teacher and a mentor. A doting father. A friend.

Goodbye Steve. Paz. And thank you.

World.title: Anti-vaccine mandate protests spread across the country, crippling Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in Ottawa, Emergency Preparedness Minister Bill Blair said the blockade at Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge is particularly alarming because a quarter of all Canada-U.S. trade moves through that one crossing, which connects Canada with Detroit and points beyond.

Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of products have been held back for three days as 50 to 75 vehicles and about 100 anti-mandate protesters camp out on the main road that leads on and off the bridge.

The Canada Border Service Agency (CBSA) has closed the bridge to commercial traffic temporarily, diverting trucks to the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia, Ont. instead. CBSA is reporting wait times in excess of four hours to make the short trip across to Port Huron, Mich.

We’ve seen the criminal acts, acts of thuggery and the obnoxiousness that they’ve inflicted on the people of Ottawa. Now they’re blocking the highways leading into our ports of entry. They’re putting their foot on the throats of all Canadians.

Labour unions representing auto workers have reported some idled Windsor plants have sent workers home while the trucker convoy holds up much-needed parts coming from the U.S.

Transport Minister Omar Alghabra said central Canada could soon see empty store shelves because so much of the region’s fresh food and produce comes into the country across that bridge.

To be honest, I find it ironic that the same people who were trying to sell Canadians fake stories about empty shelves are now causing those shelves to go empty, Alghabra said.

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens said the protesters appear to be determined to stay. They feel such a passion for this particular cause that they’re willing to die for it, he said.

Speaking briefly to reporters before question period, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said his government is working with Ontario and the City of Windsor to put an end to the blockade.

World.title: Excellent prospects for Mercosur beef exports, except Argentina
World.content:
The Argentine beef industry is optimistic about world meat production and global demand this year, with China again playing a leading market role. A report issued by Argentina’s Rosario Stock Exchange (BCR) and the Mercado Ganadero Department (Rosgan), world beef production will reach 58 million tons, representing a 1% increase over 2021.

This prospect would reverse the downward trend seen in 2021, mainly because of the recovery of the meat-packing industries in Brazil and Australia, the world’s first and third-largest meat exporters, respectively.

As for the global flow of imports, the expected average, according to analysts at BCR/Rosgan, is 10 million tons, which would imply an increase of 2.7% compared to last year.

China, which reduced the pace of international beef purchases in 2021 to 950,000 tons compared to more than 1.1 million tons in 2020 will once again represent 32% of global consumption. According to BCR/Rosgan, China accounted for 13% of global meat demand in 2017.

At that time, Argentina was in the top five beef exporters, having previously been in the top three. But Argentina has dropped out of the top ten beef exporters in recent years, owing to government restrictions on beef exports with the purpose of supporting the domestic market and helping with lower prices.

Nevertheless the Brazilian and Argentine beef markets had an unusual year in 2021. Traditional animal protein producers, the two countries witnessed declines in their exports, particularly in the last months of the year. Overall compared to 2020, Brazil beef sales dropped 9,92% while Argentine exports decreased 13,84%.

The reduction experienced by Brazil can be explained by the beef embargo imposed by China. In effect on September 2021, Brazil voluntarily suspended exports to China after the identification of two cases of mad cow disease in the country.

The World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) recognized that these were atypical episodes and that the risk to the national herd was negligible. Despite this, China insisted in freezing Brazilian beef exports for over three months until December 15.

The drop in Argentine beef shipments were motivated by the high price of the product in the domestic market, and thus the government suspended all exports in May 2021. ” As a consequence of sustained increases in the price of beef cuts in the domestic market, the national government decided to implement a set of emergency measures to better organize the sector, restricting speculative practices, improving the traceability of exports and avoiding tax evasion,” said the decree issued at the time.

Further measures were implemented, and given the deteriorating economic situation of Argentina and its impact on inflation, the country’s export ban on certain beef cuts was extended until the end of 2023.

As a result of this situation, Mercosur junior member Uruguay strongly benefitted and saw beef shipments increase 35%. The same can be said of the other Mercosur member, Paraguay, that also experienced a record year of beef exports in 2021.

World.title: Unemployment in Chile almost back at 2019 levels
World.content:
Chilean authorities have reported Monday that unemployment nationwide had fallen in 2021 to 7.2% while in the same period of 2020 it had hit 10.3%. In the middle of the social uprisings of 2019 it had been recorded at 7.1%.

“It is the eighth consecutive annual decrease in the unemployment rate,” said Leonardo González of the National Institute of Statistics (INE), which also reported the unemployment rate for women stood at 7.4%, and for men at 7.1%.

In the quarter of the year, 119,930 jobs were created compared to the previous quarter. With seasonal adjustment, González specified, the number of jobs recovered quarterly reached 49,625.

Around 1,436,000 jobs have been recovered, which represented 77.5% of all jobs lost during the worst part of the COVID-19 pandemic, with 81.8% accounting for jobs held by men and 73.1% for those carried out by women.

The INE also said 80.1% of formal jobs and 94.5% of informal jobs had been recovered.

“If we continue at this rate, we estimate that we will soon be able to recover all the jobs that were lost in the worst moment of the pandemic,” González stressed. He warned, however, that “we have been consistently seeing these rates rise, but we are not yet seeing pre-pandemic levels.”

Employment ended 2021 at 54.3%, while the labor force participation rate ended at 58.5%, an 8.1% yoy increase, driven by women (11.7%) and men (5.7%).

Jobs were boosted by construction (22.2%), commerce (8.5%) and the hotels and restaurants (30.9%).

Economy Minister Lucas Palacios said that during “2021 we met the goal of strongly recovering economic activity and also employment.”

“We have recovered 80% of the jobs that the pandemic and recession destroyed. It was necessary to create health, operational security and certainty conditions to reactivate the economy and especially investment, which is the main source of opportunities,” Palacios said.

Palacios also highlighted joint efforts by the public and private sectors. “Incentives from the State can be very relevant to promote investment and employment,” the minister explained.

Labor Minister Patricio Melero agreed the unemployment figures meant “great news” and praised “the measures adopted by the government, both in economic and health matters,” which were yielding “results which are very positive for the country.”

(Source: ANSA)

World.title: Chilean deputy likens British sovereignty in the Falklands to Chile's in Magellan
World.content:
Chilean deputy likens British sovereignty in the Falklands to Chile's in Magellan

11th Friday, September 2026 - 09:06 UTC Full article

“That is, just as the Falklands are English, the Strait of Magellan is Chilean,” Avendaño said

A Chilean lawmaker compared British sovereignty over the Falklands with Chile's over the Strait of Magellan during a parliamentary session, a position that runs counter to the official line of Santiago's government, which backs Argentina's claim to the archipelago.

Javier Olivares Avendaño, a member of the People's Party and chairman of the committee overseeing the state intelligence system, made the comparison on Tuesday in the National Defense Committee of the Chamber of Deputies: “That is, just as the Falklands are English, the Strait of Magellan is Chilean.” The People's Party is a center-right group founded in 2019 and is not part of the government.

His remarks came amid a bilateral controversy opened on August 23, when the chief of the general staff of Argentina's air force, Brigadier General Gustavo Javier Valverde, referred on a streaming program to Magellan, the south and the Drake Passage as areas of sovereignty, describing the zone as a bi-oceanic key. Chile sent a protest note and its foreign minister, Francisco Pérez Mackenna, called Chilean sovereignty over the strait indisputable, grounded in the treaties of 1881 and 1984.

Tensions eased after a call from Argentine Defense Minister Carlos Presti to his Chilean counterpart, Fernando Barros Tocornal. According to Chile's defense ministry, Presti attributed Valverde's comments to confusion and said the officer is familiar with the legislation and treaties in force.

On September 3, Presidents José Antonio Kast and Javier Milei signed a joint declaration in Santiago stating that the legal regime of the strait is the one established by those two treaties, fully in force and definitive in character. Chilean media noted it was the first time Argentina had set out in an official document Chilean sovereignty over the entire strait. At the same meeting, Kast reiterated Chile's support for Argentina's sovereign rights over the South Atlantic islands and called for negotiations with the United Kingdom to resume.

The controversy reopened hours later, when Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno described his country as bi-oceanic while discussing the naval base planned in Tierra del Fuego, and Senator Patricia Bullrich listed control of the strait among Argentina's strategic objectives. Bullrich later sent a letter attributing her comments to confusion with the Beagle Channel, acknowledging that the strait belongs entirely to Chile and asking that her apologies be conveyed to Kast.

That second round mobilized the Chilean opposition. On the same Tuesday, the chamber voted 57 to 49 with one abstention to summon Pérez Mackenna, who will become the first minister in Kast's cabinet to appear before Congress. The session is set for September 28, with a questionnaire covering thirteen subjects, including the continued force of Argentine decree 457/2021, whose text refers to joint control of the strait and which Buenos Aires has acknowledged as an erroneous formulation without repealing it.

Sovereignty over the Falklands remains disputed between the United Kingdom and Argentina, which claims the islands. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters in the archipelago chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Vance positions himself for 2028 as the Republican convention closes in Dallas
World.content:
Vance positions himself for 2028 as the Republican convention closes in Dallas

11th Friday, September 2026 - 08:41 UTC Full article

Vance focused his remarks on the Democratic Party, which he described as “the party of hate” and accused of holding the country in contempt

US Vice President J. D. Vance closed the Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday with a forty-minute speech that strengthened his standing as a contender for the 2028 presidential nomination, before an audience that chanted his name.

Vance focused his remarks on the Democratic Party, which he described as “the party of hate” and accused of holding the country in contempt. He said it is no longer the party of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, John F. Kennedy or Bill Clinton, and framed a Democratic vote in November as a threat to American prosperity. He defended birthright citizenship, the traditional family, a tough line on crime and changes to school curricula.

When an attendee interrupted to urge him to run as Donald Trump's successor, the vice president replied that they would worry about that later and that first they had to win in November. His main rival in internal polling, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, was absent: he was wrapping up a tour of Colombia, Ecuador and Peru.

Minutes earlier, security had removed a protester who tried to enter carrying Mexican and Palestinian flags. Vance addressed him from the stage: “Buddy, if you love Mexico so much, go to that country,” adding that the left had a new symbol.

The event was shaped by the pledge Trump made on the opening night on Wednesday: a payment of US$5,000 to every adult citizen, conditional on Republicans retaining control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in November's elections. “If the Republicans win, you win with us,” he said, calling it the “Trump dividend.”

The president did not specify how it would be funded. Vance later suggested it could be covered by tariff revenue, a mechanism Trump had already invoked when proposing US$2,000 checks. Estimates published by US media put the cost at around US$1.3 trillion for close to 270 million adults. Analysts and Democratic lawmakers have questioned its feasibility and legality, given that US law prohibits paying or being paid to influence voting.

Trump spoke again on Thursday, after Vance, in another forty-minute address in which he repeated arguments and promises from the previous day.

Over the two days, nineteen Republican candidates in competitive districts and states took the stage, along with former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, Donald Trump Jr., Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Texas Attorney General and Senate candidate Ken Paxton. Senator Ted Cruz attacked New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other Democratic figures, and said Islamic law has no place in the United States.

The program included a tribute to activist Charlie Kirk, assassinated a year ago, and a commemoration of the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks.

World.title: 68% of Chileans consider the Falklands British and 60% see Argentina as unreliable, poll shows
World.content:
68% of Chileans consider the Falklands British and 60% see Argentina as unreliable, poll shows

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 23:28 UTC Full article

62% of those polled disagreed with President Kast and the joint statement with Milei that, reiterates, “Chile’s support of Argentine legitimate sovereignty rights over the Malvinas Islands”.
