A majority of Chileans consider the Falklands British and regard Argentina as an unreliable partner, according to the latest Plaza Pública survey by pollster Cadem, released days after Argentine President Javier Milei visited Santiago and met his Chilean counterpart, José Antonio Kast.

The poll comes amid bilateral tension over remarks by Argentine political and military officials on the Strait of Magellan, and over Milei's speech at the Madrid Forum, a gathering of right-wing leaders held in Santiago on September 3.

Asked about the Falklands, 68% of respondents said the islands are British, 17% said they are Argentine and 15% did not answer. The result runs contrary to Chile's official position: in the joint declaration signed by both presidents at La Moneda, Chile reiterated its long-standing backing for Argentina's sovereignty claim. Sixty-two percent disagreed with Kast reaffirming “Chile's support for Argentina's legitimate sovereignty rights over the Malvinas Islands,” while 22% agreed and 16% did not answer.

Argentina maintains its claim to the islands, whose residents voted by 99.8% to remain a British Overseas Territory in a 2013 referendum.

In his speech opening the forum, Milei used a derogatory term to describe leftists and praised what he called four decades of stability and growth following the 1973 overthrow of Salvador Allende. Chilean opposition parties condemned the remarks as a vindication of the coup. According to the poll, 57% considered Milei's words a serious lack of respect toward Chilean political actors, 21% a lack of respect but not a serious one, and 18% said they were not disrespectful.

The dispute over the Strait of Magellan was triggered by comments from the Chief of the General Staff of the Argentine Air Force, Gustavo Valverde, who included the strait among areas of Argentine sovereignty, and by Argentine Decree 457/2021, which describes it as a space shared by both countries. In light of these statements, 69% of respondents believe Argentina has territorial ambitions over Chile, while 24% think it respects Chilean sovereignty in line with existing treaties. In the previous edition of the survey, in the first week of September, the figure stood at 71%.

On the 2021 decree, 54% said Kast should demand that Milei repeal it, while 37% considered the joint declaration sufficient. In it, both presidents reaffirmed the 1881 Boundary Treaty and the 1984 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, which establish Chilean sovereignty over the strait.

Sixty percent of Chileans consider Argentina an unreliable partner. By contrast, Japan (83%), Canada (80%) and England (78%) topped the list of the most trusted partners.

Respondents said Chile should prioritize trade relations with China (60%), the European Union (49%), Canada, Australia and New Zealand (46%), India and Southeast Asia (37%), Latin America (37%) and the United States (32%).

The survey also put Kast's approval rating at 35%, with 61% disapproving of his government.

World.title: Peru joins the Americas Shield during Rubio's visit to Lima
World.content:
Peru joins the Americas Shield during Rubio's visit to Lima

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 21:45 UTC Full article

Fujimori said the move relaunches joint work between the two countries and rejected the idea that it compromises Peruvian sovereignty

Peru will join the Americas Shield, the US-backed security coalition against transnational organized crime, President Keiko Fujimori announced on Thursday after meeting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Government Palace.

The announcement closed a Rubio tour of Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, Washington's largest diplomatic push in South America since Donald Trump's return to the White House. In Bogotá he had raised with President Abelardo de la Espriella the prospect of a “golden age” in bilateral relations, and in Quito he described Ecuador as the most determined partner in toughening the response to drug trafficking.

The coalition was set up on March 7, 2026, in Doral, Florida, with thirteen founding members: the United States, Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay and Trinidad and Tobago. Colombia joined during this tour and Peru does so now. In a column published this week in the Peruvian daily El Comercio, Rubio also noted that Peru becomes a major non-NATO ally, a bilateral US designation.

Fujimori said the move relaunches joint work between the two countries and rejected the idea that it compromises Peruvian sovereignty. “Peru's sovereignty is intact,” she said, recalling that the entry of foreign troops requires express authorization from Congress, a requirement she said would remain. Rubio also dismissed those objections, saying people were anticipating problems that do not exist. He added that the United States has the capacity to act unilaterally but prefers to work with partners, and that it cannot enter sovereign nations. Among the results of cooperation he cited the capture in Bolivia, with FBI support, of the leader of the Peruvian gang Los Pulpos.

Former Peruvian foreign minister Hugo de Zela has warned that the country does not benefit from being caught in the confrontation between the United States and China and should act according to its own interests.

The visit came amid friction with Beijing. China's embassy in Lima published messages saying it has never demanded that other countries take sides and that the Western Hemisphere is no one's “backyard,” and noted that Peru is the second largest destination for Chinese investment in Latin America, with a stock of US$30 billion. The messages responded to Rubio's column, in which he accused China of predatory practices, opaque contracts and unsustainable debt in the region.

The most visible point of that competition is the Chancay megaport, inaugurated in 2024 and 60% controlled by Chinese company COSCO Shipping Ports. Washington has questioned whether infrastructure on that scale could serve as logistical support for Chinese naval forces.

World.title: Gibraltar reaffirms British sovereignty on National Day, first since UK-EU treaty
World.content:
Gibraltar reaffirms British sovereignty on National Day, first since UK-EU treaty

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 21:19 UTC Full article

Crowds gather in Casemates Square for Gibraltar's National Day rally, marking 59 years since the 1967 sovereignty referendum. Photo: Jim Watt

Once again, it is the 10th of September, when Gibraltar celebrates its National Day on the anniversary of the 1967 referendum on whether to remain British or join Franco’s Spain. The result was decisive, and despite the demise of the fascist dictatorship, Gibraltar remains resolutely British.

A large crowd gathered in Casemates Square for the political rally, though it was not quite as packed as in previous years. Many people took advantage of the public holiday for a long weekend away, with some businesses closing on Friday to facilitate this.



As usual, a cross-party delegation attended from both Houses of the UK Parliament, including Amanda Martin (Labour), Martin Vickers (Conservative), Dr Al Pinkerton (Liberal Democrats), and long-time Gibraltar supporter Andrew Rosindell (Reform). Members of the House of Lords and a contingent of former MPs who hold the Freedom of the City were also present.

The UK Minister for Europe, Lord Stewart Wood, arrived late due to air traffic delays, making his first visit to the Rock for National Day.

Fabian Picardo, the Chief Minister, gave a lively speech reminding the crowd that—whatever others may think—the territory belongs to the people of Gibraltar, and nothing can change that. He indicated that this would be his final time taking to the platform as Chief Minister.

He read aloud a letter from King Charles and another from the UK Prime Minister, who reaffirmed that the UK Government remains “unwavering in its commitment to Gibraltar, to British sovereignty, and to the principle of self-determination”.

In a statement, Deputy Chief Minister Dr Joseph Garcia noted that this National Day marks the first since the UK-EU treaty was signed. He added that the agreement proves preserving British sovereignty and maintaining close ties with Europe are not mutually exclusive.

He went on to say that self-determination means Gibraltar's future can only be freely and democratically decided by its people. That principle, he stressed, is neither weakened by the treaty, diluted by closer cooperation with European neighbours, nor diminished by ongoing work with the European Union to improve citizens' lives.

Organisers announced that the evening would conclude with a fireworks and drone formation display.

By Jim Watt - Gibraltar

World.title: Falklands Legislative Assembly sends greetings to Gibraltar on its National Day
World.content:
Falklands Legislative Assembly sends greetings to Gibraltar on its National Day

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 12:23 UTC Full article

The text says the future of a people belongs to that people alone

The Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly, the archipelago's elected body, sent a message of greeting on Thursday to the government and people of Gibraltar to mark their National Day, and arranged for the flags of both territories to fly alongside one another throughout the day at Victory Green in Stanley.

In its public statement, the assembly described the two territories as kindred communities, separated by an ocean but bound by a British identity held by their own free choice and by a determination to decide their own future. The text says the future of a people belongs to that people alone.

Gibraltar's National Day commemorates the referendum of September 10, 1967, in which 12,138 voters chose to retain the link with the United Kingdom against 44 who preferred transfer to Spanish sovereignty. It is the 59th anniversary of that vote.

This year's celebration is the first since the entry into force of the treaty governing Gibraltar's relationship with the European Union, signed on July 14 in Brussels by British and EU representatives, with Gibraltar's Chief Minister Fabian Picardo and Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares present. The agreement, provisionally applied since July 15, removed routine checks at the land border with Spain, crossed daily by some 15,000 workers, and states expressly that it does not alter British sovereignty or the territory's constitutional status.

Both territories appear on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories and their sovereignty is subject to competing claims. Spain claims sovereignty over Gibraltar and Argentina claims the Falklands, and neither state recognizes the results of the votes held in those territories as settling the question. In the 2013 referendum in the South Atlantic islands, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

The message was issued during a week of rising tension over the South American archipelago, with criminal complaints and administrative proceedings opened by Argentina against oil companies and an intervention by the British prime minister in the House of Commons. The assembly did not link its statement to those events.

World.title: Iceland Foods to open first UK high street store in the Falklands in December
World.content:
Iceland Foods to open first UK high street store in the Falklands in December

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 12:00 UTC Full article

Iceland Foods operates more than 950 stores in the United Kingdom, including its The Food Warehouse format.

British frozen food chain Iceland Foods announced Thursday that it has completed a deal to open a store in Stanley, the capital of the Falklands, in what the company describes as the first UK high street retail brand to establish itself in the archipelago.

The outlet, at K4, Ross Road East, will open in early December in partnership with local retailer Kelper Stores Ltd, part of the Fortuna group, a family business with a long presence in the islands. According to the company, the store will carry its own-label frozen range alongside brands with which it holds exclusive agreements.

The announcement describes the arrangement in two different ways: the company refers to a standalone store, while the head of the local partner describes it as the first franchise store in Stanley.

Richard Walker, executive chairman of Iceland Foods, framed the opening in political terms, saying the company is “proud to be backing Britain” with the move, and said he would travel to the islands for the opening.

James Wallace, managing director of Fortuna, said the firm is “committed to investing in the community.”

Sarah Clarke, general manager of Kelper Stores, called it “a major milestone for the Falklands” and said it would broaden the range of products available to local shoppers.

Iceland Foods operates more than 950 stores in the United Kingdom, including its The Food Warehouse format.

Iceland Foods is recognised as the UK’s leader in frozen food and operates over 950 stores across the country, including The Food Warehouse locations, together with a multi-award-winning online shopping service.

It prides itself on being a convenient and friendly place to do the family’s weekly shop, as well as meet everyone’s daily top-up shopping needs for fresh, chilled, frozen food and groceries. For more than 20 years Iceland has also offered a unique, free home delivery service for in-store purchases.

Iceland was voted the UK’s favourite online grocery service at the Good Housekeeping Awards in 2021 and 2022. The retailer was also named the UK’s Best Online Supermarket in a survey by consumer champion Which? in 2022.

Iceland and The Food Warehouse enjoy exclusive partnerships with a range of leading brands including, Cathedral City, Harry Ramsden’s, Myprotein, Slimming World, Toby Carvery and TGI Fridays.

Iceland has always been a responsible retailer, operating under its ‘Doing it Right’ ethos. Recognised as the only UK supermarket to rank in The Sunday Times Best Place to Work for 2026, as well as 2025 and 2024,

Iceland is dedicated to doing the right thing in its supply chain and in the way it treats its people and customers. Iceland is also committed to minimising its impact on the environment and contributing to the communities where it operates by regenerating high streets, creating jobs, providing outstanding customer service and giving generous support to a range of good causes.

Founded in 2014, The Food Warehouse is part of Iceland Foods, which operates over 950 stores across Britain, including The Food Warehouse locations. All 200 Food Warehouse stores are large format stores with a car park, providing the value and convenience of a wholesale store without the hassle of membership.

The Food Warehouse is opening new stores up and down the country in retail parks and larger shopping districts. Each store is given a high-quality warehouse style fit out and covers between 10,000 and 25,000 sq. ft. of retail space.

The Food Warehouse offers great value, family-favourite products across frozen, chilled, fresh, branded grocery and homeware lines. With big deals, big choice and big packs across many big brands, customers can make great savings with bulk deals where savings are passed directly onto shoppers.

World.title: UK prime minister vows to be 'relentless' in defending the Falkland Islanders' choice
World.content:
UK prime minister vows to be 'relentless' in defending the Falkland Islanders' choice

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 09:26 UTC Full article

“We will always respect the rights of the Falkland Islanders to choose to be British,” Burnham said during the weekly Prime Minister's Questions

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the House of Commons on Wednesday that his government would be “relentless” in defending the right of Falkland Islanders to choose to be British, in a session dominated by defense spending and the sovereignty of overseas territories.

“We will always respect the rights of the Falkland Islanders to choose to be British,” Burnham said during the weekly Prime Minister's Questions, adding that the position “will never” change under his government. He did not mention Javier Milei or Argentina at any point in his remarks, and referred to the islands only once in a session lasting more than an hour.

“We will always respect the rights of the Falkland Islanders to choose to be British. That will never change under this Government and we will be relentless in defending that.”



Prime Minister @andyburnham restating the UK's strong support for the Falkland Islands today. pic.twitter.com/iH7qtdiH6U — FalklandsinUK (@FalklandsinUK) September 9, 2026

Burnham replied that the United Kingdom would not surrender its Diego Garcia base and that it is in discussions with the United States on the matter. On military spending, he said his government would meet the NATO commitment of 3.5% by 2035, with an interim 3% target, and that details would come in the spending review. Badenoch countered that a decade was too long to wait. Asked whether the current chancellor of the exchequer had been right to resign as defense secretary earlier this year over the government's failure to commit to that 3% target, Burnham did not answer directly.

A day earlier, International Development Minister Kirsty McNeill had sought to lower the tone in Parliament, saying the United Kingdom wants to maintain a modern and constructive relationship with Argentina across a range of shared interests.

The session came as Argentina's government steps up its campaign against companies operating hydrocarbons in waters near the archipelago. On Monday it filed a criminal complaint in federal court against five firms linked to the Sea Lion project, invoking Article 7 of Law 26,659, which carries prison terms of five to ten years, and on Tuesday it raised to 60 the number of administrative proceedings opened over alleged breaches of Article 2 of the same statute. None of the allegations has been proven.

The trigger was Milei's televised address last Thursday, in which he argued for the first time that the islands' inhabitants have no right to self-determination. The Argentine president had previously expressed a wish that the islanders would “choose to be Argentine” and said their opinion could not be disregarded.

In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the territory's status as a British overseas territory, a result successive British governments cite in response to the dispute. Sovereignty over the archipelago remains contested between London and Buenos Aires more than forty years after the 1982 war.

World.title: The ultimate guide to contemporary Mexican restaurants in Guadalajara
World.content:
Mexican Independence Day celebrations this month offer a great opportunity to celebrate and rediscover Mexican food, and what better way to do it than through five restaurants that are putting a contemporary spin on traditional Mexican cuisine?

From chilaquiles with poblano chile sauce to eggplant tamales and corn pancakes, here are some of the best contemporary Mexican restaurants in Guadalajara to try right now.

Ixtle

Located in Zapopan, Ixtle defines itself as a kitchen true to its roots: A relaxed concept that takes corn and Mexican ingredients as its starting point, reinterpreting them through international techniques and references.

In the mornings, guests can enjoy innovative dishes such as the Jarocho Breakfast, featuring eggs in hoja santa with longaniza, banana and confit mushrooms, or waffles made from maize accompanied by a blend of caramelized miso, maple syrup, honey, mascarpone and macadamia butter.

Lovers of traditional hot café de olla will appreciate Ixtle’s reinterpretation of a staple of Mexican cuisine — the café de olla latte, served cold with orange peel and a touch of foamy milk.

At night, the menu becomes more elaborate, drawing on a wider range of international influences and featuring dishes that are designed to be shared. The Mediterranean tuna tiradito, served with red peppers in pil-pil sauce and nixtamalized tomato paste, is a must-try.

Best for: Breakfasts with friends or a date night

Breakfasts with friends or a date night Location: C. Miguel León Portilla 478, Santa Fe, 45168 Zapopan, Jalisco

C. Miguel León Portilla 478, Santa Fe, 45168 Zapopan, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/ixtle_rest

Teté Cocina de Barrio

Spearheaded by siblings Mario and Karla Papa, Teté has been delighting tapatíos for over a decade through a cuisine that blends Mexico’s culinary heritage with flavors introduced by the different cultures that have settled in the country.

With an approach that prioritizes seasonal ingredients, the menu at Teté not only changes every month, but it is a complete surprise for diners, who do not know what they will have for dinner until dishes start arriving.

Guests are also in for another surprise: Teté does not have waiters. Instead, everyone does a bit of everything, with the chefs themselves guiding diners throughout the meal.

With no waiters and no menu, Teté defines itself as a restaurant that “doesn’t repeat menus, but experiences.” It’s no wonder this unpretentious restaurant in the Moderna neighborhood has made it to coveted culinary rankings around the world.

Best for: Date night

Date night Location: C. Rayón 830, Moderna, 44170 Guadalajara, Jalisco

C. Rayón 830, Moderna, 44170 Guadalajara, Jalisco Website: tete-cocina-de-barrio.mailchimpsites.com

Amorcito Mío

Located in the heart of Zapopan Centro and just steps away from the Zapopan Basílica, Amorcito Mío offers a warm atmosphere and home-cooked-style recipes.

Although the breakfast menu offers international dishes such as sandwiches and paninis, it is simultaneously a celebration of Mexican food, albeit with a twist.

Guests will be surprised by the variety of sauces featured on the chilaquiles menu beyond the traditional red and green. Expect chilaquiles with poblano chile sauce, spicy peanut sauce and a super spicy sauce made from güero chiles and habanero.

To balance the heat, Amorcito Mío offers a varied selection of Mexican breads, including pan dulce staples like conchas, as well as traditional bolillo and birote.

While breakfasts highlight authentic Mexican flavors, the menu shifts in the afternoon and evening to feature wood-fired pizzas and a blend of Italian and Mediterranean dishes.

Best for: Casual gatherings with friends

Casual gatherings with friends Location: Calle 5 de Mayo 275, Zapopan, 45100 Zapopan, Jalisco

Calle 5 de Mayo 275, Zapopan, 45100 Zapopan, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/amorcito_mi

Bruna

View this post on Instagram A post shared by BRUNA (@bruna_mx)

With a terrace surrounded by lush gardens and sculptures, Bruna generates excitement from the very first moment, offering diners an almost theatrical experience.

Since opening in 2015, chef Óscar Garza has drawn inspiration from Mexican abuelitas’ recipes and street-food flavors, reinterpreting them with contemporary techniques and an artistic presentation.

Among the dishes that stand out for their meticulous presentation is the chile en nogada, which returns to the menu each year during the patriotic month. Las probaditas de mole, literally meaning “little tastes of mole,” features a rainbow of colors and flavors that pushes the boundaries of classic mole poblano.

If you are looking for something sweet and original, be sure to try the bruleated corn cream, a dessert that blends the traditional flavor of corn with the classic French twist of crème brûlée.

Best for: Special occasions

Special occasions Location: Lerdo de Tejada No. 2418, Col. Lafayette, Guadalajara, Jalisco

Lerdo de Tejada No. 2418, Col. Lafayette, Guadalajara, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/bruna_mx

Tikuun Comedor Local

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tikuun comedor (@tikuun.comedor)

Spearheaded by chef Carlos Espinosa, Tikuun has been open for over a decade, but only recently began receiving the recognition it deserves.

Situated in the trendy Colonia Americana, it features a constantly rotating menu that showcases new preparations and seasonal variations throughout the year. Although the menu draws inspiration from different cultures and cuisines, the restaurant’s manifesto promises a distinctly Mexican essence in each dish.

Standout recent offerings include roasted eggplant with cured nopal, aged cotija, salsa macha made with chia and Kalamata olives, requesón cheese and garlic confit, as well as octopus with recado negro, chinchayote, sweet potato and beet.

The intimate, almost home-like atmosphere allows guests to savor the experience at a leisurely pace, whether ordering a la carte or opting for the tasting menu.

Best for: An intimate dinner with friends

An intimate dinner with friends Location: Emeterio Robles Gil 50, Col. Americana, 44600 Guadalajara, Jalisco

Emeterio Robles Gil 50, Col. Americana, 44600 Guadalajara, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/tikuun.comedor

Gabriela Solís is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: Is Mexico as patriotic as the US? Just look around!
World.content:
I plead guilty. Whenever the Mexican national anthem was played at this year’s World Cup, tears welled up in my eyes. It was pride. Pride that my team was participating in a flagship event of contemporary football — and that, moreover, they were performing so well, for once!

And yes, I was that ridiculous woman. And so was my mother, my sister, and even my mother-in-law, who, although born in the Soviet Union, has been Mexican longer than I have been alive. We all cried in pride. Tears flowed from our eyes in unison: “al sonoro rugir del cañón” — and that was just for the World Cup!

And I know I’m not the only one. The overwhelming response of people celebrating our victories at the Angel of Independence on Paseo de la Reforma confirms it. Thinking about that, I sincerely wonder: Are Mexicans as patriotic as people from the U.S.? This is harder to answer than I initially thought.

Proud of our roots?

Mexico is a megadiverse country. Biologically, of course, but also in terms of ethnic groups. On numerous occasions, I have written for MND about Indigenous neighborhoods that are still alive even in Mexico City, and how we still have a syncretic understanding of our relationship with God and the church. People don’t find that in the U.S., because our colonial pasts were indeed very different.

And as such, our relationship with Indigenous peoples is very different. While in the United States less than 3% of the population identifies as Native American, according to the most recent census, 19% of Mexicans identify with an Indigenous group.

Therefore, Mexico’s relationship with its Indigenous peoples is also different and very complex. Besides being inevitably tainted by racism and pigmentocratic segregation, it is ironically painful to think that we take pride in the 68 Indigenous languages ​​still spoken throughout the country.

This diversity, at first glance, gives us a very strong sense of history and identity that hardly any other country in the Americas shares. However, at the same time, “60.8% of Indigenous people live in some level of poverty,” according to the most recent INEGI survey. This equates to almost 8 million people who, due to a fundamentally racial issue inherited from the colonial period, live in some state of poverty. Painful? Yes. And deeply shameful, too.

Although there are distinctly Indigenous towns — and possibly entire states — throughout Mexico, like Oaxaca, we don’t have anything like a reserve for Native nations, as happens in the U.S. This topic alone could be a doctoral thesis, but it undeniably deserves a mention in an article about national pride. All of which brings me to the next uncomfortable issue.

The issue of malinchismo

Octavio Paz wrote a lengthy essay on this issue in 1950. In “The Labyrinth of Solitude,” the author explores our relationship with “la chingada,” that is, La Malinche: the historical figure who, despite being Indigenous, married a high-ranking officer among the Spanish invaders.

In a word, Paz thinks that our relationship with that first mother, Malintzin, shaped by the European invasion, still weighs heavily on us. Our colonial past not only shames us, but it severely affects our Mexican identity. Ouch. This leads us to what’s called malinchismo: the notion that something is better simply because it’s not Mexican. This extends to nationality, language, everyday products and even systems of thought.

How does malinchismo interact with our sense of national pride? It’s hard to say. It’s a difficult relationship that reminds us of the shame of having been dominated by European invasion, but it coexists in our national history as part of our very identity. I think it all boils down to the fact that it’s a common saying among Mexicans that, nowadays, only people from Puebla want to be Spanish.

That simply does not exist in the United States. On the contrary, it’s a grave insult to be “un-American,” right?

God bless … Mexico?

My partner lived at Penn State for a year because of his dad’s job, and he remembers with a strange feeling that the “Pledge of Allegiance” to the flag was recited every morning. In Mexico, the closest thing we have to that is what Sarah DeVries described as “Honores a la Bandera.”

Although there are points of convergence, our civic culture is more diluted: You don’t see Mexican flags in the homes of ordinary Mexicans. It’s more common to see virgins, saints or crucifixes. On the contrary, it seems, at times, that we forget our national symbols until September, or perhaps when there’s a major global sporting event, like the World Cup.

You’ll hardly find anyone in Mexico saying they’re a proud patriot, or that they’re proud of our troops. We usually never trust the police — let alone the army. Along the same lines, I’ve never heard anything like “God bless Mexico!” Perhaps because we don’t have the legacy of Manifest Destiny looming over our sense of nationalism.

You will find, though, a general feeling of pride in being a Mexican, although we have a very complicated relationship with our colonial past. Our sense of national pride, moreover, still has a very PRI-ist tinge to it — which again, might be material for an entire doctoral thesis on its own.

Proud to be a Mexican

A recent poll by YouGov shows that “70% of Americans say they are proud to be Americans; 16% say they are not.” In contrast, 89% of Mexicans expressed being proud to be Mexicans in the 2020 National Survey of Civic Culture (ENCUCI).

However much national pride those figures might inspire, we feminists do not hesitate to denounce the Mexican state as a rapist macho man, using it as a rallying cry in our gender struggles. That is perhaps one of the most frequently used slogans in the March 8 marches. And at the same time, at an official event, I wouldn’t hesitate for a second to salute my flag with pride.

Perhaps, more than certainties, this article raised more questions for our readership. It was probably meant to be that way. And that’s the wonder of the social sciences: They don’t aim to provide straight answers, but rather to expand the conversation to raise more interesting questions — no matter how uncomfortable or painful they may be.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: Corruption, bribes and who Mexicans trust the least
World.content:
In 2025, 15.6% of people who carried out a bureaucratic procedure (trámite), made a payment to a government office, requested a public service or had any other kind of contact with authorities experienced an “act of corruption,” according to the results of the latest National Survey of Governmental Quality and Impact (ENCIG).

The national statistics agency INEGI conducted the survey at 46,000 homes in late 2025 and the results were published in May.

In this “Mexico in Numbers” article, we look at where in Mexico people are most and least likely to encounter corruption when interacting with municipal, state and federal authorities. One of the main ways people experience corruption in Mexico is by being asked to pay a bribe.

We also present survey results on:

The situations in which corruption directly affecting citizens is most prevalent.

The institutions that are considered the most and least corrupt.

Where is corruption most and least prevalent?

The state where people most commonly experience corruption is Hidalgo. Around 21.5% of residents from that state who came into contact with authorities last year experienced an act of corruption, according to the ENCIG results.

The states with the next highest percentages of people who were victims of an act of corruption last year were:

Oaxaca: 20.3%

Sinaloa: 19.8%

Chihuahua: 18.4%

Sonora: 18.3%

The states with the lowest percentages of people who were victims of an act of corruption last year were:

Colima: 7%

Nayarit: 8.9%

Zacatecas: 9.4%

Querétaro: 9.5%

Tamaulipas: 10.8%

In what situations is corruption most prevalent?

According to the ENCIG results, the five most common situations in which acts of corruption occurred last year were:

When people came into contact with public security authorities, such as police: 63.5% of respondents who experienced corruption said it occurred in this context. When people were applying for property-related permits: 32% When people were making “other payments,” submitting bureaucratic paperwork (trámites) or submitting “requests”: 29.3% When people were submitting trámites to open a business: 23.5%. When people were submitting trámites to the Federal Attorney General’s Office or a State Attorney General’s Office: 22.3%

Of the five most common situations in which acts of corruption occurred last year, the only one whose incidence declined compared to 2023 was No. 4.

Which institutions are seen as most and least corrupt?

ENCIG respondents were also asked their opinions about the frequency with which various institutions engage in corruption.

Police forces are seen as the most corrupt institution. (Note: The survey didn’t differentiate between municipal police forces and state police forces.)

Almost nine in 10 respondents — 86.5% — believe that police engage in corruption “very frequently” or “frequently.”

According to survey respondents, the next most corrupt institutions are:

Political parties: 83.9% of respondents believe they engage in corruption “very frequently” or “frequently.”

Prosecutor’s Offices: 75.3%

State governments: 74.1%

Houses of Congress: 73%.

According to survey respondents, the least corrupt institutions in Mexico are:

Public schools: 31.8% of respondents believe they engage in corruption “very frequently” or “frequently.”

Public autonomous organizations: 36.9%

Civil society organizations: 41.2%

Religious institutions: 43%

The Army and Navy: 46.1%

INEGI also asked respondents their opinions about the frequency with which families, neighbors and work colleagues engage in corruption. The results were as follows:

Families: 18.7% of respondents believe they engage in corruption “very frequently” or “frequently.”

Neighbors: 19.1%

Work colleagues: 21.8%

World.title: Rubio doubles down on claims that cartels control large areas of Mexico, hinting at unilateral US action
World.content:
Listen to this article

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Mexico isn’t doing enough to combat drug cartels and suggested that the United States could act unilaterally against such criminal organizations in Mexican territory.

In remarks to reporters outside the U.S. Embassy in Quito, Ecuador, Rubio also asserted that narco-terrorist organizations — i.e. drug cartels that the U.S. government has designated as foreign terrorist organizations — control large parts of Mexico.

SECRETARY RUBIO: There are territories, vast territories in Mexico, that are not governed by the state. They are controlled by these narco-terrorist organizations. pic.twitter.com/udRGZXv0xU — Department of State (@StateDept) September 9, 2026

The secretary of state, who traveled to Quito to speak with President Daniel Noboa about security cooperation between the United States and Ecuador, had been speaking about criminal threats in the Western Hemisphere when a reporter put it to him that if he was “talking about groups that are stronger than the state and fracturing the states, it sounds like a pretty similar situation to Mexico.”

“Mexico’s bad. It’s a bad situation,” Rubio responded.

The reporter then asked the secretary of state what the U.S. government’s plan was for combating organized crime in Mexico “given the fact that the Mexican government isn’t welcoming, or draws a pretty bright line about what it will accept in terms of U.S. military involvement.”

“How can you overcome that and have this kind of more tough approach that you’re describing?” she asked Rubio.

“The case of Mexico … [is] an even graver challenge because of the size of the country, because of the power of the cartels that are there,” he said.

“I don’t think it’s any mystery to anybody that there are territories, vast territories in Mexico, that are not governed by the state; they are controlled by these narco-terrorist organizations,” Rubio said.

He added that, “in fairness, the Mexicans have done more than they’ve ever done before to go after these groups.”

Indeed, the current Mexican government has captured or killed significant numbers of alleged cartel members and leaders, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) kingpin Rubén “El Mencho” Oseguera, sent scores of prisoners to the United States to face justice and seized more than 500 tonnes of drugs and over 34,000 firearms.

However, in Rubio’s view, what the Mexican government has done is “still not nearly enough.”

“They know that, we’ve expressed that to them,” he said.

“And we hope to work cooperatively with them to do more because … the head of the snake are these cartels in Mexico,” Rubio said.

“And they are a threat to the Mexican state, and the people of Mexico will tell you that. The number one issue in Mexico, poll after poll shows, is security. Political candidates are routinely assassinated in Mexico; judges — routinely assassinated; journalists who report on the cartels — routinely assassinated by these groups. So these groups pose an enormous threat right on our border. They have drones now. They’re using drones to try to traffic drugs and people across the border,” he said.

“These groups are very dangerous, they’re very well financed, they need to be confronted,” Rubio said, referring to criminal organizations such as the CJNG and the Sinaloa Cartel.

“Our hope and our intent is to do it in partnership with Mexico. That’s the ideal. But eventually, that threat will have to be confronted, one way or the other. But our hope is to do it cooperatively with Mexican authorities,” he said.

Rubio’s “one way or the other” remark alluded to the possibility of the United States taking unilateral action against cartels in Mexico. Asked about his comments at her Thursday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum characterized them as electorally motivated given that the U.S. midterms are coming up in November.

The secretary of state is by no means the first Trump administration official to suggest that the United States could act on its own against cartels in Mexico. U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance said in June that the United States “would take military action” in Mexico “if we feel like we have to to protect our people.”

Like Rubio, Vance said that the United States wants “to work with the Mexican government,” but he asserted that the U.S. has to “reserve the right” to take unilateral action against cartel threats.

For his part, U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson told U.S. senators in March 2025, shortly before he took up his post, that on “any decision to take action against a cartel inside Mexico, our first desire would be that it be done in partnership with our Mexican partners.”

However, he added that, “should there be a case where the lives of U.S. citizens are at risk, I think all cards are on the table.”

In January, U.S. President Donald Trump said himself that the United States — whose military has targeted suspected drug boats at sea — was going to start “hitting” cartels on land. No confirmed U.S. attacks on Mexican criminal groups in Mexico have occurred since then, although CNN reported in May that the CIA facilitated a “targeted assassination” of an alleged Sinaloa Cartel member in México state in March.

Is Rubio’s cartel control claim true?

In asserting that cartels control “vast territories in Mexico,” Rubio echoed claims made by Trump and other current U.S. government officials, such as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. In 2021, General Glen D. VanHerck, commander of the United States Northern Command at the time, asserted that criminal organizations operate in “ungoverned areas” of Mexico that account for 30% to 35% of national territory. President Andrés Manuel López Obrador promptly rejected his claim.

Sheinbaum has also rejected claims about cartel control in Mexico. However, there is, according to Ioan Grillo, a Mexico-based British journalist who specializes in organized crime, a “duopoly of power” in parts of the country.

A 2024 article published on Grillo’s site CrashOut is headlined “How Much of Mexico is Governed by Cartels?”

The subheading reads, “A: None 100%. But there is a duopoly of power in chunks of the country.”

“Cartels certainly exert an amount of control in chunks of Mexico. This can be seen in squads of gunmen operating openly, running checkpoints, ordering curfews, dictating what journalists can report, charging quotas on sales of avocados, moving votes for candidates, and controlling (or assassinating) mayors,” Grillo wrote.

“Yet unlike with the Islamic State caliphate, the Mexican government still operates in those turfs. It provides electricity, sends teachers and collects garbage. And the army can still go in (while the cartel gunmen hide) and then leave (and they come out again),” he wrote.

Later in his article, Grillo wrote that in his “subjective judgement,” about “a third of Mexican states have a severe cartel presence and high levels of violence; another third have a medium (but still important) level of cartel problems and bloodshed; and a last third have levels of violence compared with regular U.S. cities, and less serious problems from gangsters.”

Since that article was published in late January 2024 — around nine months before Sheinbaum took office — homicides and other high-impact crimes have declined, according to official statistics, suggesting that Mexico’s overall security situation has improved. Nevertheless, cartels continue to operate, fight turf wars and pose major challenges to authorities in various parts of the country.

World.title: Mexico gears up for Independence Day with a military parade, concerts and of course the Grito — all set for Sept. 15-16
World.content:
More than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are preparing to march, fly and roll out new equipment in Mexico City next week as the country marks the 216th anniversary of its independence.

On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo reviewed the logistics for the capital’s Sept. 16 Independence Day parade.

In Mexico, Día de la Independencia commemorates the start of the rebellion against Spanish rule in 1810, although the nation’s War of Independence didn’t end until 1821.

The parade will include Army, Navy, Air Force and National Guard personnel, cadets, pilots, military engineers, medical workers, communications specialists, military police and special forces. It also will include horses, dogs and even eagles, according to El Heraldo de México.

Contingents will be designated “Justice and Peace,” “Sentinels of the Nation,” “Crucible of Patriots” and “Roots of Honor,” among other names, Trevilla Trejo said during his briefing on a military base in Naucalpan, México state.

The roughly 5-kilometer parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Sept. 16 with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central plaza — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes, continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

The capital’s celebrations begin the night before, when President Claudia Sheinbaum leads the traditional Grito de Independencia (“Shout” or “Cry” of Independence) from the National Palace balcony.

In conjunction, the Grammy-winning Texas-based band Intocable, whose Norteño-Tejano sound has landed them 21 No. 1 songs on Billboard’s Regional Mexican Airplay chart, will headline a free concert in the Zócalo.

Free concerts, food fairs and municipal Grito ceremonies are also planned across Mexico City’s 16 boroughs. The musical lineup includes norteño-banda group Calibre 50 (a record 27 No. 1 hits on Billboard’s regional Mexican chart) and Sinaloan balladeer Pancho Barraza (a headliner since the 1990s).

The observances will reach beyond the capital, as well, as the Grito tradition is replicated by governors and mayors nationwide.

In present-day Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato — then known simply as Dolores, where priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla called on residents to rise against Spanish rule in the early hours of Sept. 16, 1810 — Independence Day festivities are running nearly all month.

In nearby San Miguel de Allende, Sept. 16 observances include a reenactment of the start of the independence movement in 1810.

This year, the Sept. 16 national holiday falls on a Wednesday, meaning there will be no three-day weekend. Public schools and banks will close, as will many government offices and private workplaces, as it is a mandatory day of rest under federal labor law. Employees required to work are entitled to premium holiday pay. Sept. 15 remains a regular work and school day.

With reports from Milenio, Infobae, El Informador, El Heraldo de México, N+, El Sol de Bajío and ADN Noticias

World.title: Education Ministry blames screen use for Mexican students’ falling scores
World.content:
Education Minister Mario Delgado on Wednesday addressed the low scores earned by Mexican students in the latest international PISA evaluation test by blaming “the excessive use of cell phones and computer screens.”

Speaking in Mexico City during the opening of National Days of Traditional Games, Delgado expressed doubt that the results amount to a comprehensive evaluation of the Mexican educational system, though he did concede that the sample was “statistically representative.”

“The low reading comprehension scores can be explained by the fact that screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images, and teenagers find it difficult to read more complex and longer texts,” he said.

Mexico ranked 64th out of 91 countries evaluated, with a drop in math and reading scores to the lowest levels since 2009.

Before promoting team games as a partial remedy, Delgado defended the New Mexican School — the official public education model implemented under the previous presidential administration — though without providing specific pedagogical strategies.

Delgado said the Education Ministry (SEP) simultaneously implemented formative assessment programs under the New Mexican School scheme, including 7 million integrative learning exercises during the past year.

Still, officials sought to put Mexico’s poor scores in a global perspective, insisting that international reading and math scores declined by 27 points and 22 points, respectively. Such emphasis ignores the fact that the lower scores are equivalent to losing a year of learning.

Although President Claudia Sheinbaum has often criticized what she calls “the structural limitations of the PISA test (saying “it applies the same exam across countries with vastly different local characteristics”), she initiated a public debate about the excessive use of screens and the early access of children and adolescents to digital platforms. This led to new national guidelines restricting cell phone use in schools.

Delgado said that with cell phone regulation in place, new activities — such as team games — can be used to effectively get the attention of students and build cooperative learning skills.

Unlike mobile phones, which promote isolation and limit social skills, Delgado said games like yo-yo, marbles, spinning top, and cup-and-ball encourage teamwork, shared fun and the formation of new friendships.

The aim is to encourage students to spend more time playing and socializing, Delgado said, insisting that being in front of a phone limits opportunities to connect with other people.

With reports from Vanguardia, Animal Político and El Universal

World.title: Mexico’s inflation rate rises to 3.26% in August, ending 4-month decline
World.content:
Mexico’s annual inflation rate rose slightly in August compared to July, ending a four-month streak of declines.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported Wednesday that the annual headline inflation rate was 3.26% in August, up from 3.12% in July.

Month-over-month inflation was 0.20% in August, while the annual core rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was 3.88%, down from 3.95% in July.

Both the annual headline rate and the core rate came in just below the median estimates of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg.

The increase in Mexico’s annual headline rate came after inflation slowed on a month-over-month basis in each of April, May, June and July. The headline rate thus fell from 4.59% in March to 3.12% in July, a decline of 1.47 percentage points. During the same period, the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) cut its key interest rate by 25 basis points on two occasions, lowering it to 6.75% in March and 6.50% in May.

The central bank, which targets 3% inflation, appears unlikely to make any additional cuts to its key rate this year. Banxico is currently forecasting that inflation will be 3.5% at the end of 2026. It anticipates that the headline rate will gradually decline in 2027 to converge to its 3% target in the final quarter of next year.

Services inflation remains above 4%

Of the four broad categories monitored by INEGI, services recorded the largest year-over-year increase in prices in August. Annual services inflation was 4.33%, down slightly from a 4.36% reading in July. Education fees, one of the services sub-categories, rose 6.04% annually in August, the month in which students across Mexico returned to school.

Annual inflation for goods was 3.41% in August. Within that category, inflation was 4.68% for processed food, beverages and tobacco, and 2.32% for non-food goods.

Energy prices, including those for electricity and gasoline, rose 3.33% annually in August, while prices for agricultural products fell 1.53% year-over-year. The overall deflation for the agricultural products category was the product of a 5.22% decrease in meat prices and a 4.1% increase in fruit and vegetable prices.

Other need-to-know economic data

World.title: While Mexico’s northern border states deal with a heat alert, monsoon conditions drench the Pacific Coast
World.content:
Low-pressure troughs and Tropical Wave 37 were baking large swaths of Mexico on Thursday, even as the Mexican monsoon was dumping heavy amounts of rain over much of the rest of the country.

The Pacific Coast states received the brunt of the storm system, although the Gulf-side municipality of Coatzacoalcos suffered extensive flooding after being pounded by an intense storm on Wednesday.

Cooler temperatures are expected on Friday, but for Thursday the National Meteorological Service (SMN) issued a heat alert for residents in north and northwestern Mexico. Temperatures above 45 C (113 F) were forecast for parts of Baja California and Sonora, with temperatures between 40-45 C (104-113 F) in parts of Sinaloa, Coahuila, Tamaulipas and Nuevo León.

“Stay hydrated, avoid prolonged exposure to the sun and take precautions against the heat,” the SMN advised in a social media post.

The heat wave extended south to Guanajuato and Guerrero, while some regions along the Gulf Coast saw temperatures hitting 38 C (100 F) on Wednesday.

At the same time, the rainfall map showed persistent heavy rains across the length and breadth of the country, accompanied by lightning and hail in some instances.

While Sinaloa was projected to get the most rainfall through Friday, the SMN said Guanajuato could expect to see the most intense midweek rains.

The SMN said rainfall produced by the Mexican monsoon could reach 150 millimeters in Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco and Colima through Thursday. Very heavy and locally intense downpours were also forecast for Baja California Sur, Sonora and Sinaloa.

The Friday forecast also calls for continued heavy rain storms in central Sinaloa, with heavy to very heavy rainfall in Baja California Sur, Sonora, Durango and Nayarit.

The SMN said Tropical Wave 37 has been met by the arrival of Tropical Wave 38, which has crossed into the Yucatán Peninsula and southeastern Mexico from the east, increasing the likelihood of heavy rain in those regions through Sunday.

The SMN said the states of Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo will register heavy to very heavy rainfall with electrical activity during the initial approach of the new weather system.

Veracruz, Tabasco, Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero will also experience an increased probability of heavy rains with electrical discharges as the system moves west, while Michoacán, Jalisco, Colima and Nayarit will be affected by the passage of the phenomenon throughout the weekend.

With reports from El País, El Financiero, Milenio, Diario del Istmo and El Sol del Chilpancingo

World.title: Panama 2027 Budget Books US$103 Million for San Miguelito Cable Car
World.content:
PANAMA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The line item Panama’s 2027 budget assigns US$103.8 million to the San Miguelito cable car, the first of three annual tranches planned at US$133.8 million in 2028 and US$32.3 million in 2029.

— The contract On September 3, Metro de Panamá awarded the project to Doppelmayr Panamá Corp. for US$255.16 million — below the US$270 million reference price, after a single bid scored 962 of 1,000 points.

— The system About 6.6 kilometers, six stations from Balboa to Torrijos Carter, linked to Metro Line 2 at Cincuentenario, carrying 2,800 to 3,600 passengers per hour in each direction.

— The do-over A first tender, structured as a 23-year concession at US$278.7 million, collapsed on May 28, 2026, when neither prequalified consortium submitted a bid.

— The budget frame The total 2027 budget is US$35.11 billion, presented July 29 by Finance Minister Felipe Chapman with a projected deficit of 2.97% of GDP — just under the 3% legal ceiling.

— The target Contract execution runs 30 months plus trials; authorities project the cable car could start operating in 2029.

Panama’s 2027 budget books the first US$103.8 million for a cable car over San Miguelito — a project that failed to attract a single bid in May, was redesigned, and has now been awarded to the Alpine cable-car giant Doppelmayr at US$255 million.

San Miguelito is Panama’s second-most-populous district, a dense hillside sprawl north of the capital where hundreds of thousands of commuters lose hours every day on clogged avenues. The government’s answer is now written into the 2027 national budget: US$103.8 million for the Teleférico de San Miguelito, an urban cable car that will run six stations from Balboa to Torrijos Carter and plug the district directly into Metro Line 2.

The allocation sits in the Metro de Panamá investment lines of the US$35.11 billion budget that Finance Minister Felipe Chapman defended before the National Assembly on July 29 — a budget that projects a deficit of 2.97% of GDP, just beneath the 3% ceiling of Panama’s fiscal responsibility law. Panama uses the US dollar, so the figures carry no exchange-rate caveats.

From Failed Tender to Award in Ten Weeks

The budget line is only possible because the project was rescued this summer. The first tender, built as a 23-year administrative concession with a reference price of US$278.7 million, ended in failure on May 28, 2026: the opening act concluded without a single economic or technical proposal. Two consortia had passed prequalification — Consorcio Teleférico SPE, formed by Sofratesa de Panamá and Mexico’s Promotora y Desarrolladora Mexicana de Infraestructura, and Consorcio Teleférico San Miguelito-TSM, pairing Spain’s Cointer Concesiones with Doppelmayr Panamá — but neither could secure the bank backing the concession model demanded, despite ten addenda loosening bond, guarantee and financial-closure requirements.

The state changed the model instead of the project. On July 6 the Metro relaunched the contract as a turnkey, best-value tender with global adjudication at a reference cost of US$270 million — US$8.6 million lower — with the state, not a concessionaire, carrying the financing. Bidders walked the route on July 27 and held their homologation meeting on July 28.

On August 18, Doppelmayr Panamá Corp. — the local arm of the Swiss-Austrian group that built cable-car systems in Bolivia, Mexico and Colombia — submitted the process’s only economic offer: US$255,163,788.03, before the ITBMS transfer tax, which does not apply because of the Metro’s tax exemption. The evaluating commission scored the proposal 962 out of 1,000 points and recommended the award. On September 3, the Metro formally adjudicated the contract — officially Licitación por Mejor Valor No. 2026-2-80-01-08-LV-000002.

What the Money Buys

The specification describes a line of roughly 6.6 kilometers — 6,493.99 meters of referential length — with six stations: Balboa, Cincuentenario, Samaria, Mano de Piedra, Valle de Urracá and Torrijos Carter. Cabins will run at up to six meters per second and carry between 2,800 and 3,600 passengers per hour in each direction. At Cincuentenario, where the control center will monitor vibrations and weather in real time, the cable car interlocks with Metro Line 2, giving San Miguelito a one-transfer ride into the capital’s rail spine.

The rulebook is notably tougher than the one that failed. The operator must sustain 99.0% availability monthly and 99.5% annually; if the line stalls, cabins must be brought to stations within 60 minutes, a vertical evacuation must run within 30, and the emergency motor must restore service in 15 minutes or less. Industrial cybersecurity penetration tests are required before commissioning, followed by a three-month controlled trial period. The contract totals 38 months — 30 of execution, six for punch-list items, two for settlement — with an optional five-year full-service maintenance agreement; if the Metro declines it, Doppelmayr must still leave a spare-parts inventory covering the same period.

The Budget Fight Around It

The three-year payment plan — US$103.8 million in 2027, US$133.8 million in 2028, US$32.3 million in 2029 — lands in a contentious budget season. The Assembly itself is demanding US$796 million more from the finance ministry for 2027, and the Mulino administration is defending its lines against a fiscal backdrop that has already cost Panama dearly: Fitch rates the sovereign at BB, speculative grade, as The Rio Times reported when the deficit fight escalated. A US$255 million aerial line is small change against a US$35.11 billion budget — but visible, discretionary and exactly the kind of project fiscal critics circle while rating agencies watch.

What It Means for Foreigners in Panama

Urban cable cars are Latin America’s proven answer to hillside congestion. Medellín built the template, Cartagena secured US$84 million for its own line in July and Guatemala City broke ground on its AeroMetro in August — the latter also a Doppelmayr project. For expatriates, San Miguelito is not a typical residential choice; most foreigners cluster in Panama City proper, where rents now top the region. But the cable car matters anyway: it unclogs the northern corridor, extends the metro’s reach into the city’s most populous district, and signals that the Mulino government will keep spending on big-ticket mobility despite the fiscal squeeze.

The caveat is the calendar. The award still faces the contract signature and the resolution of rights-of-way along the route, on which the housing ministry Miviot and the Metro are already working. If the 30-month execution and three-month trial hold, authorities project operations could begin in 2029. Panama has heard cable-car dates before — but this time there is a signed-off award, a named builder, and a first US$103.8 million with a budget line number attached.

World.title: Delcy Rodríguez in Suriname: Oil, Agriculture and a PDVSA Seizure on the Table
World.content:
Suriname · Diplomacy

Key Facts —The visit. Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodríguez arrived in Paramaribo on Thursday night, September 10, for a state visit — her fifth official trip since taking office after the US capture of Nicolás Maduro in January. —The agenda. Talks with President Jennifer Geerlings-Simons on Friday covered oil and gas, agriculture, fisheries, tourism, education and transport, plus cooperation inside regional and international organizations. —The friction. Simons put a court-ordered attachment on PDVSA assets in Suriname — tied to the old PetroCaribe compensation mechanism — directly on the table, asking Rodríguez about recent developments. —The next step. Simons proposed convening the countries’ Political Consultation Mechanism and Mixed Commission in the first half of 2027. —The city. Central Paramaribo was kept car-free at several points on Friday for the state visit, with police traffic measures around the Presidential Palace. —The backdrop. A Starnieuws column, “Delcy, Trump and our oil,” frames the visit through Washington’s giant oil agreement with Caracas — and what it means for Suriname’s own petroleum future.

Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s acting president, made a state visit to Suriname on September 10–11 for talks on oil, agriculture and trade — a meeting that also produced the first presidential-level airing of a court attachment on PDVSA assets in the country.

Rodríguez landed at Johan Adolf Pengel International Airport on Thursday evening, where Foreign Minister Melvin Bouva received the Venezuelan delegation. On Friday morning, central Paramaribo was temporarily kept car-free at several points as police managed traffic around the state visit and the events at the Presidential Palace, Surinamese media reported.

At the palace, President Jennifer Geerlings-Simons received Rodríguez for their first in-person meeting as heads of state. An earlier attempt to organize the visit had fallen through; according to Bouva, renewed effort on both sides made this one happen.

Rodríguez told reporters that several cooperation agreements would be signed under what Caracas calls its Bolivarian Diplomacy of Peace. “We are very committed to our bilateral agenda; we will sign important agreements in different areas of cooperation. I always insist that this is the path: friendship, cooperation, a relationship where both countries and both peoples can benefit,” she said, according to the Venezuelan presidency’s press office.

Oil, Fish and Poultry: What Was Actually Discussed

Bouva, who visited Caracas in May to sign an integration roadmap with his then-counterpart Yván Gil, laid out the concrete agenda in Suriname Herald: an existing and active fishing relationship — Venezuelan vessels and fishers operate in Surinamese waters, and Venezuelan companies are investing in the local fishing sector, with at least one partnership with a Surinamese firm already in place; agricultural production; oil and gas; tourism; and better connections between the two countries.

On education, both sides are looking at capacity building, above all training for the petroleum sector — an area where Bouva says Venezuela has experience Suriname can use as its own offshore industry, led by TotalEnergies’ roughly US$10.5 billion GranMorgu project, moves toward production. The two countries’ diplomatic training institutes will also deepen cooperation. The Venezuelan presidency added that both nations expect to convene a High-Level Mixed Commission and continue recent trade-exchange agreements, including a review of Venezuela’s agro-export offer for the poultry sector.

Bouva also floated evaluating the old PetroCaribe agreement — the Chavez-era discounted-oil scheme — to see how it might be carried forward, though he made no concrete announcements on new PetroCaribe terms.

The PDVSA Attachment, Raised at the Highest Level

The sharpest item of the day came from Simons herself. She raised the case of an executory third-party attachment on assets of the Venezuelan state oil company PDVSA in Suriname, connected to the PetroCaribe compensation mechanism between the two countries, Suriname Herald reported. Simons stressed that the legal procedures are still running and that no definitive court ruling exists — and asked Rodríguez whether there were recent developments on the matter from the Venezuelan government.

“Suriname remains committed to resolving outstanding bilateral issues in a constructive, friendly and mutually respectful manner,” Simons said. She also proposed that the Political Consultation Mechanism and the Mixed Commission between the two countries meet in the first half of 2027 to deepen technical cooperation, and repeated Suriname’s condolences for the earthquakes that struck Venezuela on June 24.

“Delcy, Trump and Our Oil”

The visit landed in a charged regional context. A Starnieuws column published Friday — titled “Delcy, Trump en onze olie” (“Delcy, Trump and our oil”) — reads the trip through the recent agreement between the Trump administration and Venezuela covering some 65 billion barrels of oil: 100-year concessions on 17 oil fields holding more than a fifth of Venezuela’s reserves, with Rodríguez speaking of more than US$100 billion in investment. The column notes the deal has drawn fire from both the Venezuelan opposition and Chavismo hardliners — former PDVSA chief Rafael Ramírez called it “the biggest robbery in our history” — and asks what Washington’s grip on Venezuelan crude means for Suriname’s own oil choices.

For foreigners in the region, the significance is straightforward: Venezuela’s acting president — sworn in after US special forces captured Maduro and his wife on January 3 and flew them to New York to await trial on drug charges — is now touring neighbors to lock in trade and energy ties. After Grenada, Barbados, The Hague and India, Paramaribo is stop number five, and the first where a host president put a legal claim against PDVSA on the table in the room.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Delcy Rodríguez visit Suriname?

For a state visit on September 10–11, 2026, centered on oil and gas, agriculture, fisheries, tourism, education and transport. Venezuela’s acting president said several cooperation agreements would be signed; both sides plan a High-Level Mixed Commission and further trade-exchange deals.

What is Delcy Rodríguez’s current title?

She is Venezuela’s acting president — “presidenta encargada” — sworn in after the US capture of Nicolás Maduro on January 3, 2026. Surinamese officials refer to her as the acting or serving president; Suriname’s government protocol used “President Delcy Rodríguez” for the visit.

What is the PDVSA issue Suriname raised?

President Simons raised an executory third-party attachment on PDVSA assets in Suriname linked to the PetroCaribe compensation mechanism. Court procedures are ongoing with no final ruling; Simons asked whether the Venezuelan government had recent developments to report.

World.title: Dominican Republic Murder Rate Falls to 7.39 per 100,000
World.content:
DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · SECURITY

Key Facts — The number The Dominican Republic’s accumulated murder rate stands at 7.39 per 100,000 inhabitants through 4 September 2026, according to the joint task force’s 164th weekly crime report.

— The trend The rate has fallen every year since 2022, when it was 13.20. Last year closed at a validated 8.7, the presidency says.

— The map Authorities say 28 territories covering 80 percent of the country now record single-digit murder rates.

— The week Five murders and 34 people wounded were logged in the latest weekly period, alongside 563 robberies and 171 traffic accidents.

— The region Independent crime trackers put Jamaica near 49, Haiti and Trinidad and Tobago around 40, and Puerto Rico near 15 murders per 100,000 — all far above the Dominican figure.

The Dominican Republic is on track to close 2026 with its lowest murder rate in decades — a number the government of Luis Abinader has made the centerpiece of its security record, and one its critics say deserves a closer look at the fine print.

The Dominican Republic’s accumulated homicide rate reached 7.39 per 100,000 inhabitants as of 4 September 2026, the Fuerza de Tarea Conjunta — the joint police-military task force that produces the country’s weekly crime statistics — reported in its 164th weekly analysis, published on 11 September.

If the trend holds, 2026 will be the safest year in the country’s modern crime statistics. The comparison set released with the report shows the accumulated rate at 8.74 for the same period of 2025, 9.65 in 2024, 11.49 in 2023 and 13.20 in 2022 — an almost unbroken decline of roughly 44 percent in four years.

A Quiet Week Behind the Headline Number

The weekly report that produced the 7.39 figure counted five murders and 34 people wounded by violence in the period under review, in a country of about 11 million. It also logged 563 robberies and 171 traffic accidents — a reminder that everyday insecurity in the Dominican Republic is less about homicide than about street robbery and some of the deadliest roads in the hemisphere.

Geographically, the improvement is broad. The task force says 28 territories, together covering 80 percent of the national territory, now post single-digit murder rates — meaning the remaining hotspots, concentrated in parts of Santo Domingo and a handful of provincial cities, account for a growing share of the killings that remain.

Two Sets of Books

There is a caveat built into the number, and the government itself acknowledges it. The weekly task-force figures are operational police statistics — preliminary counts that can be revised. The presidency announced in March that 2025 closed at a validated rate of 8.7 per 100,000, based on 951 intentional homicides, after the Interior and Police Ministry’s crime-data analysis center CADSECI and its operational technical unit consolidated and validated the year’s records. Notably, that validated figure came in 0.6 points above the task force’s own preliminary estimate for the year — validation cut the number up, not down.

The 8.74 in this week’s comparison set is a different beast: the accumulated operational rate to the same September cut-off last year, not a full-year close. That distinction is exactly where the political argument lives. Opposition voices have long questioned which deaths enter the official count, how “intentional homicide” is defined against broader violent-death categories, how foreign-national victims are treated, and how often cases are reclassified after the weekly snapshot. None of that overturns the trend: available independent analyses of Dominican homicide data all point the same way. But it does mean the 7.39 should be read as a strong operational signal, not a final audited statistic.

An Outlier in a Violent Neighborhood

Set against the region, the Dominican number is striking. Independent crime-data trackers put Jamaica’s murder rate near 49 per 100,000, Haiti’s and Trinidad and Tobago’s around 40, and Puerto Rico’s near 15. Those comparisons come with their own methodology warnings — different countries count differently, and Haiti’s statistics are fragmentary in the best of times — but the orders of magnitude are not in dispute.

Within Latin America as a whole, where regional averages still sit well into double digits, a rate in the sevens would place the Dominican Republic among the safer countries on the continent. Security analysts such as InSight Crime have noted the country’s trajectory, while cautioning that low homicide rates coexist with persistent organized crime, drug transshipment and contract killing markets that rarely show up in the headline number.

Abinader’s Security Card

For President Luis Abinader, the statistics are political capital. Citizen security was one of his administration’s flagship promises, and the government now opens nearly every security presentation with the homicide curve. The validated 8.7 close for 2025 was announced from the National Palace itself — a sign of how central the number has become to the official narrative.

Critics counter that the homicide rate is the wrong single lens: robbery, extortion and femicide weigh heavily in public perception surveys, and trust in the police remains fragile. The weekly report’s own 563 robberies in seven days illustrate why many Dominicans say they do not feel as safe as the murder statistics suggest they should.

Still, the direction of travel is now long enough to be undeniable. A country that recorded 13.20 murders per 100,000 just four years ago is measuring itself in the sevens — and in a Caribbean basin where several neighbors are moving the other way, that divergence may be the Abinader government’s most durable claim on the record.

World.title: Mexico’s INE ‘Has Given In’ on Policing Elections, Council Member Warns
World.content:
MEXICO · POLITICS

Key Facts — The accusation INE council member Arturo Castillo said at the opening of the 2026–2027 electoral process that the institute “appears to have given in” on its duty to watch over and arbitrate elections.

— The context Mexico’s biggest-ever electoral process started September 10: some 102 million citizens will be eligible to vote on June 6, 2027.

— The reply Council member Arturo Chávez answered that one council member does not speak for the INE and accused critics of joining a campaign to discredit it.

— The alliance Sergio Aguayo, Denise Dresser, Mauricio Merino, José Woldenberg and hundreds more signed a call for a Democratic Alliance for Election Observation.

— The flashpoints Early Morena campaigning, “pre-folded ballots” left over from 2024, and whether government social-program workers may register as election observers.

— The president’s answer INE president Guadalupe Taddei closed the session saying the institute “will not be intimidated by absolutely anyone.”

Mexico’s electoral referee opened the 2027 campaign season by arguing with itself — a sitting council member says the INE has surrendered its job of policing the parties, while a civic alliance of academics and journalists organizes to watch every step of the vote.
