World.title: ‘Abuse of power’: Von der Leyen rapped after backing space mega deal
World.content:
“Endorsing a merger at a conference covered by the media, without any substantive review, is an abuse of power and misconduct,” the French MEP wrote on X.

Von der Leyen was referring to Project Bromo, a joint venture between satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales to compete, at least in part, with the Starlink satellite-internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which recently went public in the U.S. and is valued around $2 trillion.

“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” von der Leyen said.

Her words would have been music to the ears of the summit host, French President Emmanuel Macron, who has publicly backed the project together with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

But they raised red flags with the antitrust community in Brussels, where the project has yet to be formally notified or assessed by the EU executive’s competition department led by Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera.

“What is the point of Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera and the Directorate General for Competition if it is the president of the Commission who unilaterally decides a case?” Yon-Courtin asked.

World.title: Sweden’s NATO missions are at risk if the left wins election, warns PM Kristersson
World.content:
Until recently, Sunday’s upcoming vote seemed like it would be a comfortable victory for Andersson’s Social Democrats and their political allies in smaller parties on the left. But their poll lead shrank dramatically in the past two weeks to as low as 2.6%, within the statistical margin of error.

Far-right friends

Kristersson’s center-right coalition has been governing for the past four years with the support of the far-right Sweden Democrats. He defended his decision to cooperate with a party opponents claim is too extreme despite its internal efforts to clean up its past neo-Nazi links.

“I have full respect for the fact that there are eight parties in the Swedish parliament,” said Kristersson. “None of these parties are even close to a majority of their own. If you cannot unite parties on specific topics and ambitions, then you will simply not get anything done at all.”

Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, the first woman to serve as Swedish PM, leads the polls. | Tim Ross/POLITICO

Under leader Jimmie Åkesson, the Sweden Democrats are in second place behind Andersson’s Social Democrats in the polls. Åkesson has said he’s eyeing up the chance of becoming prime minister at the next vote, due in 2030.

If Kristersson returns as prime minister after Sunday’s election, he has said he’s ready to give Sweden Democrat politicians roles as ministers in his government for the first time. It would be a major change for Sweden — and the left-wing bloc has campaigned against it.

Kristersson suggested that being part of a team would limit the opportunities for any individual ministers to go rogue with extremist policies.

“In Sweden, we have a collective decision-making process in government,” he said. “I would never say that one minister is not important, but every minister is part of a team that jointly makes all the decisions — so there is very little room for people to play in a role of their own.

“And since I will be the person that is forming that government, and the person that will appoint every one of them, I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government.”

World.title: UK MPs reject bill legalizing assisted dying bill despite previous support
World.content:
The bill, introduced by backbench Labour MP Lauren Edwards, would have legalized assisted dying for adults aged 18 or over who are judged by two doctors as expected to die within six months.

It will now make no further progress and follows members of the Scottish Parliament rejecting similar legislation in March and a previous vote by MPs against assisted dying in 2015.

Assisted dying is currently illegal in the U.K. and assisting someone to end their life is punishable by up to 14 years in prison in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

The vote was a matter of conscience, meaning parties did not whip their MPs who could vote as they wished.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was not an MP when Leadbeater's bill was previously debated, deliberately abstained to avoid swaying the views of MPs.

Nonetheless, Burnham argued soon after becoming PM that fixing palliative and social care should come before legalizing assisted dying.

“It is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care,” he said in July.

Isabel Loubser contributed to this report.

World.title: Iran-backed Houthis seize Red Sea port, putting another key trade route at risk
World.content:
At its narrowest, the strait is only about 30 kilometers wide. Yemen’s internationally recognized President Rashad al-Alimi warned Thursday it “must not be allowed to become another Strait of Hormuz.”

The Iranian-supported rebel advance raises the prospect of simultaneous disruption at two of global trade’s most vital chokepoints, potentially compounding shipping delays, supply shortages and inflationary pressure worldwide.

Tehran on Friday voiced support for Yemen’s "independence, national sovereignty and territorial integrity," while blaming the country’s crisis on blockade and foreign military intervention. The Iranian foreign ministry's statement, published on official state-run news agency IRNA, did not address the Houthi advance or Bab al-Mandeb.

The Houthis’ military capabilities have also drawn fresh scrutiny. A weapons cell based in Northern Yemen, a large part of which is controlled by the Houthis, used Anthropic’s Claude AI to develop guidance, navigation and control software for rockets and ballistic missiles, the tech giant reported in a memo published Thursday.

Western concerns are growing over the ramifications of the Iran war spreading further across the region.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot warned Friday in a post on X that “Bab al-Mandab is not a bargaining chip.”

World.title: US excludes French groups from MAGA-aligned grant program
World.content:
The grant program was formally advertised in the summer after U.S. State Department officials held talks with MAGA-aligned think tanks and advocacy groups about funding opportunities earlier this year. That led French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot to warn against what he described as potential “foreign interference in [European] electoral processes.”

The country is beefing up its arsenal to fight online disinformation and foreign interference ahead of the 2027 presidential campaign, with a law set to be considered by the Senate in October.

A spokesperson for the State Department said the program “does not and will not fund political parties, in Europe or elsewhere” and added that the allocation of grants “was still in active deliberation.”

The U.S. administration, most prominently Vice President JD Vance, has repeatedly framed the EU’s hate speech laws and election safety measures as attempts to curtail free speech and civil rights.

Its high-profile support for Hungary’s autocratic former leader Viktor Orbán and its pledge to support like-minded “patriotic European parties” in its National Security Strategy have raised fears of election interference ahead of several key elections in Europe.

The spokesperson for the State Department said the strategy objectives included “collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Nicolas Conquer, the founder of the MAGA-aligned French think tank Western Arc, has applied for the funding. He said he had yet to receive a formal response to his application.

World.title: EU should sanction Israeli settlements like Russian-occupied Crimea, Kallas says
World.content:
“Especially today, on the eve of the Jewish New Year, it is hard to believe that [she] would draw a direct parallel between The Western wall and the Jewish Quarter in Jerusalem and the situation in Crimea, regardless of her personal worldview,” the mission said.

The EU foreign policy chief has long backed a push from several member countries to pressure the European Commission to ban trade with territories illegally occupied by Israel — an issue that divides capitals and has become a flashpoint in the rift between Kallas and the Commission’s president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Kallas’ backing has so far failed to force the Commission’s hand. In July, only a minority of EU foreign ministers called on the Commission to bring specific measures for member countries to vote on. While a handful of countries including the Netherlands, Belgium and Sweden have pushed for bloc-wide restrictions, the Czech Republic has vowed to oppose any new sanctions — withholding the unanimity required among EU capitals.

But the debate was reignited Tuesday when eight EU countries, including France, Spain and Ireland, joined the U.K. and Canada in a pledge to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements.

“All EU Member States agree that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law,” Kallas said after the announcement. “The Israeli Government’s settlement expansions in the West Bank are undermining the prospects for a viable two-State solution.”

Kallas’ positions have previously drawn the ire of Israeli officials. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar vowed to “sever all contact” with the EU’s top diplomat in June, after reports that she had compared Israel’s treatment of Palestinians to apartheid-era South Africa.

World.title: ‘The Europe she fought for will miss her’: Politicians pay tribute to Emma Bonino
World.content:
A veteran of Italy’s fight for civil and women’s rights, Bonino played a key role in the campaigns that led to the legalization of divorce and abortion in the country during the 1970s.

In 2017, she co-founded the liberal More Europe party, which paid tribute to her on Friday. “Activist, parliamentarian, minister, European commissioner. Always radically free,” party leader Riccardo Magi wrote on X. “Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedoms.”

Carlo Calenda, leader of the liberal Italian Action party, said: “The last great protagonist of the civil battles that led to the modernization of this country,” adding that “a piece of Italian and European political history is passing away.”

Bonino’s endeavors extended beyond Italy. She served as a European commissioner in the 1990s, notably overseeing an increase in humanitarian aid to countries and regions affected by some of the most devastating conflicts of the decade, including the Balkans, Rwanda and Afghanistan.

“Emma Bonino has never waited for the world to be ready. She has always chosen to move forward, showing the way to others,” wrote European Parliament President Roberta Metsola. “The Europe she fought for will miss her.”

World.title: Hamas planned Berlin-Vienna attacks for Oct. 7 anniversary, indictment shows
World.content:
Federal prosecutors said last year that they had arrested men linked to the Palestinian militant group who were suspected of planning attacks on Israeli and Jewish targets in Germany. The indictment, which has not been made public, reveals that Vienna was also an intended target — and that the attacks in the two capitals were to be coordinated. The principal targets included Israeli diplomats, Jewish community centers and pro-Israel demonstrations.

Seven men have been charged in connection with the plot and remain in pretrial detention, according to the indictment. One of the accused was working as a confidential informant for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. The files show that the informant continued reporting to his intelligence handler while allegedly failing to disclose the full extent of his own involvement in obtaining ammunition for the group.

The indictment portrays the plot as part of a broader shift in Hamas’ operations in Europe. Intelligence assessments cited in the filing say plans existed even before the Oct. 7, 2023 attack to establish and train operational cells on the continent, using Turkey as a base and directing attacks remotely from abroad.

The prosecutors alleged the weapons operation was also coordinated from Lebanon, where a Hamas operative allegedly oversaw one of the procurement channels linking members of the network across Europe.

According to the indictment, the objective was to move beyond the fundraising, propaganda and logistical activity that had long characterized Hamas’ presence in Europe and develop the capability to carry out attacks against Israeli and Jewish targets in the West.

The plot began to unravel on Oct. 1, 2025, just six days before the planned attacks, when German authorities arrested three suspects in Berlin during the handover of a cache of weapons that prosecutors say had been assembled for the operation.

World.title: French father jailed for threatening to behead his son’s teacher
World.content:
A French court has sentenced a man to six months in prison after he threatened to “cut off the head” of a teacher at his son’s school last week.

 

The defendant confronted his son’s teacher in the school car park in the southwestern town of Le Fauga last week, after the nine-year-old was moved to another class because of his behaviour.

He threatened to decapitate the 58-year-old teacher before entering the school, where he repeated the threats in front of the headteacher.

Remarks of 'great violence'

The court sentenced the defendant to six months in prison, to be served immediately, a harsher sentence than the six months under electronic monitoring sought by the public prosecutor.

The presiding judge, Fabrice Rives, condemned the “extremely worrying remarks” and described them as being of “great violence”, explicitly referring to the murder of Samuel Paty.

In that case, Paty, a history and geography teacher, was beheaded in 2020 by an 18-year-old radical Islamist of Chechen origin after showing his class caricatures of the Prophet Mohammed.

At the hearing, the defendant apologised, saying he had “not realised the seriousness” of his words.

Describing himself as “very, very protective” of his children, he said he was not a violent person and did not know what had come over him that day.

Teacher 'traumatised'

The teacher is currently on sick leave and unsure whether she will return to the classroom, according to her lawyer, Jocelyn Momasso-Momasso.

He said she was “traumatised”, adding that she had told him: “I didn’t 

At the hearing, the defendant said he had already agreed to move two of his three children who attended the school to another establishment.

World.title: France joins Slovakia in asking to delist Russian oligarch Usmanov
World.content:
The French government has joined Slovakia in seeking the delisting of Russian-Uzbek businessman Alisher Usmanov, causing “huge frustration” among other EU countries, four EU diplomats told Euronews.

 

Slovakia has long pushed for Usmanov and another Russian oligarch, Mikhail Fridman, to be removed from the EU's sanctions list targeting individuals close to Vladimir Putin's regime and the military-industrial complex sustaining the war in Ukraine.

But Bratislava is no longer alone. Paris has also called for Usmanov, who has been under EU sanctions since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, to be delisted.

Usmanov is an Uzbek-born Russian billionaire who built his fortune through investments in metals, mining, telecommunications and technology and is considered close to the Kremlin.

The French move has caused “huge frustration” among other member states, particularly against the backdrop of escalating hybrid threats in Europe, including the latest case of an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany.

“It raised a lot of questions about the motivation — seems mostly economic reasons at play here. Not a lot of understanding on the side of other member states,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the talks.

The EU sanctions regime currently targets more than 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial complex and its contribution to the invasion of Ukraine. The regime is due for renewal on 15 September, with member states under pressure to reach an agreement by then.

Individual listings have so far been renewed every six months, but a 12-month renewal is now on the table. Sectoral sanctions already shifted from six-month to 12-month renewal cycles in July.

In several meetings of EU ambassadors, Slovakia has opposed the renewal, pushing for both oligarchs to be delisted and the six-month timeframe to remain in place.

The Slovak demands are not new. Bratislava has repeatedly called for the delisting of the two high-profile Russian oligarchs, including when the sanctions were last extended in March.

EU sanctions require unanimous approval for renewal, meaning a single country can veto an extension. Slovakia's opposition has already caused frustration among member states, but France's new position is likely to complicate the talks further.

Paris presented Usmanov's delisting as a political compromise, betting that Slovakia would not abandon its two delisting demands as it did last time.

EU ambassadors are due to meet again on Monday to discuss the renewal and will be under pressure to reach a political agreement before the 15 September deadline.

A spokesperson for France's permanent representation to the EU said Paris supported the renewal of sanctions, but declined to comment on the discussions, citing confidentiality.

World.title: Russia sends sanctioned ships to Mediterranean as NATO tracks 'Syrian Express' convoy
World.content:
Russia's navy has returned to the Mediterranean for the first time in two months, ending what military sources described as the first interruption to its Mediterranean presence since 2013 — with ships reportedly detected switching off their tracking transponders before passing through the Strait of Gibraltar.

 

Speaking on condition of anonymity, a senior European military source said the "Syrian Express" ships had arrived at the Syrian port of Tartus on Monday.

The informal name "Syrian Express" refers to Moscow's maritime logistics network that transfers military supplies, weapons, and equipment between Russian ports and Tartus.

It has been running intermittently since Russia's military intervention in Syria in 2015, frequently involving sanctioned vessels that have also been associated with Russia's broader shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to circumvent Western sanctions.

The latest Russian convoy included the sanctioned cargo vessel Sparta, the sanctioned tanker General Skobelev, and the replenishment ship Akademik Pashin, all escorted by the destroyer Admiral Levchenko.

Tight European surveillance

Despite its return to the Mediterranean, Russia's navy remains under tight European surveillance.

The ships in question were closely tracked by the Italian Carabinieri frigate as they sailed through the central Mediterranean after they were spotted at Gibraltar.

Euronews obtained exclusive photos of the Italian frigate alongside the Russian ships.

Euronews obtained exclusive photos of the Italian Carabiniere frigate, alongside the Syrian express ships Military source

Tracking data from the specialised website MarineTraffic indicates that the vessels switched off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders — which automatically broadcast ships' identity, position, speed, and course — before passing through the Strait of Gibraltar.

Britain deployed three ships — HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn — to monitor the convoy as it sailed through the English Channel.

The military source told Euronews that in recent months, Syrian express ships have begun cutting off AIS transponders even "more frequently" than in the past, with this practice almost becoming "systematic".

Russia retains post-al-Assad presence in Syria

Tartus is Russia's only naval base outside the former Soviet Union and its sole resupply and maintenance point in the Mediterranean.

The Soviet Union established the facility in 1971 under a lease agreement with Damascus, using it to sustain its Mediterranean fleet during the Cold War.

Russia intervened militarily in Syria in September 2015, entering the country's civil war on the side of Bashar al-Assad at a moment when his forces were losing ground to opposition groups.

Moscow initially said its strikes were targeting the so-called Islamic State terrorist group, but international organisations documented that the majority of Russian air strikes hit opposition-held civilian areas, with the Airwars monitoring group assessing that those strikes resulted in the deaths of more than 14,000 Syrian civilians.

The nine-year campaign in Syria was the Kremlin's most significant military participation in a war outside the former Soviet Union before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

When the al-Assad regime finally collapsed in December 2024, Russian warships evacuated from Tartus within days — a precautionary move to avoid being seized or denied departure.

In August, Damascus announced it had reached a deal with Moscow to retain Russia's future presence in the two military bases it has in the country.

On 9 August, Syria’s state news agency SANA quoted the Foreign Ministry as saying the Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval base would become “joint training and capacity-building centres” under new arrangements aimed at preserving "mutual interests".

The senior European military source outlined several factors which are hindering Moscow's ability to maintain its presence in the Mediterranean including Russia's ageing navy, European sanctions against its shadow fleet, as well as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones targeting its Black Sea fleet.

European and Ukrainian pressure on the shadow fleet is also pushing Russia to deploy military escorts for its oil tankers.

World.title: UK lawmakers reject assisted dying bill for England and Wales
World.content:
UK lawmakers on Friday rejected legislation that would have allowed terminally ill adults in England and Wales to choose to end their lives.

 

Following an impassioned four-hour debate in the House of Commons, the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was rejected by 286 votes to 270.

The outcome marked a notable reversal from last year, when an almost identical bill passed with a majority of 23 votes.

The bill would have allowed adults in England and Wales with fewer than six months to live to apply for an assisted death, subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

The vote brings an end to a two-year debate in Parliament over assisted dying, during which the House of Commons had backed the measure on two previous occasions. That support was not enough for it to become law, as it was effectively filibustered by unelected lawmakers in the revising House of Lords chamber.

During Friday’s debate, lawmakers shared personal stories and arguments both for and against the proposal. The government remained neutral, allowing MPs to vote according to their consciences rather than along party lines.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham did not take part in the vote, saying he did not want to “unduly influence the debate”.

Concerns over safeguards

Opponents called the bill unsafe, citing the risk of coercion of vulnerable people and insufficient safeguards for people with disabilities.

Opposition to the bill had been voiced by the leader of Catholics in England and Wales, Archbishop Richard Moth, who called it “wrong in principle” and “deeply flawed,” as well as the Church of England’s Archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists also raised “serious concerns”, citing “too many unanswered questions about the safeguarding of people with mental illness."

World.title: NATO's deterrence increasingly undermined by lack of response to Russian 'hybrid' attacks
World.content:
Incidents of Russian-orchestrated hybrid war attacks across NATO territory are entering a new dangerous, kinetic phase, leaders across the continent agree.

 

At a meeting in early September, EU Foreign Policy Chief Kaja Kallas said Russian President Vladimir Putin's aim is to "scare us away from supporting Ukraine."

"He will not succeed," she told journalists at a meeting of EU foreign ministers.

However, others in European diplomatic circles have told Euronews that the lack of a powerful deterrent response is leaving the continent vulnerable to an escalation in Russian attacks.

Germany’s decision to formally blame the Kremlin for planting an explosive-laden drone in Leipzig airport in August marked Berlin's most direct confrontation with Moscow after years of hostile interference.

Germany shut the Russian consulate in Bonn and terminated an agreement that had allowed the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin to remain open despite long-held suspicions of espionage activities.

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the offences and intelligence findings establish Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said in Berlin after the incident.

More recently, a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was almost hit by a Russian drone as he started his journey to attend the state funeral of King Harald in Oslo on 7 September.

'The Kremlin has the measure of us'

“How is it these (incidents) do not meet the threshold for NATO to respond?” Ed Arnold, senior adviser at British Foreign Policy Group, put it to Euronews.

“By doing nothing, we are chipping away at the deterrence value of NATO.”

Arnold pointed out that if the military-grade explosives in the drone at Leipzig at detonated, they could have been fatal. The drone wasn’t correctly installed and failed to blow up.

“The incident at Leipzig wasn’t foiled by security services, the explosives didn't detonate,” he said. “NATO needs to have a comprehensive response now, because the Kremlin has the measure of us.”

The ambiguity over NATO’s response stems partly from the lack of certainty as to whether the United States would support a collective response to an attack on NATO territory.

A US intelligence assessment in August reported that Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve with a limited assault on NATO territory within a few years, whether via a small-scale land incursion or a serious cyber-attack on critical infrastructure – in either case, a situation too serious to go unanswered.

Arnold argued that the uncertainty over Washington's commitment will only fuel Putin’s appetite to risk the possibility of a direct confrontation with NATO, playing as it does into Putin's campaign to prove that Article 5 of the NATO charter – “an attack on one is an attack on all” – is hollow.

"He knows that the best bet to achieve this is the current White House administration," Arnold said. “Putin is a strategist not a tactician. He still can't beat the Ukrainians in a conventional war, but he can see that the Trump administration are susceptible to Russian charm."

Charm offensive

US Envoy Steve Witkoff spoke in glowing admiration to Putin during diplomatic talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine last week.

"So first of all President Putin, thank you so much for having us," he said. "We were sitting outside just now… and we were all talking about when we retire, we'll have all these incredible stories and incredible memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all.”

Kurt Volker, who served US ambassador to NATO under the first Trump administration, is now advising Ukrainian authorities on security matters. He told Euronews the alliance needs to be at a much higher state of readiness for an attack which would undeniably elicit an Article 5 collective response – and that it must be made clear to the Kremlin that there is now “zero tolerance” of its continuing shadow-war activities.

Instead, he pointed to drone incursions in Romania and Poland over the last year and the apparent lack of consequences.

"We’re left questioning - 'where is the line' that if Russia crosses it, we would respond."

“Remember when there were 19 drones in Polish territory and that was shocking, and now we have an armed drone fast circling over Romanian airspace and into Ukraine and nobody says anything. This all has a creeping effect."

Poland took the relatively rare decision to trigger Article 4 of NATO’s charter in the aftermath of the drone incursion last year.

An Article 4 process is the prelude to triggering the demand for a collective allied response. It draws all allies into a formal consultation if they suspect their territorial integrity is under threat. The goal of the process is to consider a joint response with the backing of allies after all the information is shared. Unlike Article 5, it does not commit the alliance to a mutual defence response.

Asked why there have been so few Article 4 formal consultations since despite the Kremlin's increasingly aggressive activities, Volker said that whenever an official process is drawn upon but no outcome materialises, it further exposes NATO's “level of disunity”.

“If you have Article 4 but then there’s no outcome, then maybe it's a better idea not to have the meeting in the first place,” he said.

In response to such criticisms, NATO officials have also pointed to the fact that Germany did not trigger an Article 4 emergency consultation.

"Germany might do this, but until they do, it's still a matter for the German government to respond and not the alliance," an official told Euronews.

Russia undeterred

“The deterrence isn’t working,” said Laura Galante, former director of the US' Cyber Threat Intelligence Integration Centre. “When you have a drone in a civilian airport, we can see this threat in clear focus."

She agreed with others who spoke to Euronews that there hasn’t yet been a moment where NATO has successfully coalesced around a response to Russian incursions or attacks – and she also pointed to the “backpaddling” by Washington on whether it is fully committed to collective security of NATO.

Galant says it’ll be up to Europe – particularly countries like Finland and Sweden which have strong, well-equipped militaries and a comprehensive security posture – to take the lead in the event of a major attack.

Even the use of the term "hybrid war" is now widely viewed as insufficient as it minimises the severity of Russia's orchestrated actions, which include not just frequent drone incursions but also arson, sabotage and assassination attempts.

“We have to find also a way how to tackle the non-conventional warfare,” Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs, told the 2026 Riga Conference on Thursday.

“We very often refer to that as hybrid warfare. And the more I have myself done that many times. Now I think that we are all wrong."

Rinkēvičs argued that the "hybrid" framing creates "a feeling in our societies that it has nothing to do with the real and clear and present danger".

Meanwhile, on 11 September, the Kremlin threatened to target Lithuania with Russian nuclear weapons if Vilnius allows nuclear arms to be stationed on its territory.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov made the remarks as he commented on Vilnius's recent openness to remove restrictions on hosting nuclear weapons.

“This was to be expected. It will mark a very serious escalation of tensions, because if you deploy nuclear weapons on your territory, they are aimed at someone," he said at a press conference. "Obviously, these weapons will not be aimed at the West. They will be aimed at the East – that is, at us."

“If there are nuclear weapons on its territory that are aimed at us, then, accordingly, that country’s territory will also be in the crosshairs of our nuclear weapons.”

World.title: Norway's Princess Astrid dies two days after funeral of brother King Harald
World.content:
Norway’s Princess Astrid, the older sister of the late King Harald, died on Friday at the age of 94, the Norwegian Royal Palace said in a statement.

 

"Aunt Astrid was an important source of support for King Harald and the rest of our family. We learned a great deal from her, and she was never afraid to speak her mind," King Haakon VIII ⁠said ​in the ​statement.

"Her passing is a great loss to us. We will miss her."

The King added that Princess Astrid had stepped into the role of First Lady at just 22 following the death of his grandmother, Crown Princess Martha.

He said she was particularly committed to caring for and including the most vulnerable members of society and carried out her duties with loyalty, dedication and “an infectious sense of humour.”

Norway's Princess Astrid leaves the Oslo Cathedral after a funeral service for Norway's King Harald V in Oslo, Wednesday, 9 Sept., 2026. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)

The Princess made her last public appearance at King Harald’s funeral on Wednesday, as Norway bid farewell to the long-serving monarch, with crowds lining the streets of Oslo and foreign royals and world leaders attending the ceremony.

World.title: Podcast: Eco-anger, France in space, world's first photograph
World.content:
A climate expert experiences eco-anxiety firsthand after living through France's hottest summer on record. France tries to find its place in the new space race. And the story of the earliest known photograph still visible today.

Advertising

Eco-anxiety is on the rise in France after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves led to wildfires, scorched crops and the deaths of at least 7,000 people as well as livestock and birds. Juliette Decq, a climate adaptation consultant, says fear is a normal response to the reality people are now facing. A mother of two young children, she experienced that reality firsthand when her own home became unsafe. She talks about her anger over France’s lack of preparedness, not least in schools, but also about the solidarity she witnessed in her local community as they helped people protect themselves. Eco-anger, she says, can be a force for change. (Listen @0')

Historically a leader in Europe’s space programme, France is reassessing its role in space. Although French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on the International Space Station, France’s space ambitions haven’t focused on human space flight. But as the US and China ramp up their Moon missions and space becomes increasingly industrialised, France is looking to find its place. Space policy analyst Xavier Pasco explains how Europe is positioning itself as a regulator in a rapidly changing sector that has, until now, remained largely unchecked. (Listen @20'10'')

French inventor Nicéphore Niépce took the earliest surviving photograph in July 1827: a scene from a window that might have taken days to make. He fell into obscurity, and the photo itself was lost. Now it's returning to France, as part of a celebration of 200 years of photography in his honour. (Listen @14'15'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

World.title: Ukraine: Russian strike on Kyiv gas station kills 2
World.content:
With fighting on the front lines mostly stalled, Russia has been increasingly hitting petrol stations and other civilian targets. Ukraine has also been attacking Russia with drones, killing three people on Friday.

At least two people were killed in Kyiv after Russian jet-powered drones struck a petrol station on Friday.

A 12-year-old boy was among 12 people who were injured by the attack, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one of the injured was a first responder who was "wounded in a double-tap strike."

Russia has turned to using jet-powered drones in near-constant attacks on Kyiv Image: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

Russia increasingly targeting petrol stations with new, faster drones

Friday's drone strikes come a day after what is thought to be the first Russian attack on a Kyiv gas station during the war.

Russia has struck around 300 petrol stations in Ukraine in recent months, most of which were in or near frontline areas.

The attacks on petrol stations come amid a spike in Russian assaults using new, faster and harder-to-intercept jet-powered drones to strike logistics centers, warehouses and commercial supply chains.

Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine condemns escalating Russian 'terror'

Zelenskyy said Russia was escalating these strikes on civilian energy infrastructure, calling them "increasingly terrorist in nature."

"Maximum attention must be focused on protecting the skies, finding solutions to protect people, and scaling up countermeasures against Russian drones," the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.

The CEO of Ukrainian oil giant Ukrnafta, which owns the gas station and one other that was also struck on Friday morning, condemned Russia for "yet another deliberate strike on civilian facilities."

"There is no military objective in such attacks. This is terror against the civilian population," Bogdan Kukura said.

Russia has not publicly commented on the latest attacks, but has consistently denied targeting civilians.

Ukraine, Russia striking logistics, energy targets

More than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion and with the fighting on the front lines in eastern Ukraine mostly stalled, Russia and Ukraine have been increasingly hitting logistics, energy and other economic targets in a bid to dent the other's war effort.

Ukraine has also stepped up its own drone attacks inside Russia. Overnight, two people were killed in Russia's Tula region, while one person was killed in Kursk on Friday, officials said.

Tula's regional governor Dmitry Milyayev added that three people were injured in the attacks.

Ozon, Russia's second-largest e-commerce platform, said a Ukrainian drone had struck a logistics hub in the city of Saratov, starting a fire.

Kyiv says its strikes against e-comms targets are aimed at disrupting Russia's supply lines Image: REUTERS

More than 20 warehouses belonging to Ozon and Wildberries, Russia's other leading online retailer, have been hit in Ukrainian attacks in recent weeks.

Kyiv says the strikes are justified as part of its campaign to undermine Russia's war effort, which has also seen Ukraine target Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure.

World.title: US commemorates 25 years since 9/11 terror attack
World.content:
A quarter century has passed since Islamists hijacked four commercial jets and turned them into weapons against the US. On Friday, ceremonies in New York, Pennsylvania and Washington DC marked the dark anniversary.

Commemorations are being held across the United States on Friday to mark the twenty-fifth anniversary of the deadliest attacks ever carried out on US soil.

Events are taking place at the sites of the attacks — in New York City, Washington DC and Shanksville, Pennsylvania — and elsewhere around the nation to honor the 2,977 people killed that day.

The main ceremony is being held in New York, where Islamists from the terror group al-Qaeda flew two hijacked commercial airliners into the twin towers of the city's famous World Trade Center — a symbol of American economic power.

New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani, Governor Kathy Hochul and former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden are in attendance as well as current Vice President JD Vance.

Friday's event will feature wreath layings and vigils, punctuated by several moments of silence, marking the moments of impact and collapse and honoring the memory of the dead.

Family members will read out the names of the people killed that day, as well as six that were killed in a 1993 al-Qaeda bombing in the building's basement.

The attacks of September 11, 2001, killed nearly 3,000 people, changing New York, the US and the world Image: Angelina Katsanis/AP Photo/picture alliance

This year, the ceremony also acknowledged more than 600 firefighters who died from illness related to the toxic air and dust emanating from the burning structures of the site.

In Washington, President Donald Trump spoke at a ceremony at the Pentagon, the symbol of the US' military might, which was also targeted with a hijacked airliner that day.

In his remarks, Trump referenced his ongoing war in Iran, saying the US will never forget 9/11, adding, "that's why we fight today."

Other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. It was there that passengers stormed the cockpit of a hijacked United Airlines jet in midflight, forcing the plane to crash in an empty field and keeping attackers from hitting their final target, the US Capitol.

25 years later: Keeping the memory of 9/11 alive To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU and NATO allies honor victims

European Union and NATO allies also commemorated the event.

European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday expressed admiration for "victims, their families and those who rushed to help others."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen underscored the strength of democracies, pointing out that the attackers had failed to rob democratic nations of their freedom.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte posted on X that allies had, "stood together" that day, "invoking Article 5 for the first and only time in NATO's history."

Rutte added, "America's friends and allies in NATO stood with you then and we stand with you today."

US President Trump has often threatened to attack NATO allies and voiced doubt about alliance members' commitments to helping the US in times of need.

How did the 9/11 terror attacks shape modern America? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The world after 9/11

The audacious attack quite literally changed the world, stunning the US and triggering a chain of events that impact people's everyday lives to this day.

The incident sparked the Bush administration's "War on Terror," which drew the US into its longest-ever military conflict in Afghanistan and shattered trust in the nation when Bush insisted on invading Iraq, which was not involved in 9/11.

America's reputation suffered as a result of extrajudicial policies such as renditioning and "enhanced interrogation" at secret CIA prisons, as well as its creation of a detention facility in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where suspected terrorists were held for years in dystopian conditions without trial.

The aftereffects of the wars are still costing the US billions and the debacle of Iraq irreparably damaged the solidarity the US was shown in the immediate aftermath of 9/11.

The attacks changed airport security measures, as well as the US government's ability to surveil citizens — leading to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security, one of the biggest agencies in the US government, and passage of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and the USA Patriot Act.

Further, the event dramatically changed attitudes towards Muslims.

There was much controversy this year over whether Mamdani, for instance, should attend the New York ceremony. Republicans argued against it but the mayor insisted he would do so out of love of city and country and respect for those who died that day and in the years after.

This year's ceremony honors those who have died in the aftermath of the attack

Mamdani's election as mayor shows just how far parts of the country have come since that day and the young Muslim Democrat this week opened a new chapter in the story of 9/11 by releasing tens of thousands of documents showing that leaders had hidden information about the toxicity of air in the city after the attack.

As asbestos and toxic smoke blanketed the city for months officials told residents and clean-up workers that they had nothing to fear.

In fact, the toxicity of dust, rubble and smoldering plastic and metal has led to at least 9,400 additional deaths according a federal medical monitoring program.

World.title: Iran pursues cautious escalation ahead of US midterms
World.content:
Tehran appears to be boosting pressure on Washington ahead of the crucial midterm vote, but shows little desire to return to a full-scale war.

The war with Iran "is going to end immediately after the [US midterm] election because they can't hold out any longer," US President Donald Trump said of Iran's leaders on Wednesday.

Speaking at the Republican midterm convention, the first such event to be held at a massive arena in Dallas, Texas, Trump described the November 3 vote as "one of the most important elections of your lives," and once again defended the war against Iran.

The US president restated his argument that he had launched the attacks to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon. He also promised that oil prices would fall as soon as the US had won the war.

But even if Trump's promises are taken at face value, rising gas prices are sure to hurt Republicans' electoral prospects in the midterms.

On Wednesday, Brent crude — the global benchmark for prices — jumped to over $100 (€86) per barrel. The fighting escalated again this week, with the US striking Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for Iran's targeting of a US warship.

Iran's tightrope walk

"Iran still appears to see escalation primarily as a controlled instrument of coercive bargaining, rather than as an end in itself," said Mohammad Ghaedi, a Middle East expert and professor at the Department of Political Science at George Washington University.

"Iran is trying to impose costs on the United States without raising those costs so dramatically that Washington feels compelled to return to full-scale war," he explained.

"That helps explain why the number of missiles fired at US naval vessels has remained relatively limited."

The regime wants to demonstrate that it can threaten US forces and disrupt the maritime traffic in the region, the expert said, "but it also wants to keep the confrontation below a threshold that could trigger a much larger American response."

How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A return to the Islamabad truce?

Tehran's preferred outcome would be a return to the Memorandum of Understanding signed in Islamabad in June, Ghaedi said, referring to a preliminary deal that paused the full-scale conflict.

At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in late August, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian reiterated that, if the United States returns to the memorandum, Iran would return as well.

From Tehran, however, this scenario seems increasingly unlikely.

Ghaedi said the first provision of the memorandum presents a major obstacle, as it requires an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon — "something Tehran sees as unlikely before Israel's elections."

Trump reportedly urged to limit US response

Israel is going to the polls to elect a new parliament on October 27, just days before the US is set to hold its midterm vote. In Tehran, many believe that a decisive turning point in the conflict will not come until after these two elections.

On September 2, the Reuters news agency reported that senior advisers to President Trump were urging him to limit any escalation of the conflict, fearing political repercussions for the Republicans at the midterms.

The White House is reportedly considering expanding the military action after the elections.

Is the lull in fighting between Iran and the US over? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tehran, Ghaedi said, "has little interest in pushing the conflict into a much higher level of escalation."

"If Democrats gain control of Congress and try to constrain Trump's conduct of the war, Iran would be even more cautious about doing anything that could create a rally-around-the-flag effect or push Democrats closer to Trump."

Will Iran bend to economic pressure?

While military developments are hard to predict, the US will likely continue to boost economic pressure on Iran.

But Ahmad Alavi, an Iranian economics professor based in Sweden, warns that economic pressure alone would not result in political concessions.

"If the leadership of the Islamic Republic concludes that the goal of the pressure is not to change its behavior but to weaken or overthrow it, it might view concessions as a greater threat to its survival and resort instead to escalating military actions," he told DW.

Tehran would be more willing to make concessions if there were a genuine prospect of easing pressure and an established channel for negotiations, he added.

Gulf states search for Hormuz solution

Meanwhile, Oman and several other Gulf states are once again seeking a diplomatic solution to the conflict.

The foreign ministers of the Gulf states are planning to meet with their Iranian counterpart in Salalah, Oman, next week, to try to reach a deal that would temporarily ensure the safety of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported.

However, such an agreement would likely require Washington's approval, given the prolonged US naval blockade against Iran.

Is Iran set to become an economic outcast? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran keeps up hard line in public

Iran's leaders have continued to signal defiance as the conflict drags on.

"We will continue the war until final victory," Ali Nikzad, deputy speaker of parliament, told reporters on September 9.

Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), also demanded on September 8 that the US "completely cease hostilities" and refrain from further threats if it wanted to end the current situation.

At the same time, he threatened a more comprehensive Iranian response should the US attacks continue.

On September 10, the IRGC released a video that, according to Iranian sources, shows the capture of a US Anduril Dive-LD unmanned underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz. The vehicle is said to have been deployed on a covert mine-clearing mission.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
World.content:
New Delhi's "America Plus" approach sees India deepening its ties with China and Russia, while also trying to keep BRICS from turning into an anti-Western platform.

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.

The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi's year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.

Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.

India's difficult BRICS chairship To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi's diplomatic gains.

New Delhi and Beijing locked in 'armed coexistence' and competition

Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.

Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India's engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi's longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.

"These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers," Kantha told DW.

However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.

India's geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powers Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.

International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.

The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.

Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.

"The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard," said Kantha.

"It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple 'elephant and dragon' story," he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world's two most populous nations.

BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow

India's presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.

With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.

Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair's statement instead.

With Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.

"Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground," says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.

"BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common," he added.

Fears of Chinese dominance

The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.

Tracking the tense relationship between India and China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. However, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.

India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.

What is BRICS Pay? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation," Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking 'de-dollarization.'"

"Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements."

India's 'America Plus' strategy

Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.

EU-India trade agreement: consequences for the economy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India's diplomatic course is not a pure "multi-alignment" approach but an "America Plus" strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.

"India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons," said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.

But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.

"A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia's growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance," he said.

In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.

The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India's power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
World.content:
Uber's departure from Nigeria and Uganda has left countless customers high and dry. But what about drivers? With fuel prices, maintenance and other operating costs rising, many say they're struggling to make a living.

A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending over a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect.

With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — namely Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa.

"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail.

In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.

Ride-hailing apps have gained in popularity across Africa over the past decade, but not all of them seem to be profitable Image: Afolabi Sotunde/REUTERS

A difficult market to crack

Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale. The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond.

However, it's not only Uber that is having to deal with its frustration over the current situation:

Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility, especially in markets like Nigeria.

In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20 — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable.

Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers

Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good," while firmly stressing that the high commission rates were adding greatly to his existing woes.

He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€ 20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport."

"Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty-handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick up another client]," he explained.

"At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough."

Uber makes UK drivers workers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in the megacity Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business model.

The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other drivers who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income.

"But the amount I take home won't add up like before again."

In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged several strikes and protests over soaring operating costs, low fares and working conditions, as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have also been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran.

Their pleas and concerns, however, remainlargely unheard, as they find themselves having to prepare for a bumpy ride ahead.

Dollars versus naira

Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision; however, the decision comes against the backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded the purchasing power of millions of people while pushing them deeper and deeper into poverty.

This also makes such consumers less likely to use the transport company.

Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means that fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience."

Rising fuel costs due to the war in Iran coupled with Nigeria's abolition of the state fuel subsidy have led petrol prices to skyrocket Image: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

Effiong added that while Uber's cost base is dollar-linked, the drivers' revenue is the shrinking naira, leading to the overall maths not working anymore, and forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins.

Thia is despite the fact that Nigeria's ride-hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year.

"These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted.

Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does actually operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets."

The complex economics of ride-hailing

There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution. But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit also creates a loss of a service many users had considered a safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options.

Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives."

"But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added.

Spain restricts ride-hailing services To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber:

Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing dynamics change in order to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond?

In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, even resorting to violence at times as part of ongoing local taxi wars.

Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets?

As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end.

In some markets, the competition between ride-hailing apps and traditional taxi services can have brutal consequences Image: Daniel Irungu/dpa/picture alliance

Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: BRICS Summit 2026: Putin, Modi reaffirm partnership
World.content:
Skip next section Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain'

09/11/2026 September 11, 2026 Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain'

Speaking to DW about the BRICS Summit, former UN diplomat Shashi Tharoor said that the expansion of the bloc has made it the voice of the Global South.

The BRICS coalition started out with four member countries; Brazil, Russia, India and China but now has 11 members and partner countries after the economic bloc decided to open up membership for more countries in 2023.

Tharoor noted that while Iran joined the coalition, US strategic partners Egypt and Ethiopia also joined

"The expansion that took place in Johannesburg turned out to be one in which both sets of geopolitical points of view were accommodated," Tharoor noted in an interview with DW.

He argued that, "in some ways the expansion has made it much more the voice of the global south."

However, he also said that while the majority of the world is represented in the new 11-member BRICS, the chances of having a consensus has also decreased.

"I would say that BRICS is functioning, but the contradictions remain, and some contradictions have become even more apparent," he said.

He said that when BRICS leaders met this year, they "could not agree on any particular language, and so the chair, India, issued a chair statement instead… it wasn't just Iran, it was also Ukraine that they couldn't agree on."

Tharoor noted that the bloc has a "built-in set of geopolitical divergences which will crop up whenever issues divide the members."

World.title: Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
World.content:
The Houthi takeovers of Mokha, Dhubab and Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threaten to push Yemen deeper into the Middle East war. The Iran-backed group has made advances against Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia.

Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen's internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone attacks with Saudi Arabia.

On Thursday, the Houthis seized the port city of Mokha and by Friday had taken control of the town of Dhubab and the island of Perim, Yemeni government sources told the news agency Reuters. Mokha, Dhubab and Perim had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's government. All three are strategically located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

With Iran having blockaded the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become increasingly important as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports. As the Houthis are aligned with Iran, control of and potential attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives Iran additional leverage in its war with the United States.

The government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced on Thursday that troops were reorganizing and consolidating their defenses in Mokha in coordination with other anti-Houthi forces.

The conflict has also spilled into Saudi Arabia, a close US ally and regional rival of Iran's. This week, the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four cities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia responded with dozens of airstrikes across four Yemeni provinces.

"This is actually a full-scale war," Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "It hasn't been given that name yet but we are marching there full time," Al-Muslimi said.

Houthis 'much stronger'

The latest escalation, which started in July, ended a period of relative calm after years of war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to support Yemen's government in 2015 following the 2014 Houthi insurgency. The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and the Saudi-backed government ended in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce. However, the country remains de facto split.

The Houthis control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and most of the country's north, as well as parts of the center, and now also much of the western coastal stretch, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim. The internationally recognized government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council, is based in Aden. Many senior officials operate from Saudi Arabia. Government-aligned forces control parts of the south and east, while tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.

The political landscape was further fragmented in December, when secessionists backed by the Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), seized areas in the south and east. The fallout between Saudi Arabia, which aims to keep Yemen united, and the UAE-backed secessionists ended with the termination of Yemen's joint defense pact with the UAE and the withdrawal of Emirati forces from the country. The STC was dissolved in January.

Elham Manea, the director of the Middle Eastern and Gulf Studies Research Competence Area at the Institute of Political Science at the University of Zurich, told DW that the current situation is very different from that of 2015. "The Houthi movement is militarily and institutionally much stronger," Manea said, "while the camp opposing it, that is, the internationally recognized government, remains more fragmented."

The Houthis targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and said Riyadh retaliated across four provinces in Yemen Image: Al Masirah/REUTERS

What's Pakistan's role?

Manea said Saudi Arabia had changed its approach. In 2015, Riyadh joined the war in support of Yemen's ousted government. "Now, it is providing greater military, technical and logistical support to the internationally recognized government and forces aligned with it," Manea said.

The key question is whether Saudi Arabia is preparing for a war aimed at defeating the Houthi group or seeking to change the military balance, restore deterrence and eventually negotiate from a stronger position.

"At present, I consider the second scenario more likely," Manea said.

Al-Muslimi offered a similar view: "The Saudis would like to avoid war at any cost."

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has not yet been invoked. Reuters reported on Thursday that Pakistani officials said no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed, but the government would act when the time came.

Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based political consultancy Azure Strategy, told DW that she doubts Pakistan would join the conflict directly. "But the escalation in Yemen will increasingly test its ability to stay out," Gower said. "Islamabad does not want to antagonize neighboring Iran," she added, "and will try to preserve its role as a mediator, while meeting its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia through intelligence, advice and other forms of military support short of direct participation."

Thousands of civilians fled their homes this week, while nearly 200 were killed in the fighting, according to international bodies Image: AFP

Humanitarian toll rises

Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy to Yemen, said the country was facing the "harsh reality" of a return to war.

The UN Development Programme estimated that 377,000 people had died as a result of Yemen's conflict between 2014 and late 2021. Of these, approximately 154,000 deaths were directly caused by combat and violence.

The current conflict has already killed nearly 200 people, according to the World Health Organization. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) also warned that around 18,500 people have been displaced. "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's chief of mission, said in a statement. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before," he said. "Every time fighting flares up, they lose whatever little they had managed to rebuild."

This view is echoed by Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. "When you have a country in which nearly two-thirds of people are in need of aid, any additional precarity and displacement will have a real civilian cost," she said.

"Thousands of civilians were killed in the fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis between 2014 and 2022, and warring parties repeatedly demonstrated extreme disregard for civilian life," she said. "The renewed fighting now threatens to repeat the devastating civilian casualty events of the earlier years of the war," she added.

World.title: Germany charges 7 suspected Hamas members over attack plot
World.content:
Prosecutors say the suspects had moved beyond general preparations and were already pursuing a concrete plan for a deadly attack on Israeli or Jewish targets.

German federal prosecutors on Friday charged seven suspected members of the Islamist militant group Hamas.

The men allegedly plotted to carry out a deadly attack on Israeli or Jewish targets in Germany or Austria.

What are the charges?

The men are accused of helping procure weapons, membership in a foreign terrorist organization, and taking part in preparations for act of violence endangering the state, the Federal Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said on Friday.

Investigators believe the suspects, who were arrested in Germany and abroad over recent months, were already pursuing a concrete attack plan.

The men are accused of helping obtain guns and ammunition for an attack targeting representatives of Israel, Jewish people or people regarded as pro-Israel.

The plot allegedly became concrete by July 2025 and was intended to take place on the second anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel.

Prosecutors say that one of the suspects recorded a video claiming responsibility in advance and announcing the planned attack in the name of Hamas.

How Europe, the US can better protect Jewish communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

All seven men also face weapons charges, while three are additionally accused of violating Germany's War Weapons Control Act.

What weapons had allegedly been obtained?

By the time three of the suspects were arrested in Berlin on October 1, 2025, prosecutors say the group had obtained:

one functioning fully automatic rifle

13 functioning handguns

more than 700 rounds of ammunition

Part of the arsenal was allegedly moved to Vienna and stored there by another suspect who is being prosecuted separately.

According to prosecutors, all seven belonged to Hamas and several were tasked by senior Hamas officials with securing the weapons.

The suspects were arrested between October 2025 and May 2026 and remain in pre-trial detention.

Another alleged participant, Mohammed A., was arrested in London on November 3, 2025, at the request of German authorities.

He has not yet been transferred to Germany and is being prosecuted separately.
