World.title: No puedo hacer frente a la derrama para la instalación del ascensor. ¿Pueden embargar mi casa? ¿Podría no usarlo para no pagar?
World.content:
Pregunta. En el edificio donde vivo la comunidad de propietarios ha decidido la instalación de un ascensor, pero me encuentro en la situación de no tener recursos para hacer frente a la derrama. ¿Pueden embargar mi vivienda? ¿Puedo solicitar que no me den acceso al ascensor a cambio de no pagar? C. Manuel F.

Respuesta. Los acuerdos válidamente adoptados por la junta de vecinos son obligatorios para todos los propietarios, tal y como establece el artículo 17.9 de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal.

En el caso de aprobarse la instalación de un ascensor, el pago de las cantidades correspondientes deberá realizarse en los términos acordados por la junta y reflejados en el acta. Asimismo, la comunidad de propietarios puede reclamar judicialmente el abono de las cantidades pendientes, ya sean gastos ordinarios o extraordinarios. Para ello, puede acudir al procedimiento monitorio y, si no logra cobrar la deuda mediante cuentas bancarias u otros bienes del deudor, podría solicitar el embargo de la vivienda y, en último término, su subasta para satisfacer el importe adeudado.

Este es el marco legal aplicable. No obstante, la ley no impide que los propietarios alcancen acuerdos específicos. Como hemos indicado, las cantidades deben abonarse conforme a lo acordado por la junta y recogido en el acta. Por ello, es perfectamente posible que la propia junta apruebe un calendario de pagos distinto, más amplio o flexible, para aquellos propietarios que no puedan asumir las cuotas en las mismas condiciones que el resto.

En cuanto a la posibilidad de eximir a un propietario del pago de la instalación del ascensor a cambio de limitar su uso, la ley tampoco prohíbe expresamente este tipo de acuerdos. Sin embargo, su redacción y ejecución exigen una especial precisión. En ese caso, el acuerdo debería reflejarse de forma detallada en el acta, recogiendo tanto la aprobación de la instalación como la excepción aplicable al propietario afectado y las condiciones concretas de dicha limitación. Por ejemplo, debería especificarse si el ascensor no tendrá parada en una determinada planta, si no se facilitará llave o sistema de acceso al propietario excluido, si la limitación podrá levantarse mediante el pago de determinadas cantidades o cualquier otra circunstancia necesaria para evitar interpretaciones o conflictos futuros.

Este tipo de acuerdo sería válido en el ámbito interno de la comunidad de propietarios. No obstante, para que pueda producir efectos frente a futuros adquirentes de la vivienda es necesario acceder al Registro de la Propiedad.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Un arcoíris de sal en el corazón de Cabo de Gata
World.content:
Una visita guiada por las salinas de este parque natural en Almería permite conocer la cosecha del mineral y, de paso, adentrarse en un entorno con una biodiversidad impresionante y en paisajes desérticos

La magia se produce al caer la noche. El agua del mar, embalsada durante días y calentada por el sol, disminuye entonces su temperatura con rapidez. Sobre su superficie, cuando todos duermen, nace una fina lámina salada que se cosecha con delicadeza al amanecer. Nace así la flor de sal, una exquisitez por su valor gastronómico y organoléptico. La llamativa transformación ocurre en paisajes sorprendentes como las salinas de Cabo de Gata, una extensión de 400 hectáreas de terrenos inundables junto al desierto de Almería que, desde la primavera de 2025, se puede visitar. Además de conocer la extracción de este mineral e incluso recogerlo, la ruta permite disfrutar de la elegancia de los flamencos y adentrarse, acompañados de la singular salicornia, en la historia de uno de los parques naturales más asombrosos de la geografía ibérica. “Es un lugar increíble”, confirma Arantxa Roldán, guía en este territorio marciano.

Para llegar hasta las salinas hay que atravesar, primero, un bosque de pitas y ramblas donde un puñado de heroicos árboles resisten en una tierra seca que parece gritar por una gota más, un último sorbito para sobrevivir a la sequía y el calor. Son las condiciones a las que se adapta el azufaifo, joya botánica “fácil de ver gracias a los senderos públicos cercanos al centro de visitantes de Las Almoladeras”, cuenta el director del parque natural Cabo de Gata-Níjar, Salvador Parra, quien recomienda allí una parada para hacerse una idea sobre el ecosistema formado por la Sierra de Gata y su orla costera de charcos salinos. Desde ellos llegan los ecos de los flamencos rosados que se pueden avistar desde el mirador junto al pueblo de El Cabo, donde arranca una línea de mar totalmente recta que, más de seis kilómetros después, llega hasta el Arrecife de las Sirenas y sus curiosas formaciones volcánicas.

Vista de las salinas de Cabo de Gata, una extensión de 400 hectáreas de terrenos inundables. Nacho Sánchez

El paisaje huele al salitre que llega con la brisa marina. En las dunas crece la siempre viva, el narciso marítimo y un insólito azafrán local de llamativa floración invernal a ras de suelo. Es un terreno plano, donde solo levantan las viejas sierras volcánicas de color oscuro, pero también una enorme y blanca pirámide. Es una garbera, una forma de almacenar la sal al aire libre. En este rincón almeriense espera a su exportación, por barco, al norte de Europa, donde se usa para quitar el hielo de las carreteras. Es el principal destino de las alrededor de 40.000 toneladas anuales —sin tratar— que se extraen en estas salinas, aunque también se utilizan para piscinas, salazones cárnicos y consumo humano. De flor de sal, su mejor versión, son unas 17 toneladas al mes. De cerca, brilla. “Y parece más salada”, dice, entre risas, José Luis Díaz Segovia, uno de los visitantes. Tiene razón, porque por estructura y pureza, tiene un sabor más intenso.

De los romanos al cine

El poblado para trabajadores de las salinas que hay junto a la playa. Nacho Sánchez

“Este humedal tiene más de 2,6 millones de años de historia, pero la explotación salina no arrancó hasta la época romana”, relata Roldán en los primeros minutos de la visita. Fueron ellos quienes, según subraya la guía, construyeron los casi seis kilómetros de canales que permiten que el agua del mar se concentre en más de un centenar de balsas. A principios del siglo XX, una familia catalana, Costa, se hizo cargo de la explotación y construyó el pequeño poblado que hay junto a la playa, con una treintena de viviendas donde residían los salineros y hoy lo hacen sus descendientes. En él destaca, alta y de perfil erosionado, la iglesia de San Miguel de las Salinas y el antiguo cine, que ocupaba un sencillo edificio de madera. En los años noventa, la salina pasó a manos del Grupo Molins, de capital francés, que tiene instalaciones similares en el Puerto de Santa María y Torrevieja. Y que en abril de 2025 decidió impulsar las visitas guiadas a pie por este entorno salado.

Arantxa Roldán, guía en las salinas del Cabo de Gata, en un momento de la visita. Nacho Sánchez

El agua va y viene por los canales al dictado de los técnicos de la compañía: gracias a las esclusas, mueven miles de litros a su antojo con facilidad. La cosecha de sal se realiza entre mayo y septiembre por un equipo de una treintena de empleados que cubren cada centímetro de su piel para evitar el impacto del sol. Ya no lo hacen a mano y con bueyes, sino con herramientas y camiones. Da igual. Las balsas de evaporación siguen hipnotizando con sus colores. Desde los tonos azulados clásicos de las zonas con menos concentración salina hasta las tonalidades moradas y lilas gracias a bacterias y microalgas. Son más llamativas en los cristalizadores, esteros más pequeños donde hay hasta 300 gramos por litro. El arcoíris se completa con el verde de la salicornia, especie vegetal apreciada en gastronomía que aquí se deja en paz. Más allá, los prismáticos permiten ver las tonalidades rosas de los portentosos flamencos y unas pequeñas cigüeñuelas que aletean a toda velocidad.

Un visitante en las salinas de Cago de Gata. Nacho Sánchez

La ruta a pie dura alrededor de una hora. La versión más sencilla cuesta 10 euros, pero hay otras opciones que permiten desde recolectar flor de sal (45 euros) hasta vivir experiencias gastronómicas o celebrar catas durante la caída del sol. Es un atardecer que el fotógrafo almeriense Javier Lozano conoce bien porque lleva disfrutándolo, a pie de playa, desde su infancia. “Pasar la tarde en esa zona del Cabo de Gata es único” reconoce este enamorado de las salinas y de todo el parque natural. “Hay pocos sitios en el Mediterráneo donde mires a tu lado y no veas edificios. Y este es uno de ellos”, afirma quien también celebra la luz, azulada en las mañanas, cálida en las tardes, única cuando hay calima. “Hay un toque africano muy especial. Entiendes que estás viendo algo distinto y no sabes ni qué es, pero se nota en cómo se refleja en el mar, en los edificios. Por eso el cine ha venido tanto a Almería”, destaca quien celebra el agua cristalina y de gran salinidad que hay en este litoral. En el entorno de las salinas, de hecho, se han rodado series recientes como Entre Tierras o La Casa de Papel, ficciones que intentan, sin éxito, superar esta realidad.

World.title: Cabinet to stop employers docking foreign workers’ pay for rent
World.content:
Employers will no longer be allowed to deduct rent from foreign workers’ minimum wage from July 2028, social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has told parliament.

Under current rules, employers and agencies can withhold up to 25% of the minimum wage – around €144 a week – to cover accommodation, provided the housing is certified.

The scheme is used mainly for the estimated 600,000 to 900,000 foreign workers in the Netherlands, most of them from Poland, Romania, Hungary and Ukraine, who work in meat processing, distribution centres and greenhouses.

Research by the ministry found employers regularly deduct the full 25% even when the quality of the housing does not justify it, Vijlbrief wrote in a letter to parliament on Thursday.

He said employers are using the deductions as a “business model” and told Nieuwsuur that too many people are being exploited.

Employers will still be able to provide housing, but will have to charge for it separately and at a fair price, the minister said. Ending deductions will also make it easier for inspectors to check whether workers are actually being paid minimum wage, he said.

The decision is the cabinet’s third on the issue in little over a year. Eddy van Hijum, former social affairs minister, proposed phasing out the deductions from January 2026, but his successor Mariëlle Paul of the VVD reversed that decision, arguing that workers would struggle to find housing without employer involvement.

Trade union federation FNV called the move a “perverse profit model at the expense of migrant workers”, and parliament has twice voted for the deductions to go.

Vijlbrief acknowledged that the ban will mean foreign workers will have to find their own accommodation amid the housing crisis. As a result, the ban will come with a rent protection bill, which has yet to reach parliament. Both are scheduled for July 1, 2028.

The measure is part of a wider package to tackle the exploitation of foreign workers, including a ban on temp agency staff in the meat industry, also from mid-2028. A long-delayed licensing system for staffing agencies is set to take effect in 2027.

World.title: Cabinet backs EU-wide minimum age for social media
World.content:

The government has backed an EU-wide minimum age for social media, ahead of proposals from Brussels expected next week.

The Netherlands and Spain have sent joint proposals to the European Commission calling for a single minimum age across the bloc, with privacy-friendly age checks.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is expected to outline how the bloc can can limit social media by children in her annual State of the Union speech to the European Parliament next Wednesday.

“In the physical world we do not accept that products are unsafe for children,” junior digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts (D66) said in a statement. “The same standard must apply online.”

D66, VVD and CDA agreed in their coalition agreement to push for an enforceable European minimum age of 15. The joint paper with Spain does not name an age, but Aerdts told broadcaster NOS that 15 remains the Dutch position.

Australia became the first country in the world to bar under-16s from platforms such as Facebook and Instagram in December 2025. France’s ban on under-15s took effect this month, and the UK has announced a ban on under-16s from 2027.

The proposal faces criticism, including from privacy advocates worried about how age verification would work in practice.

Brussels unveiled an age-check app in April, but a security researcher demonstrated a way to bypass it within hours of the launch, and the commission had to issue a patch.

World.title: Feyenoord bans 47 fans over Cambuur fireworks barrage
World.content:
Feyenoord has banned 47 supporters from De Kuip stadium over the fireworks barrage that injured seven Cambuur fans during last month’s match in Leeuwarden, the club said on Friday.

The 47 have also had their away-match cards blocked and have been reported to football association KNVB for a nationwide stadium ban.

The bans follow several weeks of investigation, including video footage analysis. They include the people who set off the fireworks and those who are accused of coordinating the attacks. Many reportedly held up banners or hid beneath them to avoid the cameras.

“It cannot be ruled out that criminal proceedings will follow in due course,” the club said. Any further action on a national ban would then be decided by the KNVB on the basis of information from the public prosecution department.

Seven home supporters suffered burns, eye injuries and hearing damage when fireworks were fired from the away section towards the pitch and the home stands in the 12th minute of the August 23 game, which Feyenoord went on to win 5-2 after a 20-minute stoppage.

Feyenoord general manager Robert Eenhoorn described the incident as “simply terrible”. The club did not take supporters to its subsequent away games at NEC Nijmegen and PEC Zwolle, and Cambuur barred visiting fans for its home match against FC Twente before lifting the restriction.

World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Belgian police have arrested three suspects in an ongoing investigation into an international horse meat fraud ring, and carried out raids at 24 locations, including seven in the Netherlands.

According to the Belgian Federal Police, a horse trader in East Flanders was at the centre of a ring which faked passport and microchip information to export horses used in racing for slaughter.

European regulations stipulate that animals destined for a slaughterhouse must be fitted with a microchip that tracks, among other things, whether or not they have been treated with medication.

An investigation by Belgian authorities revealed a large number of horses exported from Ireland to mainland Europe had modified or manipulated microchips.

During the raids, more than 1,000 horses were checked and many were seized. Police also confiscated electronics and more than €100,000 in cash.

The operation was carried out with the assistance of Europol, together with Dutch, French and Irish authorities.

In 2013, the Netherlands was embroiled in a horse meat scandal after it was found in products said to be 100% beef in Britain, Sweden, Ireland and Poland. The Netherlands is a major processor of horse meat imported from abroad.

World.title: Van Weel accused of neo-colonialism in Bolle Jos extradition row
World.content:
Sierra Leone’s chief minister has accused Dutch justice minister David van Weel of “neo-colonialism” after he appeared on a national television show to demand the extradition of fugitive drugs lord Jos “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers.

Van Weel spoke by video link from The Hague on broadcaster AYV’s State of the Nation programme on Wednesday, saying that the Netherlands had lodged a formal extradition request more than a year ago but no progress had been made.

Leijdekkers is suspected of hiding in Sierra Leone after footage of him at a church service with the president surfaced online last year. It’s alleged he is in a relationship with the president’s daughter and has a child with her.

Major drug shipments passing through West African ports are also suspected to be orchestrated by Leijdekkers’ organisation, including the biggest cocaine shipment ever seized earlier this year, and last week a 4,000 tonne seizure in France that had sailed from Ghana.

“Show the pictures”

Sierra Leonean minister David Moinina Sengeh, the president’s most senior official, responded on the same programme, saying the pressure the Netherlands was putting on the country was “scandalous” and amounted to “neo-colonialism.”

Sierra Leone is an independent country, he said, and Van Weel should stop appearing on television and threatening to cut EU aid – adding that the country did not live on European money, Nieuwsuur reported.

“Hand on heart, our security intelligence does not know where Leijdekkers is,” Sengeh said. “We cannot go by what these guys are saying or what some people are using others to say. If they know, show the pictures.”

Sengeh also accused the Netherlands of double standards, saying Freetown had twice asked The Hague to extradite a political activist and social media commentator known as Adebayor, who lives in the Netherlands and whom Sierra Leone accuses of inciting violence during riots there in 2022.

“We sent the attorney-general there. We sent the foreign affairs minister there,” he said. “They refused extradition. Have they given us that due respect to come?”

Van Weel: “ridiculous”

Van Weel told Nieuwsuur in Dutch that the neo-colonialism accusation was “ridiculous” and that the fierce reaction showed his strategy was working. He said he had not yet received a call from Freetown indicating any acceleration of the extradition process.

The interview is the latest step in a pressure campaign that has escalated since the spring. In June, Van Weel asked the EU to halt development aid to Sierra Leone, worth €352 million for the 2021 to 2027 period, though the request has so far failed to win support from other member states. In July he travelled to Ghana to build a coalition of West African countries to lean on Freetown.

Leijdekkers has been sentenced in absentia in the Netherlands and Belgium to terms Van Weel says total around 80 years.

World.title: Cardiologists in Amsterdam and Nijmegen raided over corruption
World.content:
National fraud investigation service FIOD has raided the homes of six cardiologists in Amsterdam and Nijmegen on suspicion of corruption, and property worth at least €1.5 million has been seized, current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported on Friday.

The FIOD believes the doctors took money from medical supply companies, under the guise of research funding, in exchange for giving those suppliers better deals. The money may have been pocketed by the doctors and funnelled through holding companies, the FIOD said.

The raids were announced on Thursday but no details were given as to which hospitals were involved, only that they were in Noord-Holland and Gelderland. Eight addresses were searched but nobody was arrested.

Nieuwsuur and research platform Investico identified the doctors through land registry records. Two work at the OLVG hospital in Amsterdam; the other four were, until recently, at the CWZ hospital in Nijmegen.

Long-running row

The Nijmegen doctors were sacked by the CWZ last year after a dispute over money. The hospital said in May 2025 they had taken €2.7 million in “sponsorship” from medical suppliers over five years, at a time when it was buying equipment from the same companies.

The FIOD has not said whether that dispute is connected to its investigation.

Zwolle

In 2022 the FIOD raided the homes of five cardiologists at the Isala hospital in Zwolle who were suspected of taking €3.2 million from a German pacemaker maker. Waiting lists there more than doubled after two of the doctors were suspended. That case has still not come to court.

Later that year Nieuwsuur found dozens of cardiologists were taking millions from device makers without their hospitals knowing. The FIOD says tips from within the medical sector and media reports prompted the new investigation.

Neither hospital had responded to a request for comment on Friday.

World.title: All you need is a Beatles lyric, TU Delft researchers find
World.content:
Researchers at TU Delft have found Beatles lyrics and song titles in more than 3,000 titles of scientific articles, according to a new paper in the open-access journal PLOS One.

Gabriel Budel and Rob Kooij of TU Delft teamed up with Michiel Tjepkema, co-host of the Dutch Beatles podcast Fab4Cast, to look for the lyrics here, there and everywhere across the scientific disciplines.

They identified 2,237 exact references and 963 examples of creative wordplay in data from the academic database Scopus.

The most used songs were “The Long and Winding Road” (798 mentions), “With a Little Help from My Friends” (209) and “Here, There and Everywhere” (129). The most cited paper was “Attention is all you need”, the 2017 paper that introduced the architecture behind ChatGPT – and a play on “All You Need Is Love”.

According to Budel, it’s not all too much. “Some of these are genuinely brilliant. ‘The lung and winding road’ is a paper on long Covid that changes one vowel,” he said in a statement.

The undertaking was not a hard day’s night. The team used a large language model to identify the lyrics, but they couldn’t just let it be. “The three of us then went through every selected title by hand to determine if it really was a Beatles pun,” Budel said.

The group didn’t stop until they got enough. They also found lyrics from Michael Jackson and Elvis Presley, though far fewer than the Beatles.

The researchers weren’t all shook up by their findings. Pop culture references can help reach a wider audience and improve readability, they said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices. Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Bratysława ⤵️ Polska i grupa #V4 nie pozwoli na żadne zmiany i na żadne propozycje instytucji europejskich, czy innych państw, które mogłyby wpłynąć na pogorszenie sytuacji energetycznej w naszych państwach. Ceny energii w tym regionie muszą spaść. pic.twitter.com/BFnRx8Clse — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 10, 2026 In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry. They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings. “Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin. “Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.” Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system. “We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said. According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS). The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”. The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament. While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system. In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies. Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path. They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position. Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind. In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time. Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal. Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Nevertheless, Braun’s party, Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), continues to enjoy support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years, for statements he made suggesting that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are "fake" https://t.co/PCssZt5eXD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 25, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. However, “a red line has [now] been crossed”, he added, quoted by news website Interia. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. Infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak later confirmed that they were working on “radical” measures to toughen penalties for those who violate the rules at rail crossings. He revealed that one proposal being considered is suspending for three months the licence of any driver who ignores red lights at rail crossings. However, critics noted that the ministry had already announced such plans in July 2025, and had failed to implement them since then. – Chcemy wprowadzić przepis, na podstawie którego każdy kierowca, który wjedzie na przejazd drogowo-kolejowy kiedy jest zapalone czerwone światło, straci prawo jazdy, zostanie mu ono zatrzymane na trzy miesiące. However, 24% of Poland’s accidents took place at rail crossings, compared to 16% in Germany. In total, Poland had by far the highest number of deaths caused by accidents at rail crossings (45), ahead of Germany (26), France (20) and Hungary (18). When taking into account the size of countries’ rail networks, Poland had 4.3 rail deaths (from all causes, not just accidents at crossings) per thousand kilometres of track, which was the fifth-highest figure in the EU, behind Portugal (6.2), Hungary (5.8), Slovakia (5.7) and Lithuania (4.6). Last week, in dramatic scenes captured on camera, a train carrying almost 300 passengers hit a truck at a rail crossing in Gdańsk, luckily resulting in no injuries. World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek… — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026 On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade. “Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.” “We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation, including DiNanno, was in Poland this week to discuss potential locations for the base. World.title: “We remember where Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” says Polish FM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
