World.title: Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Commission did not open proceedings against Pashinyan
World.content:
Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

The Corruption Prevention Commission refused to open administrative proceedings against Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. Commission members said the complaint contained no “obvious signs of violations of the code of conduct”.

Semyon Babayan, head of the human rights NGO Public Informant, had asked the commission to assess the prime minister’s alleged “violations of the code of conduct”.

“Pashinyan’s public rhetoric and the wording he often uses grossly violate the legally established integrity system and the ethical standards that public officials must follow,” the applicant said.

He presented the commission with 11 such examples. One of them was the word “immoral”, which the prime minister used to describe the Catholicos of All Armenians.

According to the human rights activist, “it insults the feelings of believers and violates the requirement for religious neutrality”.

However, the commission found that the wording remained within the permissible limits of freedom of expression.

For a long time, Nikol Pashinyan has demanded that Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II step down. He claims that the Catholicos has broken his vow of celibacy and has a daughter. The prime minister also believes that the Catholicos has links to foreign intelligence services and follows their orders. On 24 August, Nikol Pashinyan called the Catholicos “immoral” while speaking in parliament. He also referred to the Patriarch by his secular name, Ktrich Nersisyan. He has used this name for him since launching his campaign to reform the Church. In protest, opposition MPs banged on their desks every time the Catholicos’s name was mentioned. “Your Catholicos is immoral. If you are not bothered by the fact that the man who heads the Mother See is sexually active, then keep banging your desks as much as you like. There is no other way to have a child — even in the Church. There is only one way to have a child: sexual intercourse,” Pashinyan said.

Commission says the word “immoral” falls within the bounds of political speech

The commission commented on the use of the word “immoral” against the Catholicos, citing case law from the European Court of Human Rights. It stressed that political speech enjoys a broader scope of protection.

Commission members assessed the prime minister’s wording as falling within what is permissible in the context of political debate:

“The use of exaggeration, generalisations and even shocking or striking expressions is characteristic of political speech during political debates — in this case, a speech delivered from the parliamentary rostrum.”

They also noted that, according to the European Court of Human Rights, freedom of expression covers not only positive and favourable statements, but also those that may “offend, shock or disturb”.

The Corruption Prevention Commission therefore concluded that the prime minister’s statement should be considered in the broader context of political debate.

The decision also gives the meaning of the Armenian word “պիղծ”, which Pashinyan used, citing academician Eduard Aghayan’s Explanatory Dictionary of the Modern Armenian Language. It notes that the word primarily means “unclean, immoral, vicious”, while in a religious context it means “heretical, unacceptable, ungodly”.

As for the statement “your Patriarch is immoral”, commission members found no attack on the faith or a religious group. In their view, Pashinyan made an “assessment of the alleged conduct” of a specific member of the clergy:

“Pashinyan’s statement sought to criticise not the person, but a specific phenomenon — namely, the alleged violation of the vow of celibacy.”

The commission also stressed that the word “immoral” carries a negative connotation but “does not cross the line into vulgarity or profanity”. Its members also found no calls for violence or threats in Pashinyan’s speech.

According to the decision, the prime minister’s speech was “predominantly critical in nature, as is characteristic of political debate”.

What other violations did the human rights activist identify?

Semyon Babayan also told the commission about 10 other “serious violations” that he believes the prime minister had committed:

“Violation of the principle of separation of powers: a public statement that ‘there is no judge who would not do what I tell them to do’, which directly undermines the independence of the judiciary and trust in democratic institutions.

Use of offensive language: using crude, street-level rhetoric in public against opponents or citizens — conduct that is clearly incompatible with the ethics expected of a senior public official.

Unsubstantiated assessments and ‘back-of-the-envelope estimates’: arbitrarily citing percentages related to corruption and bribery, such as 70% or 100%, without referring to official or verified factual data.

Erosion of public trust: using threats and divisive rhetoric from a high state platform, which contributes to the spread of intolerance.

Threats to ‘smear [people] across the asphalt’: publicly calling for the use of force in a personalised and punitive manner, outside the framework of legal procedures.

The phrase ‘whimpering judges’: humiliating members of the judiciary and systematically discrediting the institution.

Statements that citizens would be ‘brought to their knees’ because of their political views: entrenching a culture of communication based on force and a commanding tone that is unbecoming of a statesman.

Segregation of fellow citizens by labelling them ‘persons of Armenian origin’: violating the principle of national unity and artificially dividing society.

Showing preferential treatment towards members of his own team: violating the principle of equal integrity standards for the sake of political expediency.

Erosion of the integrity and image of a public official: maintaining a marginal, sarcastic and aggressive tone in public debate, undermining the duty of a public official to set an example of appropriate conduct.”

The commission found no signs of an obvious violation in any of the examples cited.

Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

World.title: Property prices in Armenia rise again: new wave of emigration from Russia and other factors
World.content:
Armenia is seeing another wave of people relocating to the country, amid reports over the past two months of a possible mobilisation in Russia. As a result, both rents and property prices have risen again. On average, prices for rentals and properties for sale have increased by 20%.

At one point, prices were rising almost every day. This was evident from listings on popular online property sales and rental platforms. The biggest boom has been in the rental market. Activity is also increasing in cities near Yerevan, including Abovyan, Masis and Nor Hachn.

Most of those arriving are Armenians who had been living in Russia. They say they are moving to avoid being called up for military service and because of the uncertainty they have faced in recent months.

Amid the large influx, it has become difficult to find affordable and mid-range rental properties. This is also linked to students from the regions moving to the capital as the new academic year begins.

A Russian man found a job but cannot find a flat

Dmitry Popov arrived in Armenia with friends three weeks ago. They first stayed in Yerevan, then moved to Lori Province, where they found jobs in the towns of Alaverdi and Tumanyan.

He decided to stay in Yerevan, where he has acquaintances who offered him a place to stay. He has already found a job as a courier with one of Yerevan’s companies. He is now negotiating his pay with his employer. Meanwhile, Dmitry has been looking for a one- or two-bedroom flat in the outer districts of the capital. He cannot afford a place in the city centre because rents there are very high.

“At first, I was looking for a place for up to $500. Now I’m looking for one for $700. I still haven’t found anything because I need basic amenities — furniture and household appliances. Even when I find a flat with an average-quality renovation, it turns out there is no fridge, washing machine or comfortable sofa,” the young man explains.

He knows that the latest influx of migrants from Russia is largely driving the rise in prices.

After the initial influx and surge in prices during the first months of the Russia-Ukraine war, the property market began to stabilise. Prices fell slightly as many Russians returned home or moved to other countries. Now they have risen again.

“To be honest, I really like Yerevan. The city has its own rhythm, an interesting cultural scene, good food, friendly people and convenient public transport. I managed to find a job within a few days. Now I just need to find a flat. If I can’t find one in Yerevan, I’ll look in nearby towns. I’m asking local people how public transport works in the suburbs, what rental options are available and how lively those places are,” Dmitry says.

He says he did not have many options: he could either move to Yerevan or Tbilisi:

“I’ve visited both cities many times and had already been considering moving to one of them before the recent tensions in Russia. My friends who have lived in both cities recommended Yerevan, even though it is more expensive than Tbilisi. They said people in Yerevan are friendly, welcoming towards Russians and willing to help. They also said it would be easier to find a job here. By the way, they also suggested moving to other Armenian cities, such as Gyumri, Dilijan and Vanadzor.”

He says relatives in Russia call him to ask whether they should move to Armenia for the long term. He recommends it, although he also tells them about the problems.

He has already decided that if he manages to earn more in the future, he will buy a one-bedroom flat in Yerevan.

Factors affecting prices

Andranik Harutyunyan, director of Silver REA real estate agency, says apartment rents have risen by around 15% compared with last year. This is an average estimate, as prices vary significantly between different parts of the city and types of apartments.

The same applies to the property sales market. According to the estate agent, it is difficult to establish a single rate of price growth and compare it with last year’s figures:

“It is quite difficult to assess price changes in the primary market because developers sell apartments in residential complexes at different prices depending on the stage of construction. The secondary market is also seeing a noticeable increase in demand.”

Harutyunyan notes that members of the Armenian diaspora are showing greater interest in apartments on the secondary market. For them, buying property is a form of business investment. By renting out a property, they can earn a higher annual return than they would by keeping the same amount of money in a bank.

“Those who moved to Armenia after the Russia-Ukraine war began are also active. Some have been living here for about a year and have decided to settle permanently. Another group consists of people who had ties to Armenia in the past but have now decided to move their businesses and families here.

Interest is also being driven by the growing value placed on property assets in Armenia in recent years. As a result, demand for housing remains high in both the primary and secondary markets,” the real estate agency director says.

Apartment price trends by administrative district

According to data from the Cadastre Committee, property prices continued to rise across all of Yerevan’s administrative districts in the second quarter of 2026. However, the pace of growth varied. The biggest increases came in Nork-Marash, Shengavit and Ajapnyak.

Nork-Marash recorded the sharpest increase, with the average price reaching 553,000 drams ($1,527) per square metre. Compared with last year, this represents a 24% rise.

Apartment prices in Shengavit rose by around 19% over the same period, while prices in Ajapnyak increased by 16%. More construction and relatively affordable prices have helped drive demand in these districts.

Price changes were more moderate in other parts of the city. Growth has been relatively slow in the Small Centre and neighbouring Arabkir, largely because prices there were already high.

Overall, property prices in Yerevan continue to rise. However, the strongest growth is occurring in districts with development potential and relatively more affordable prices.

Property prices in Armenia rise again

World.title: How does Georgia’s parliament work? SJC analyses current legislative processes
World.content:
The Social Justice Center (SJC) analyses the work of Georgia’s 11th Parliament between 25 November 2024 and 26 June 2026. It notes that the parliament’s work has, on the one hand, undermined democratic institutions and rights and, on the other, expanded the executive branch’s discretionary powers and strengthened the centralisation of power.

The organisation’s director, Tamta Mikeladze, published the report’s main findings:

During this period, parliament adopted 276 legislative packages or initiatives. Almost half went through an accelerated procedure, while around 10% followed a simplified procedure. This means parliament adopted around 60% of legislative acts through accelerated or simplified procedures. The executive branch submitted more initiatives than parliament itself, showing that the legislative agenda was largely driven by government initiatives.

Almost half went through an accelerated procedure, while around 10% followed a simplified procedure. This means parliament adopted around 60% of legislative acts through accelerated or simplified procedures. The executive branch submitted more initiatives than parliament itself, showing that the legislative agenda was largely driven by government initiatives. During the same period, the parliament, which was almost entirely made up of members of the ruling Georgian Dream party, did not adopt a single opposition legislative initiative , including those submitted by the Gakharia for Georgia parliamentary party. After Gakharia for Georgia entered parliament, lawmakers formally opposed legislative initiatives in only 38 cases. In all other cases, they adopted the initiatives unanimously.

, including those submitted by the Gakharia for Georgia parliamentary party. After Gakharia for Georgia entered parliament, lawmakers formally opposed legislative initiatives in only 38 cases. In all other cases, they adopted the initiatives unanimously. The quality of the legislative process is also problematic. Explanatory notes generally did not indicate that broad consultations had taken place and often lacked relevant sectoral or comparative legal analysis. Of the 276 initiatives, local or international experts took part in only six cases, while just eight initiatives provided for the harmonisation of Georgian legislation with legal instruments of the Council of Europe, the EU or the UN.

Against this backdrop, the parliament’s work can be divided into several main areas:

● Restrictions on civil society and repressive controls – 7 legislative changes. Alongside the laws on “transparency of foreign influence” and “registration of foreign agents”, parliament amended the law on grants. These changes effectively placed civil society organisations under full state control and criminalised certain forms of their activity. Parliament also created an Agency for the Management of State Grants, restricted NGOs’ participation in state decision-making, tightened the rules for issuing and receiving grants, broadened the legal definition of a grant, and introduced new criminal and financial sanctions.

● Media and freedom of expression – 6 direct changes: rules on foreign funding changed, the Communications Commission gained wider powers, new requirements for broadcast content were introduced, coverage of court proceedings was restricted, and financial oversight mechanisms were strengthened.

● Five separate changes concerned freedom of assembly and expression, increasing administrative and criminal liability for actions related to protests.

● Public service – 8 changes. Institutional safeguards for civil servants were weakened, while political appointments and the discretion of senior officials gained greater importance. The Civil Service Bureau was abolished, and opportunities for employment under administrative contracts were expanded. At the same time, new financial benefits and mechanisms for obtaining permission to engage in certain activities were introduced, with access to them largely dependent on decisions by senior officials. This creates a risk of not only politicisation but also clientelist governance.

● Education and academia also became targets of centralisation. Changes adopted in 2025-2026 strengthened the government’s influence over university funding, student numbers, academic programmes, and the reorganisation and institutional structure of universities. The limited involvement of academics in the process points to a broader problem with academic freedom.

● Ideological and propaganda-related measures – 7 major legislative changes. These included the introduction of a new crime, “treason against the state”; the removal of the term “gender” from legislation; tougher drug policies; changes to labour and immigration rules for foreigners; and expanded mechanisms of state control. What these changes have in common is not only tougher policies in specific areas, but also the incorporation of political and ideological concepts into the legal framework.

It is also important to look not only at what parliament adopted, but at what it left off its agenda. During the reporting period, issues concerning the rights of children and prisoners, public procurement and corruption prevention, environmental protection and civil safety, healthcare, urban planning and construction, education, regional policy, agriculture and tourism were pushed into the background or postponed. As a result, parliament’s agenda was clearly dominated by restrictive and controlling legislation. At the same time, its positive legislative agenda, covering a broad range of public interests, was significantly weakened.

Tamta Mikeladze: “The parliament’s work is therefore, on the one hand, directed against democratic institutions and rights, while on the other, it strengthens the executive branch’s discretionary powers and centralisation.

The theoretical frameworks of ‘autocratic legalism’ and ‘sham law’ are important for describing this process. In such a system, a law may formally meet the technical requirements of a legal act, but it loses its primary function: limiting state power and reducing arbitrariness. The law no longer acts as a mechanism for constraining power. Instead, it becomes a tool for maintaining and consolidating power.

In short, Georgia’s process of autocratisation, after years of oscillating between hybrid democracy and hybrid authoritarianism, is now aggressively and systematically affecting the legal sphere itself for the first time. It is fundamentally changing the law’s substance and nature.

We still have no adequate understanding of how difficult it will be to rehabilitate the state, political system, legal system and society after the crisis and the authoritarian period that Georgian Dream has inflicted on them.”

On legislation in Georgia

World.title: Georgian blogger says Interior Ministry wants to punish him for insulting Russian propagandists
World.content:
Civil rights activist and blogger Tornike Razmadze says Georgia’s Interior Ministry has summoned him to court to impose a fine or administrative detention because he insulted Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov in response to their insults against Georgian King Erekle II.

Georgia’s recently established Hate Speech Unit at the Interior Ministry has accused Razmadze of violating Article 166, Part 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The provision covers swearing in a public place and carries a fine of 500 to 3,000 lari ($185–1,110) or administrative detention for up to 20 days.

According to the activist, the case concerns a video he posted several weeks ago in which Russian propagandists discussed Erekle II, calling him a “king who crawled on his knees”. Margarita Simonyan, in particular, claimed that King Erekle had begged the Russians for help “on his knees” and that modern Georgians would likewise get down on their knees and ask Russia to take them under its protection.

Tornike Razmadze explains that this was why he used obscene language against Simonyan and Solovyov — more precisely, against their mothers.

According to the blogger, Simonyan and Solovyov effectively insulted the ruling Georgian Dream party as well. What angers him most is that, instead of taking offence at the Russian propagandists, the government wants to punish the person who insulted them. Razmadze sees this message from the authorities as the most important aspect of the whole case.

The activist also appealed to Georgia’s Public Defender (Ombudsman):

“I am not asking you for protection or support. I have one simple request: record your position on the case opened against me. I simply want to hear your position.”

However, the Interior Ministry’s Hate Speech Unit said the case had nothing to do with kings or propagandists. It said Tornike Razmadze was accused of insulting Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

“Insulting comments on social media by citizen Tornike Razmadze and Anna Bdeyan directed at Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze were identified. Administrative proceedings have been launched against them under Articles 166 and 173,” the Interior Ministry said.

The blogger’s lawyer, Mikheil Zakareishvili, in turn, says the Interior Ministry deliberately added Article 173, which concerns insulting a public official, to the charges. He says the original reports did not contain such wording. The lawyer is convinced that the case was opened specifically because of the insults directed at Simonyan and Solovyov.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) considers the case against Razmadze another example of restrictions on freedom of expression. The association says prosecuting people over statements made on social media violates their fundamental constitutional rights and freedom of expression.

What is the Hate Speech Unit

The new Hate Speech Unit at Georgia’s Interior Ministry began operating on 1 June 2026. According to the ministry, its main task is to identify public statements that demean human dignity or are offensive and may constitute administrative offences.

Over the past three months, the unit has fined dozens of people. Vakhtang Sanaya, a journalist and presenter on Formula TV, became the first person to receive a two-week administrative detention sentence. Activist Giorgi Akhobadze also received a one-month detention sentence for a Facebook post.

World.title: Russian Orthodox Church calls on pilgrims to ‘boycott’ New Athos Monastery in Abkhazia
World.content:
The Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) has called on pilgrims not to visit the New Athos Monastery in Abkhazia.

The ROC considers the monastery’s abbot, Father Dorotheus, a schismatic.

However, this did not stop Sergei Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff of the Russian presidential administration and the Kremlin’s point man for Abkhazia, from visiting the monastery.

The Moscow Patriarchate’s chancellor, Metropolitan Grigory, has sent a circular letter to all bishops of the Russian Orthodox Church warning that Russian pilgrims must not attend services at the New Athos Monastery. The services there are led by defrocked hieromonk Dorotheus (Dbar).

“We are concerned about cases in which Orthodox pilgrims from dioceses of the Russian Orthodox Church visit the New Athos Monastery and take part in services held there. Pilgrims often go to confession and receive communion there without knowing that they should not.

I ask you to take measures to ensure that pilgrims travelling to holy sites in Abkhazia with your blessing are always informed that they must not engage in prayer or Eucharistic communion with the monk Dorotheus. They should also be informed that the sacraments performed in schism have no spiritual grace,” Metropolitan Grigory wrote.

Archimandrite Dorotheus

Archimandrite Dorotheus heads the Holy Metropolis of Abkhazia, one of two unrecognised Orthodox churches operating in the republic. A graduate of Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and a doctor of theology, he is highly popular in Abkhaz society and well known in church circles.

His “rival” is Father Vissarion, who heads the Abkhazian Orthodox Church (AOC). He is the only serving Abkhaz cleric ordained by the Georgian Orthodox Church during the Soviet era. Despite its unrecognised status, the AOC enjoys the active support of the Russian Orthodox Church.

The ROC, by contrast, has opposed Archimandrite Dorotheus and officially defrocked him in 2023 for refusing to submit to its authority.

The Holy Metropolis of Abkhazia and the AOC have been engaged in a long-running and bitter conflict.

Father Vissarion has also addressed not Russian but Abkhaz believers, saying they should not take part in services at New Athos.

Father Dorotheus himself believes that the Moscow Patriarchate’s letter was prompted by Archpriest Nikolai Balashov, an adviser to Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Russia. According to Dorotheus, Balashov has consistently worked in the interests of the Georgian Orthodox Church for decades.

“Similar circulars have appeared repeatedly. Yet their authors stubbornly refuse to acknowledge the main point: pilgrims who visit the New Athos Monastery are not there ‘out of ignorance’. The overwhelming majority of them knowingly take part in the services I conduct.

These people know the church bureaucracy well and can see that it contains no spiritual truth — only political and administrative manipulation,” Father Dorotheus wrote on his social media page.

Dorotheus believes another factor also prompted the AOC leadership to step up its activity. On 28 August 2026, Abkhaz President Badra Gunba and Sergei Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff of the Russian presidential administration, made an unofficial visit to the New Athos Monastery.

According to Dorotheus, this was the first time since 2011 that such high-ranking officials had visited their monastery.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: First day of diplomatic corps visit to Karabakh and East Zangezur concludes (PHOTO)
World.content:
SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 11. On September 11, the first day of the visit by representatives of the diplomatic corps accredited in Azerbaijan to Karabakh and Eastern Zangazur included visits to and inspections of a number of sites in the cities of Khankendi and Shusha, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

In accordance with the visit program, representatives of the diplomatic corps first familiarized themselves with the ongoing works at the Khankendi Railway and Bus Terminal Complex. The participants were briefed on the work being carried out at the complex.

The delegation then visited the Cultural Center in Khankendi, where Assistant to the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Hikmet Hajiyev welcomed the participants of the visit.

Representatives of the diplomatic corps visited the Victory Park and took a commemorative photograph in front of the Victory Arch.

As part of the visit, the participants also familiarized themselves with Karabakh University. They were briefed on the facilities created at the university and its activities. The representatives of the diplomatic corps then visited the sewing factory of *AzCotton LLC*, operating in Khankendi, and familiarized themselves with the enterprise’s activities.

The visit continued in the city of Shusha. Representatives of the diplomatic corps were briefed on the restoration and reconstruction works being carried out in the city. The diplomats inspected the construction of the New Shusha Mosque. They then visited Jidir Duzu, Karabakh Street and Shusha Central Square, as well as the “House of Sadigjan” and the Upper Govhar Agha Mosque. They also inspected the shot-up busts located in Shusha Central Square.

The diplomats viewed the exhibition “Heydar Aliyev and Karabakh” at the Shusha Creative Center. Afterwards, they visited the Shusha fortress walls and took a commemorative photograph in front of the walls. Representatives of the diplomatic corps familiarized themselves with the facilities created in the first residential quarter and met with residents of Shusha.

The participants of the visit attended an official reception held in Shusha on the occasion of the Independence Day of the United Mexican States.

The visit will continue on September 12.

World.title: Hajiyev: Azerbaijan, Mexico have major potential to expand economic ties
World.content:
SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 11. There is significant potential for further developing economic, trade and investment ties between Azerbaijan and Mexico, Hikmet Hajiyev, Assistant to the President of Azerbaijan and head of the Foreign Policy Affairs Department of the Presidential Administration, made the remarks at an official reception in Shusha marking the Independence Day of the Republic of Mexico, Trend’s correspondent deployed to Karabakh and East Zangazur reports.

Hajiyev said there are broad prospects for developing relations between the two countries in economic, trade, cultural, humanitarian, investment, energy and other areas.

“There is a certain geographical distance between our countries, but this geographical distance is certainly not a problem for us. Both countries are firmly determined to ensure that our relations develop successfully across various areas,” he said.

According to the presidential aide, contacts between the relevant institutions of the two countries are continuing, particularly in the development of economic, trade and investment ties.

“There are the necessary opportunities to unlock this rich potential and develop it in the interests of our countries,” Hajiyev emphasized.

He added that Azerbaijan highly values Mexico’s dynamic development in Latin America and its role as one of the leading countries in the G20.

World.title: Azerbaijan highly values Mexico’s steadfast support for its territorial integrity – Hikmet Hajiyev
World.content:
SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 11. Azerbaijan highly values Mexico’s continued and steadfast support for the country’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

Hikmet Hajiyev, Assistant to the President of Azerbaijan and head of the Foreign Policy Affairs Department of the Presidential Administration, made the remarks at an official reception in Shusha marking the Independence Day of the Republic of Mexico, Trend’s correspondent deployed to Karabakh and East Zangazur reports.

“We highly value Mexico’s determined position in supporting our country’s territorial integrity and sovereignty when Azerbaijan’s lands were under occupation, and the Azerbaijani people greatly appreciate this,” Hajiyev said.

He noted that these principles play an important role in the foundation of friendly relations between Azerbaijan and Mexico.

The presidential aide emphasized that Azerbaijan and Mexico currently maintain close political ties and an active political dialogue, with regular political consultations held between the two countries.

“Regarding most of the fundamental issues on today’s international agenda, the positions of Mexico and Azerbaijan are almost identical. Our countries support friendship, partnership, interstate relations based on the norms and principles of international law and mutual respect, as well as justice and fairness in international relations,” Hajiyev added.

World.title: Mexico seeks to intensify investment, trade ties with Azerbaijan – ambassador
World.content:
SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 11. Mexico intends to intensify investment and trade exchanges with Azerbaijan.

Mexico’s Ambassador to Azerbaijan Victoria Romero made the remarks at an official reception in Shusha marking the Independence Day of the Republic of Mexico, Trend’s correspondent deployed to Karabakh and East Zangazur reports.

The ambassador said Mexico and Azerbaijan are dynamic economies located in two strategically important regions of the world.

“Our economic relations have strengthened significantly, but there is still great potential and ample room for further development in this area. We want to intensify investment and trade exchanges and continue bringing more of our country’s most distinctive products to Azerbaijan,” Victoria Romero said.

The diplomat also highlighted the expansion of political dialogue and growing institutional contacts between the two countries. According to her, both sides are interested in identifying new areas of cooperation.

World.title: US Embassy thanks Azerbaijan for contribution to joint fight against global terrorism (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. Today, the U.S. Embassy Baku community gathered to honor the nearly 3,000 lives that were lost in the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001 and its aftermath.

Together, we reflected on the lives of the victims and their families, the first responders who ran boldly toward unimaginable danger, and all the lives forever changed after that tragic day.

We also remembered how countries around the world, including Azerbaijan, stood with the United States after the attack. U.S. and Azerbaijani service members served side by side as part of coalition forces in Afghanistan. We are grateful for Azerbaijan’s contributions to our shared fight against global terrorism.

Twenty-five years ago, the United States was attacked by terrorists who sought to threaten the American way of life. Out of the darkness, we saw the timeless truth of American character shine for the world to see. The terrorists did not succeed – they could not weaken the spirit of our people.

World.title: 'Nothing to hide': Brazil's presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro under corruption investigation
World.content:
Brazil's right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro says he has "nothing to hide" in a corruption investigation that was revealed just weeks before voters go to the polls.

Senator Bolsonaro, the leading right-wing challenger to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in next month's election, is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering tied to failed lender Banco Master.

The senator is the eldest son of former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest for a coup plot against his then-successor Lula.

The probe was opened in July by Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee who has recently been hailed as a hero by many on Brazil's right, including Flavio Bolsonaro himself.

The investigation centres on the financing of a film about his father Jair Bolsonaro, which Flavio Bolsonaro insists "is completely legal."

The development could further shake an already volatile presidential race, with multiple opinion polls showing Flavio Bolsonaro and Lula statistically tied in a simulated second-round runoff.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will go up against Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in next month's election. (Reuters: Adriano Machado)

The judge opened the probe at the request of federal police as part of a broader investigation into the failed bank

But details of the investigation only became public after Chief Justice Edson Fachin ordered the proceedings related to the Banco Master case unsealed late on Thursday.

Justice Mendonca complied with Justice Fachin's request, releasing thousands of pages of court records.

Further details and the broader implications of the newly unsealed documents were not immediately clear, as parts of the case, including details of the investigation into Senator Bolsonaro, remained under secrecy as police actively investigate.

Brazil's institutions have been shaken by the fallout from the expanding probe and alleged ties between banker Daniel Vorcaro and central bank officials, senior government members, opposition politicians and Supreme Court justices.

Probe stems from film financing

The investigation into Flavio Bolsonaro stems from questions over an investment he allegedly solicited from Mr Vorcaro, owner of Banco Master, to help finance "Dark Horse," a film about his father that stars US actor Jim Caviezel.

Questions about the film's financing emerged in May, prompting the senator to acknowledge seeking financial backing from Mr Vorcaro, while denying wrongdoing. The disclosures cost him support in opinion polls at the time.

Brazil's former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is the father of Flavio, was sentenced to 27 years jail for leading a conspiracy aimed at keeping him in power. (AP: Luis Nova)

The unsealed documents show the federal police then requested an investigation, authorised by Justice Mendonca, to examine whether Senator Bolsonaro committed money laundering, illicit foreign exchange and corruption.

The unsealed police report confirms much of a report by news website The Intercept Brasil from May that first detailed communications between the senator and Mr Vorcaro up until the banker's first arrest in November 2025.

"Brother, I am and always will be with you," Senator Bolsonaro told the disgraced banker in an audio message at the time, according to the report.

Police said data extracted from Mr Vorcaro's mobile phone showed he transferred about $US12 million ($16.7 million) in 2025 to a US-based fund linked to former lawmaker Eduardo Bolsonaro, the senator's brother, who now lives in Texas, as part of efforts to finance the film.

One screenshot included in the documents suggests Eduardo Bolsonaro advised Mr Vorcaro's team on the management of the funds in the United States.

Investigators are seeking to determine the origin of the money, the companies used to channel it, and its ultimate beneficiaries.

Flavio Bolsonaro and his brother have always denied wrongdoing.

Flavio Bolsonaro is the son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro. (AP: Eraldo Peres)

Supreme court crisis

The new developments intensify a crisis rattling Brazil as voters head into an unusually tight election campaign in which any major development could tip the balance in favour of either left-wing Lula or Bolsonaro.

Justice Fachin has sought to resolve a public clash between justices Mendonca and Alexandre de Moraes, who has also been mentioned in the Banco Master probe, that thrust the court into one of its most severe internal crises in decades.

Mendonca made public documents from the investigation earlier this month, including dozens of messages that police say Mr Vorcaro sent to Justice Moraes. The disclosures prompted calls for an unprecedented investigation into a sitting Supreme Court justice over allegations that Moraes acted as an adviser to the banker.

Justice Moraes, in response, accused Mendonca of abusing his authority.

Justice Fachin scheduled a full-court session for Tuesday, when the court's 10-member bench is expected to discuss allegations regarding Justice Moraes's relationship with Mr Vorcaro.

'Disclose everything': Lula

Senator Bolsonaro's supporters have attempted to link Lula to Justice Moraes, who pursued former President Bolsonaro over a 2023 coup plot and secured his conviction last year.

During Independence Day rallies in Sao Paulo on Monday, a giant inflatable balloon depicting Mendonca towered over crowds gathered to support Bolsonaro's campaign.

Seeking to distance himself from the crisis at the court, Lula publicly supported unsealing the investigation hours before Justice Fachin's decision.

"Whenever there is an allegation involving the judiciary or politics, it should be made public so everyone knows what is happening," he said in an interview with SBT TV on Thursday.

" Investigate everything, disclose everything, regardless of who it hurts. "

Reuters/AFP

World.title: Nepal estimates reconstruction after deadly floods to cost nearly $7 billion
World.content:
The reconstruction bill after the deadly floods that hit Nepal last month will amount to $US4.78 billion ($6.67 billion), its foreign ministry says.

Spokesman Lok Bahadur Chhetri said that $US57.67 million ($80.43 million) was needed for short-term reconstruction and recovery over the next six months.

Approximately $US4.71 billion ($6.57 billion) was required for long-term reconstruction adapting to a rapidly changing mountain environment, he added.

"Given the scale and extent of the damage, the government is also undertaking a comprehensive post-disaster needs assessment to determine the full extent of loss and damage and the requirement for recovery, rebuilding and reconstruction," Mr Chhetri told reporters on Friday.

A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding along the Trishuli river in Nepal. (AP: Rajesh Kumar Singh)

At least 12 hydropower projects have been engulfed in mud and debris, and whole villages wiped off the map, after a glacier collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border caused a tsunami-like surge of water, mud and debris to submerge parts of the country on August 26.

The devastation in the valleys below the glacier includes cross-border trade routes, roads, bridges, houses and other infrastructure which was swept away.

Rescuers in Nepal have retrieved 1,385 bodies, while around 5,130 people remain missing, the country's disaster agency said on Friday. In Tibet, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to Chinese state media.

The combined toll is 1,428 people dead and more than 5,649 missing, including around 800 foreigners, among them tourists and pilgrims.

Eight Australians who were originally declared missing in the flood have been found, with 35 still unaccounted-for.

If you want to help support the thousands affected by the crisis, the ABC is supporting the Emergency Action Alliance member charities and their local partners. You can find more information here.

UN estimates $220 million in building damage alone

Nepal's leaders are asking wealthier countries and global agencies for financial help in the wake of the floods, arguing the reconstruction costs show how climate change hits poor countries which do little to cause it.

The Nepal government is finalising a report detailing the extent of the damage, losses and funding requirements for temporary shelters, schools and essential infrastructure, officials said.

A man stands on a mud-covered street, alongside damaged houses, following deadly flash floods and a mudslide in Nepal (Reuters: Tyrone Siu)

A UN preliminary assessment estimated building damage from Nepal's floods at $US158 million ($220 million) alone, warning that total losses — including damage to roads and bridges, agricultural land and humanitarian costs — would be far higher.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah said earlier that Nepal must "strongly raise" with the international community the disasters it has experienced as a result of climate change.

He is expected to take his first foreign trip as leader to address the UN General Assembly on the issue this month.

Nepal's disaster management chief Dharam Raj Uprety told Reuters the estimated cost will be shared with the World Bank and Asian Development Bank, along with the embassies of countries and blocs including the United States, Britain, India, China, Japan and the European Union.

"It's not only a disaster induced by flood, it's massive. A disaster induced by climate change," he said.

Locals seek compensation for lost livelihoods

Nanimaya Senchuri lost her farm in the flood. (Supplied: ActionAid)

Nanimaya Senchuri was one of many in Nepal who lost their farmlands in the floods, buried under mud and debris.

She was inside her house, which she shares with her daughter, when the Trishuli River came crashing down nearby.

"In all my life, I had never seen a flood like this," she said.

As a result, she lost two large plots of farmland, her paddy crop and her banana plantation almost ready for harvest.

The farm not only provided food for Ms Senchuri and her family, but was also her source of income.

She was not sure whether she, and everyone else affected by the natural disaster, would receive compensation needed to rebuild farms and livelihood.

Flood reconstruction costs 'a shared responsibility'

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, contributes a fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions compared to industrialised nations.

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide — increasing the risk of such disasters.

Scientists say glaciers in the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are melting faster as global temperatures rise.

Houses damaged by recent flash floods stand amid thick layers of sludge, mud and debris in Nepal's Nuwakot district.

Nepalese officials have publicly framed the disaster as an example of the disproportionate impact of climate change on poor countries.

Nepal expects global agencies and other partners to "recognise this kind of event and take accountability on that" — though it is not for the country to dictate who should contribute how much — Prakash Pokhrel, a geologist for the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.

"We need not say what is causing climate change because you already know why climate change is happening and who is contributing the most to it," Mr Pokhrel said.

" Countries like Nepal don't contribute significantly to climate change, but they are facing this level of disaster. So why should it not be a shared responsibility among the global community? "

Houses damaged by recent flash floods stand amid thick layers of sludge, mud and debris in Nepal's Nuwakot district. (AP: Dar Yasin)

China accounts for roughly a third of global emissions, with the United States and Nepal's other neighbour India also among the world's biggest emitters.

China is willing to provide assistance within its capacity for Nepal's post-disaster reconstruction, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Thursday.

Mr Guo said Beijing had immediately extended assistance to Nepal, while rescue and relief work was ongoing back home on its side of the border.

"We believe that under the leadership of the Nepalese government, the Nepalese people will be able to overcome the disaster and rebuild their homes at an early date," he said at a regular news briefing.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Norway's Princess Astrid dies aged 94 two days after King's funeral
World.content:
Norway's Princess Astrid, an older sister of the late king Harald, has died at the age of 94, the royal palace said in a statement, two days after the King's funeral.

Her brother Harald died last month, aged 89, after more than 35 years on the throne, and the princess made her last public appearance at his funeral on Wednesday.

"Throughout her long life, Princess Astrid represented the Royal House in a warm and dutiful manner," King Haakon VIII said in the statement.

"His Majesty the King has received with great sadness the news of the passing of Princess Astrid," the Palace said in a statement.

"The Princess fell asleep today, Friday 11 September, at the age of 94."

The Palace released a statement on Friday stating Princess Astrid of Norway had died aged 94. (Reuters: Peter Nicholls)

The death of the King

King Harald V of Norway died in late August, announced by the European country's royal court.

"King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, 28 August," the royal palace said on its website.

Norway’s King Harald V was laid to rest after a funeral procession through Oslo on Wednesday. (AP: Ole Berg-Rusten Name/NTB via AP, Pool)

The King was laid to rest after a state funeral and ceremony on September 9.

Royal dignitaries seen at the funeral included Britain's Prince William, Japan's Crown Prince, the kings of Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden and Spain.

Spain's Queen Sofia, Britain's Princess Anne, and Britain's Prince William leave the Oslo Cathedral after a funeral service for Norway's King Harald V in Oslo. (AP: Markus Schreiber)

Also paying their respects were European heads of state, the presidents of Germany and Finland, France's prime minister, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Representing the United States was Allison Hooker, Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, the Norwegian government said.

King Harald, who was Europe's oldest living monarch, was taken to hospital on August 17.

The palace said he was treated for a bacterial infection in his blood.

"A whole nation is in mourning, and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway," the country's Prime Minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said in a statement following the King's death.

The new King of Norway

His 53-year-old son who succeeded the throne, is now King Haakon VIII.

King Haakon adopted the motto, "All for Norway," a cry that dates back to his great-grandfather.

His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child became Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and the heir to the throne.

King Haakon and Queen Mette-Marit wave to the crowd from the balcony of the royal palace, on the day of the funeral of Norway's King Harald V. (Reuters: Claudia Greco )

In recent years Haakon has stepped in as his aging father's health began to fail.

He ascends the throne faced by the task of stabilising the nations monarchy and boosting the royal family's popularity after his wife's past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson's rape conviction.

Queen Mette-Marit, 53, the King's commoner wife is recovering from a lung transplant she underwent in June.

Last week, the Queen had to cancel plans to attend her husband's oath ceremony in parliament due to complications after her operation.

World.title: 'Landmark' NT novel wins best fiction at Prime Minister's Literary Awards
World.content:
A novel based on the oral history of Yolŋu people from north-east Arnhem Land has been named as this year's fiction pick at the Prime Minister's Literary Awards.

Darwin-born author Leonie Norrington and co-authors Djawundil Maymuru, Merrikiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs and Djawa Burarrwanga have won the $80,000 fiction prize for their book A Piece of Red Cloth.

Told from the perspective of Yolŋu people, the book tells the story of a grandmother's quest to protect her granddaughter from Macassan trepang fishermen during the 1600s, while they learn to interact with foreigners.

Leonie Norrington says winning the award is a "recognition of history". (ABC News)

The Prime Minister's Literary Awards judges labelled the novel as a "landmark achievement in fiction", writing it "is also an urgent example of intercultural work, setting a high benchmark for collaboration between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal writers".

"It is a profound work of remembrance and re-imagination, fusing oral history, novelistic technique and deep cultural knowledge," the judges said.

Having grown up in the Barunga community, Dr Norrington said her Aboriginal mother Clare Bush inspired her to write A Piece of Red Cloth before she died.

Dr Norrington said her Aboriginal mother wanted the Yolŋu people's story told to help people in other parts of the country to understand the country was "alive" and we are "one with the earth".

"If we only have what she called 'Captain Cook history', then we're always going to have a frontier mentality about our country," she said.

"We can exploit the country because we're not from the country.

Prime Minister's Literary Awards announced Kate Wild's book about the fatal shooting of Kumanjayi Walker and the ensuing murder trial, The Red House, is one of six PMLA winners.

"We could belong to the country and then have more respect for the country and for the first peoples of the country, not just as the first people who lived here, but the people who emerged at the same time as the country."

Speaking to Radio National in 2025, local custodian Merrikiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs said the book explores cultural traditions that are still apparent in modern communities while re-telling the story of how Yolŋu people had been trading with countries overseas for centuries.

Merrkiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs accepted the award in Canberra on Thursday. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"All I can is that we still live like this, like what's happening in the book today," she told the program.

"Even if we are modern people, we still go out bush, we till dig for that yams, for those roots get it up oysters, still live it, still eat it."

Dr Norrington said winning the award was a "recognition of history" and hoped her book could be a driving force for action.

"Our history has been read by the Prime Minister of Australia and now things can change," she said.

Leonie Norrington and Merrikiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs were part of the group that collaborated to write A Piece of Red Cloth. (Supplied)

"I think if I was going to have a message to the prime minister, I think it would be that Australia is a terribly, terribly dry and very fragile country and we need to look after it.

"The future generations of Australia really rely on us making good decisions about what we do with this very fragile land."

A Piece of Red Cloth wasn't the only NT winner at the prestigious awards — Kate Wild's book The Red House, about the fatal shooting of Kumanjayi Walker in Yuendumu and the murder trial of police officer Zachary Rolfe, won the non-fiction category.

World.title: Putin and Iranian president arrive in India for summit focusing on war
World.content:
Vladimir Putin has arrived in India for talks ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit dominated by economic challenges and conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine, with the leaders of China and Iran set to attend.

War, global trade turbulence and oil are expected on the agenda at the two-day annual summit which opens on Saturday, when Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to arrive.

It will be Mr Xi's first visit to India since 2019, marking the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours.

The visit comes six years after a deadly military clash between China and India along their disputed Himalayan border.

Xi Jinping is making his first visit to India since 2019. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

Ties between both nuclear-armed China and India have warmed in recent months, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.

But deep mistrust remains within their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating the relationship.

"One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said in a post on social media on Friday, welcome arriving leaders.

Modi calls for end to Ukraine war India's PM Narendra Modi tells Putin the war in Ukraine needs to end.

Mr Modi is due to hold talks later on Friday with Mr Putin, who last visited India in December 2025. Moscow is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.

India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important relationships and most controversial fuel supplier in recent years, as the war in Ukraine drags on.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also expected on Friday, and is also set to hold talks with Mr Modi.

Posters of leaders in attendance of the BRICS summit line the streets of New Delhi. (Reuters: Francis Mascarenhas)

Gulf conflict is the 'fault line'

The BRICS summit was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions typically dominated by Western powers.

It has since expanded to include Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.

"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V Pant, a professor of international relations and vice president of India's Observer Research Foundation.

" What was seen until last year as an achievement, the expansion of BRICS, today looks like a big constraint on BRICS. "

It will be Mr Pezeshkian's first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly in conversations.

Econimist Shilan Shah said the war in Iran would provide a stern test of the expanded group's cohesion.

Mr Shah noted the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.

United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi are all expected to be in attendance.

India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war".

World.title: Freo surge home to claim semifinal classic against Cats
World.content:
The Flagmantle dream is still alive for 2026 after ruckman Luke Jackson produced a Herculean display to lead Fremantle to a pulsating 14-point semi-final win over Geelong in Perth.

In front of 59,725 fans at Perth Stadium on Friday night, Fremantle skipped out to a 38-7 lead before Geelong hit the front in the third quarter on the back of three quick goals to Oliver Henry.

(Getty Images)

Staring down the barrel of a straight-sets finals exit, Fremantle lifted when it mattered most, with Jackson the biggest hero of them all.

Jackson kicked two late goals in the third quarter and set up another for Patrick Voss to give Fremantle back the lead.

In a pressure-filled final term, Geelong cut a 24-point deficit back to eight points with 75 seconds remaining.

But Wharfie Time — played for just the second time this year — sent the crowd into a frenzy, with Voss kicking his fourth goal from the ensuing centre clearance as Fremantle sealed the 18.12 (120) to 16.10 (106) victory.

The win set up a preliminary final against the Swans in Sydney next week.

Henry kicked a career-high five goals for Geelong, while Shannon Neale chipped in with three.

Geelong had made eight preliminary finals in the past 10 seasons, but having to travel to Perth for this year's semi-final proved a bridge too far.

Bailey Smith racked up 29 disposals and 751m gained, while Patrick Dangerfield followed up his five-goal haul against Carlton with two majors and two goal assists.

Jackson (25 disposals, 35 hitouts, eight clearances, two goals) was a clear best-on-ground, while Voss's four goals were also crucial.

Shai Bolton made up for his quiet display in last week's 32-point loss to Hawthorn with two goals from 26 disposals.

AAP

World.title: Bennett bemoans Bunker as Knights stun Souths in elimination final
World.content:
Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett has called out the Bunker as not being good for the game after a controversial no-try call in his side's elimination final defeat to Newcastle on Friday night.

The Knights tore out of the blocks and overwhelmed South Sydney 20-10 in a fiery and dramatic finals clash at the Sydney Football Stadium.

But Bennett was left deeply frustrated at full time, pointedly asking "who is refereeing the game" after Jayden Sullivan had a try taken off him with the Rabbitohs trailing by just 10-6.

Following some neat interplay with Latrell Mitchell on the left, Alex Johnston dropped the ball under pressure from Jermaine McEwen as he ran down the line, before kicking on to allow Sullivan to dot down.

Ashley Klein awarding the try on field for a strip tackle however, Bunker official Chris Butler overruled Klein and said it was in fact a loose carry and that McEwen had slapped the arm of Johnston, not the ball.

Around 10 minutes later, Dom Young came perilously close to putting his foot on the line as he scored to extend the Knights' lead with the Bunker agreeing with the on field official's call, provoking Bennett's ire.

"I think anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock on," Bennett said of the Johnston incident in his press conference.

"The ball got knocked out of his hands.

"The referee awards the try, the Bunker flies in and says no try.

"Then 10 minutes later, Dom Young goes down the sideline, I'm not sure whether he put his foot on the line or not, but the bottom line is the bunker says we go with the referee's call.

"I want to know who's refereeing the game, that's the first thing I want to know. Is it the referee? Or the Bunker?"

The Knights and Souths went toe-to-toe in a thrilling contest. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Bennett, a long-time critic of the Bunker, said the entire process was not good for rugby league.

"It's just not what the game needs," he said.

"I've been in it [the game] a long time, seen a lot of things, and I don't think the Bunker enhances our game.

"I'm happy to live with the referee's call. Always have been, always will be.

"The ref I know is doing his job properly, he'll make a mistake, I'll live with that. My players will make mistakes, I'll live with that.

"What I can't live with is this thing called the Bunker that's supposed to be 100 per cent perfect, but it's not perfect.

"One's a try because the referee says it's a try, the other one is no try because the Bunker says it's no try.

"I wanna know who's running the game."

Knights refuse to be bullied in tense tussle

Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai tore into each other in the opening minutes. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Despite the controversial calls, Newcastle appeared well worth their win, the Knights coming out adamant they wouldn't be bullied by the star-studded Souths squad.

Dane Gagai and Latrell Mitchell set the tone early, their ferocious scuffle in the corner seeing Mitchell throw a punch that mercifully for both men missed its target.

Incredibly, neither man was sent to the bin and, in a throwback to games of yesteryear, from the restart Gagai ran the ball straight back at a crazy-eyed Mitchell, winning the battle and, eventually, the entire war against his former teammate.

Unfortunately for Souths, that missed right hook was as close as Mitchell came to making any impact in the game, the star centre strangely quiet with just seven touches in the first half.

Souths lost talismanic veteran Cody Walker to a calf injury before half time and missed the veteran's poise and creativity.

The Rabbitohs did rally, Campbell Graham scoring not long after, and David Fifita was held up as Souths rallied behind their stricken five-eighth, who retreated to the sheds in tears.

When Sullivan's try was taken away from the Rabbitohs by the Bunker, the home support must have known it was not their day.

Having the try taken off them was doubly disappointing because it was the only time in the game that Mitchell and Johnston linked up in the way Souths needed them to if they wanted to progress.

Newcastle scored not long after, with Johnston then leaving the field with a groin injury, and that was all she wrote.

The Knights will play the loser of the game between the Dolphins and the Warriors as the fairytale season for last year's wooden spooners continues for at least another week.

Look back at how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Being a renter, Jenny missed out on solar boon but that is about to change
World.content:
Australia could soon follow in the footsteps of Germany and the United Kingdom as it prepares to lift a ban on plug-in solar and batteries, unlocking access to the technology for millions of apartment dwellers and renters for the first time.

The move was discussed during a meeting of the country's energy ministers, where they agreed to explore pathways to support the "safe deployment" of plug-in solar across the country.

'Crazy' battery charging fires gas power Australia is leading the world in the adoption of batteries. But in one state, storage is fuelling some perverse and pricey outcomes.

The systems, which are also commonly referred to as 'balcony solar', were legalised in the United Kingdom last month and New Zealand has flagged plans to do the same within 12 months.

Germany is a world-leader in plug-in solar, with an estimated one in 10 households having a system installed.

It can technically be sold in Australia but not legally plugged in and used.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen said a third of Australians have solar on their roof, making the technology "more popular than the backyard pool".

"Now we're taking the next step, by looking at how even more Australians can take advantage of free, abundant sunshine to cut their energy bills — even if they don't have a roof.

"All state and territory ministers are on board and will work with the Commonwealth to look at how plug-in solar and batteries can work in Australia to give apartment dwellers more control over their energy bills."

Chris Bowen says a third of Australians have solar on their roof. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Heidi Lee Douglas is the CEO of Solar Citizens, a community organisation that's been campaigning for plug-in solar to be legalised, and welcomed that Australia was now a step closer to that reality.

"This commitment to make plug-in solar and plug-in batteries legal in Australia is great news for more than a third of Australians who rent or live in apartments, and also for low-income households so they can access some of the bill-busting benefits that cheap clean solar home owners enjoy," she said.

"We want to see a firm timeline and deadline by December at the next energy ministers meeting for when plug-in solar and batteries will be available for use in every state and territory.

" Australians are looking for every opportunity to bring down their power bills. "

Heidi Lee Douglas is the CEO of Solar Citizens and says plug-in systems would finally bring more social equity for the technology. (Supplied: Solar Citizens)

What are plug-in solar and batteries?

Plug-in solar systems and batteries can be plugged into regular power points and do not require installation by an electrician.

The power generated by the panels is fed into the home network via an inverter and a standard plug and helps offset electricity used by appliances.

Overseas, they are commonly attached to apartment balconies or installed in backyards and produce between 600-800 watts of power, typically at a cost of up to $1,300.

They are a popular choice for people who live in an apartment and cannot mount rooftop solar as well as renters, many of whom have never considered the possibility of accessing renewable energy.

More than 30 per cent of Australians are renting, which equates to almost 3 million households.

Maiya Irving-Mackinnon is a renter from the Sydney suburb of Marrickville who estimates her electricity bills have increased by about 15 per cent, or $200, over the past 12 months.

Maiya Irving-Mackinnon, a renter from the Sydney suburb of Marrickville, is keen to reduce her power bills by having a plug-in solar panel. (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

"Solar has never really been something that we can consider as a renter because we can't install anything on the roof or on a ground floor apartment," she said.

"I would really like to have the option to install solar panels and for that to be subsidised but it's not really something that's been available for a renter before.

" During the day, if we were able to run our electronics at a reduced cost, if not for free, then I think that would make a really big difference to our energy bill. "

Experts have suggested the payback period for plug-in solar systems ranges from four to ten years.

Ms Lee Douglas expects some households will save up to $1,000 a year on electricity bills.

"The average plug-in solar panel will allow you to save about $300-$400 a year, and plug-in batteries will easily double that," she said.

Importantly, renters would be able to take the panels and batteries with them when they moved.

Barriers to overcome

Plug-in solar systems don't need installation; they are as easy to plug in as a kettle or toaster. (Supplied: Holger's Pictures)

The federal government will now work with the states and territories to "identify measures that enable the safe use" of plug-in solar and report back on next steps by the end of the year.

The federal government is yet to indicate whether it is considering offering subsidies or rebates for the technology.

Solar Citizens is calling on plug-in solar and batteries to become legal in Australia by July next year.

But there are still barriers to overcome ahead of then, including ensuring safety standards are up to scratch for when products begin to enter the market.

Executive director of the German Plug-In Solar Association Craig Morris said Australia could look to the safety standards that Germany has developed as a starting point.

"The risk of too many companies coming in and some of them not being serious has gone down," he said.

"If you go back just five years, I think we had a number of companies that you didn't really know too much about them and maybe they were just trying a quick buck.

" But I think in the meantime, the big boys have taken over and pushed out some of the smaller firms. "

Benchmark power price drops Surging levels of renewable energy and better reliability from coal-fired generators are set to give consumers a break, with benchmark power prices to fall up to 10 per cent for consumers and more for small businesses.

Bringing landlords and body corporates on board to allow plug-in solar to be hung on balconies or stationed in backyards is another challenge that would need to be addressed in Australia before the technology is legalised and rolled out.

In Germany, tenants need to get permission to install plug-in solar but landlords need a good reason, such as planned facade renovations, to reject the request.

Mr Morris said ultimately, adoption of plug-in batteries would be crucial in allowing the full benefits of plug-in solar to be fully realised.

"What we're ultimately offering, which is plug-in solar with batteries, or maybe even plug-in batteries without solar, offering flexibility from households," he said.

"The batteries would charge and discharge not in order to optimise our consumption of the solar power we generate, but to optimise operation of the local grid.

"And this can save money across the board, across the country for everyone, even if you don't have a system, because we're going to optimise the usage of these public power lines."

World.title: Chalmers makes more tax tweaks to temper budget blow
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Chalmers makes more tax tweaks to temper budget blow Paul Sakkal September 12, 2026 — 4:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has made another tweak to fix the fallout from Labor’s budget tax rises, but a leading business group says the revised reforms remains harmful and sap confidence across the economy. The government moved on Friday to address concerns from a range of influential businesspeople and some Labor figures that Labor’s new inflation-adjusted model for taxing capital gains could hurt fast-growing new businesses and worsen Australia’s productivity and investment. Treasurer Jim Chalmers on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Under the changes, companies operating for up to 15 years will be able to qualify for a CGT concession, up from 10 years, while investors will need to hold eligible shares for three years, down from five. The concession will also no longer be capped. And a research and development refund scheme for biotech firms will be accessible for 15 years, up from 10. Tech Council of Australia chief executive Kate Cornick said the changes would “help ensure the risks that founders, talent and investors take to build and back early-stage companies are rewarded.”



“As a nation we have a lot of catching up to do on R&D, and the proposed [changes] ... are a solid step toward getting us back on track.” Related Article Exclusive

Federal budget ‘A problem for every single business’: Labor insider adds to backlash over CGT overhaul Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar said the overhaul did not alter the overall impact of Labor’s tax package on businesses. “We are almost four months on from the federal budget and the policy settings continue to move on a day-by-day basis, this is eroding confidence across the economy,” he said. A media release from Chalmers’ office said the changes were “all about supporting small businesses and start-ups, including in the biotechnology and medical technology sectors. These reforms will deliver more innovation, encourage more entrepreneurship and deliver certainty for investors.”



Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said Chalmers had been “forced by the prime minister into his fourth humiliating backdown over his budget”. “The backdown is welcome, but it is embarrassing that certainty and confidence has been jeopardised for so many businesses because we have an out-of-his-depth treasurer.” In the May budget, Labor scrapped negative gearing on existing properties and created new rules to stop tax minimisation by using trusts. It also moved from a flat 50 per cent CGT discount to an inflation adjusted model that could lead to lower taxes for investors in low-growth, high-dividend blue-chip shares but higher taxes on quicker growing firms that create dynamism. Labor promised before the last election it would not pursue such policies, but said it changed its position due to the urgency of solving the housing crisis. House prices have continued their pre-budget tumble due to a combination of high-interest rates and the tax changes. Labor has already walked back a tax on trusts that the Coalition weaponised into a “death tax” scare campaign, got rid of a tax that would have penalised people whose spouses died, and backtracked on elements of a new minimum tax on trusts.
