World.title: ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSeptember 11 attacks ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on Maria Tsvetkova , Idrees Ali and Joseph Ax Updated September 12, 2026 — 2:51am ,first published 11:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day. In New York, family members of the victims joined Vice President JD Vance, former president George W. Bush, who was in office on 9/11, and ex-presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8.46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Centre’s North Tower. A woman and child pause at the memorial on Friday morning. Spencer Platt/Pool Getty Images North America via AP The site of the World Trade Centre attacks, pictured on Friday, now the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, a sombre recitation that lasts for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001.



Elsie Caldwell carried a photograph of her son Kenny Caldwell to hear his name and all the others read aloud. She last spoke to him that morning a quarter-century ago. “Mom, I just want to let you know that I love you,” Caldwell said he told her in a final phone call. She is one of many relatives of victims whose remains never were recovered. Other moments of silence, marking when the other three planes hijacked by al-Qaeda terrorists crashed and the two towers collapsed, followed. For the first time, a seventh silence was observed to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward. Sombre ceremonies were held across the country to mark the 25th anniversary. Bloomberg New York City Fire Department (FDNY) members visit the memorial ahead of the ceremony. Bloomberg



An attendee with a tattoo of the Twin Towers at the memorial in New York on Friday. Bloomberg US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wiped away a tear as he revisited the place where the attacks killed 658 of his then-colleagues – including his brother, Gary Lutnick – at the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald. Gregory Carafello came to the ceremony to honour the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald. Carafello himself was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate. “Everyone should realise that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families,” he said. “These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work.” Former president Joe Biden, Vice President JD Vance and former president George W. Bush. AP Photo/Pamela Smith



Former President Bill Clinton, former First Lady Michelle Obama and former President Barack Obama listen to speakers at the memorial in New York. Olga Fedorova/POOL EPA via AP At the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, where American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building’s west flank, killing 184, senior military leaders gathered amid heavy rain to watch the unfurling of an American flag before US President Donald Trump chronicled some of the stories of those aboard who perished in the crash: a woman pregnant with her first child, a family of four headed to Australia, three sixth-graders on a field trip. “In those harrowing days after the attacks, we saw the authentic spirit of our nation,” Trump said at the ceremony. The president and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who also delivered remarks, both used their speeches to make the case for the Iran war, which they have defended as necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump at a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein



An American flag is unfurled at the Pentagon early on Friday morning. Bloomberg US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth watched the flag unfurling ceremony as rain fell at the Pentagon. Bloomberg “We salute our first responders and law enforcement, and we love them,” Trump said. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.” Trump added: “September 11th reminded us of the terrible power of hate. The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail, and to win.” A ceremony was also being held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington.



Related Article September 11 attacks The day that changed America and shaped the world we know today The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security. But for many whom the attacks directly affected – the victims’ families, first responders and rescue workers – the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter-century ago and the heartbreak that followed. Loading Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower.



Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him to her father’s grave last week and was attending a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday. “This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing that they won’t ever get to know each other,” Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. “My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather. Related Article September 11 attacks Australians remember lost loved ones 25 years on from September 11 attacks “We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added. The attacks initiated the “war on terror,” which led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements – a promise being tested by the current Iran war.



At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks. At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colours Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected. Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Rudy Giuliani, former mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony. Bloomberg Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died.



Patrick Whalen’s father, also named Patrick, was a New York City firefighter who responded to the attacks and continued working at Ground Zero for months amid the dust and rubble. In 2020, he was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer linked to exposure to toxic carcinogens, and died in 2021. Related Article September 11 attacks John Howard witnessed the 9/11 attacks as PM. It changed his leadership forever “The government told him it was safe to breathe, and, obviously, it was not true,” the younger Whalen said after a New York City Fire Department memorial service this week. Information that the air at Ground Zero was safe to breathe came from the US Environmental Protection Agency. Its former administrator, Christine Todd Whitman, apologised in a 2016 interview with The Guardian, saying the agency did its best with the knowledge it had. The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show. Twenty-six have died this year alone.



A woman mourns at the September 11 memorial plaza in Lower Manhattan. Dave Sanders/Pool The New York Times via AP A mourner places a flower on one of 2753 empty chairs in New York’s Bryant Park, each signifying a life lost in the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Centre. AP Photo/Heather Khalifa People walk in the Oculus near the memorial on the 25th anniversary of the attacks. AP Photo/Angelina Katsanis Reuters with AP Twenty-five years on from September 11

World.title: Bring on the the Zak attack: The Cats’ semi-final showed they sorely need it
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Bring on the the Zak attack: The Cats’ semi-final showed they sorely need it Andrew Wu September 12, 2026 — 2:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

There’s a good reason why Geelong are neck deep into getting Zak Butters. It was on show in Perth. Finals expose weaknesses and the Cats were found wanting again in the engine room, as they were when they were pounded by the Brisbane Lions in last year’s grand final. Their premiership dream unravelled last year against the power of Will Ashcroft, Lachie Neale and co. This time they were upended by the clean hands of Caleb Serong, the slick wheels of Shai Bolton and Hayden Young, and the might of Luke Jackson. Patrick Voss and Bailey Smith aren’t exactly shrinking violets. AFL Photos Geelong’s fate was ultimately decided by the belated tolling of the bells for “Wharfie Time” but the bursts at the start of the game and the final few minutes of a rollicking third quarter left them reeling.



Apart from that, as Geelong coach Chris Scott pointed out, the Cats matched the Dockers. The problem was Freo slammed seven goals in those periods. In a game decided by 14 points, those passages were critical. The opening spurt spat out three goals in four minutes for the Dockers, allowing the tension that had gripped their faithful last week to be released in a cacophony of roars and electronic hip-hop that accompanied each goal. Patrick Dangerfield stood strong in the finals yet again. AFL Photos Bolton, one of numerous star Dockers who were quiet in their qualifying final debacle, set them alight, getting out the front of stoppage twice for goals. It’s for games like these the Dockers paid the big price to lure him from Richmond. Bolton’s impact was dulled slightly after this – it had to be after such a fast start – but he still finished with 26 disposals. In his quieter patches, the Dockers had Serong, Young, Andrew Brayshaw and Murphy Reid running the show.



The Cats relied too heavily on Bailey Smith, who did not stop running, but lacked sufficient support. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The ‘Butters rule’ the AFL should introduce to fix a shonky system As brave as Max Holmes was to get up for two finals after ankle surgery, he did not produce the scything runs that make him a dangerous midfielder. He limped off just before half-time though played out the game for a modest 18 disposals. “So to come back and play two finals the way he did was ultra-impressive and speaks to his professionalism,” Scott said afterwards. “But I think it was more a matter of a couple more weeks would have had him closer to himself.” The Cats were walloped 23-13 out of the middle and conceded 12 goals from stoppage. They gave up 11 goals from this source in last year’s grand final.



Should Butters, one of the league’s best clearance winners, choose the hoops over the red, white and blue of his boyhood club the Western Bulldogs, he would stiffen a Cats on-ball brigade that often gets found out in big games. For periods in the second term, the Cats had taggers Oisin Mullin and Mark O’Connor in the centre square alongside Shaun Mannagh, who made his reputation as a dynamic half-forward. As honest as Mullin and O’Connor are, not many premiership contenders will fear Geelong’s midfield with both stoppers in there. “They’re a good centre bounce team. That’s an area we need to improve,” Scott said. Loading



“If you take out the first three to four minutes, and the centre bounces in general, and then that patch, it wasn’t even with three minutes to go in the third quarter, it was probably the last 90 seconds, we were probably on top for the rest of the game. They were two brief periods that really hurt us.” The Cats were also punished by Jackson, who made the most of his advantage in experience, size and strength against Mitch Edwards – a 21-year-old in just his 20th game and second final. When the coaches’ votes come out next week, it would be a surprise if he did not get the maximum of 10. View post on X The big man with the mullet gave his midfielders first use of the ball, won the ball himself at ground level, and kicked two clutch goals from ruck infringements when the Dockers surged late in the third quarter. There is little he cannot do.





As well-beaten as they were around the ball, the Cats hung tough, forcing the Dockers to win the game three times. Not much went right for them. They were stiff not to have Ollie Dempsey’s volley from close range ruled their way. Replays appeared to show the ball ricocheting off Matt Johnson’s arm onto Dempsey’s boot, but the ARC deemed there was insufficient evidence to overrule the goal umpire’s soft call. “From what I’m told, everyone has the same opinion that Ollie did,” Scott said diplomatically when asked for his assessment of the decision. The vision of Scott punching the window of the box in bemusement will become rich online meme material.



Chris Scott could barely believe his eyes after a shot on goal from Ollie Dempsey was ruled a behind due to “inconclusive evidence” to overturn the umpire’s call. Seven “Sometimes I punch the wall when I’m happy,” Scott said. “Sometimes I punch the wall when I’m annoyed.” Jeremy Cameron battled manfully for two goals and 15 disposals. He will undergo surgery to fix the lingering issues on the arm he broke in last year’s grand final and which has hampered him all year. Tom Stewart, the man who Scott rates as the best player at the club, was held to 14 disposals against the influential Patrick Voss – who energised the crowd with four goals, including the sealer with seconds left. Stewart did not take a mark in the first quarter when the Dockers surged. Along with Holmes’ struggles, that’s three of Geelong’s best players having midrange nights when more was needed from their top-liners.



Patrick Dangerfield was ominous at times but lacked the supply to dominate as he did last week, while Ollie Henry played his best game, booting five. If they win Toby Greene’s signature, their forward line will cause migraines for opposition defences. It is testament to their resilience that the game was still alive with 75 seconds on the clock, prompting the Dockers to toll the bell for Wharfie Time to spur their team home. “There are a lot of teams in history after a start like that who would’ve turned up their toes and been beaten badly,” Scott said. “Obviously, we were being outplayed. To hang in and give ourselves a chance late in the game, in some ways be a fraction unlucky at various times, I think is a credit to our players. “It’s less about our off-field stuff and much more the ability of those guys to hang in. They’ll all be really hurting at the moment.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wayne Bennett has never liked the bunker. He wants it gone after Friday night
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Wayne Bennett has never liked the bunker. He wants it gone after Friday night Christian Nicolussi September 12, 2026 — 12:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Wayne Bennett blasted the NRL bunker after Alex Johnston was ruled to have knocked on at a vital stage during the Rabbitohs’ 20-10 loss to Newcastle, and declared: “The quicker they get rid of the bunker, the happier I’ll be.” South Sydney lost Cody Walker to a calf injury, then lost to an impressive Knights who now march on to week two of the finals for a showdown against the loser of Saturday’s Warriors-Dolphins clash. Loading Approaching the hour mark at Allianz Stadium on Friday night, Latrell Mitchell squeezed a pass for Johnston who appeared to have the ball stripped from him by Knights backrower Jermaine McEwen. Play was allowed to continue, Johnston kneed the ball forward, then Jayden Sullivan kicked it further ahead before scoring.



Referee Ashley Klein awarded a try, but bunker official Chris Butler had other ideas, claiming McEwen was trying to make a tackle, and Johnston simply lost the ball. Rather than potentially go ahead 12-10, Souths were on the back foot, and 10 minutes later conceded a try to Dominic Young, who appeared to put his right foot on the touchline. Did Jeremaine McEwen strip the ball from Alex Johnston? Nine Bennett complimented Newcastle on playing a “tremendous game”, and was mindful to not deflect from the result, but he was also clearly frustrated with the bunker, which was meant to eliminate every contentious call. “Anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock-on,” Bennett said.



“The ball was knocked out of his [Johnston’s] hands. “The referee awards a try, then the bunker buys in and says it’s no try. “Ten minutes later, Newcastle winger Dom Young goes down the sideline, I’m not sure if he put his foot on the sideline, but the bottom line is the bunker comes back and says, ‘we’re going with the referee’s call’. “I want to know who is refereeing the game, that’s the first thing I want to know. “Is it the bunker or is it the referee?



“In the case of Alex Johnston ... you can look at that 50 times, everyone can come up with a different opinion. It’s just too technical. It’s not what the game needs. Cody Walker hobbles off with a calf injury. NRL “I’ve been in the game a long time, I’ve seen a lot of things, and I don’t think the bunker enhances our game to the [level] we believe it does.” Bennett said he was happy to live with referees’ making poor calls, just as he was prepared to cope with mistakes made by his own players. “But the bunker was meant to be 100 per cent bulletproof, and it’s not,” he said.



“It won’t stop here tonight. There will be more instances through the play-offs, I can promise you.” Related Video Video icon 1:05 Joey pleads with Rabbitohs to extend Walker Bennett was also confused by a call in the first half to penalise Mitchell when he appeared to be struck first by Knights centre Dane Gagai. The Mitchell-Gagai duel was one of the great match-ups of the evening. Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook thought “common sense prevailed” with the decision to strip Souths of the Johnston and Sullivan try, while Cameron Smith said during the live commentary it did not deserve to be a try.



The Knights looked like a team that was fresh from the bye the previous week, and looked in more sync in attack. Souths were not helped by Walker breaking down on the half hour, with the playmaker immediately signalling to the sideline for help. He would have been unlikely to play on next weekend had Souths progressed, but Bennett confirmed the club was keen for him to play on in 2027, even though a deal was yet to be formally struck. Aside from Walker, then Johnston failing to finish the game with a groin complaint, Souths had enjoyed a good run with injuries at this time of year. World.title: Dockers avoid a violet crumble, advance to a prelim final after Chris Scott left fuming from no-goal call
World.content:
Dockers coach Justin Longmuir says he has breathed a sigh of relief. His side was facing a straight-sets exit after finishing the season on top of the ladder.

They jumped out of the blocks at Optus Stadium with a six-goal opening term, but had to withstand a Geelong fightback during the third term. At one stage, Geelong held an eight-point lead.

But a four-goal burst to close out the third term set up their 14-point victory. It was a huge improvement from last week’s shock loss to Hawthorn.

“I thought we played a clearly much better brand of footy [than last week],” Longmuir told Channel 7.

“We played to win tonight, and you know, it got a bit hairy in the third quarter, and we clearly didn’t start the third quarter well. But I’m so proud of the way the players fought back at the back end of that third quarter.

“Clearly, it was an important part of the game. We lacked a bit of composure at times in the last quarter, but yeah, really proud of the week we had, and really proud of the effort.”

Longmuir will now begin preparing for next week’s preliminary final clash against the Swans in Sydney.

World.title: Fremantle v Geelong player ratings: ‘The Unicorn’ weaved his magic yet again, but these Cats guns will rue one that got away
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Fremantle v Geelong player ratings: ‘The Unicorn’ weaved his magic yet again, but these Cats guns will rue one that got away

Loading

All the pressure was on the Dockers as they desperately tried to avoid being the second top-of-the-ladder side in as many seasons (after the Crows last year) to bow out in straight sets. And in the Cats, they faced a proven finals foe that was never going to give in. That’s exactly what makes the Dockers’ 14-point win so impressive. Steve Barrett (Fremantle) and Marc McGowan (Geelong) run their eye over every player in from this semi-final. Josh Treacy lifted after his performance against the Hawks. AFL Photos



Fremantle (3) Caleb Serong: Predictably had Oisin Mullin for company, and eventually quelled the tag in a fine – and anticipated – return to form after he was below his usual standard against Hawthorn. His magnificent 55-metre goal in the fourth quarter all but sealed a preliminary final berth. 7.5/10 (5) Heath Chapman: Struggled to contain Ollie Henry, especially in the third term when the Cats were gathering steam, and his decision-making was shaky at times. He did salvage his night with a strong finish. 5.5/10 (6) Jordan Clark: One of Fremantle’s few bright spots in their qualifying final meltdown was industrious against the Cats, his old side. He generated tremendous run out of defence, racking up 621 metres gained and wasting almost none of his 25 touches. 7/10



(8) Andrew Brayshaw: One of the Dockers’ prime movers through the middle, his performance won’t create headlines, but he was as consistent as ever across four quarters and used the ball smartly. 7/10 Luke “the Unicorn” Jackson was nothing short of brilliant for the Dockers. AFL Photos (9) Luke Jackson: When Fremantle needed something special, their “Unicorn” delivered. After running amok in ruck in the opening term, he was becalmed in the second, before unleashing a match-winning third quarter for the ages. The big fella booted two goals for the term and contributed to three others. Titanic. 9/10 (10) Shai Bolton: The Dockers needed a bright start, but they couldn’t have dreamt of a better one than what their exciting No.10 crafted, twice bursting away from Bailey Smith in the middle and booting two goals in the opening 80 seconds. He continued to give Geelong fits, even when the disciplined Mark O’Connor ran with him. 8.5/10 View post on X



(13) Luke Ryan: Had his hands full with Patrick Dangerfield at times, but still managed to consistently provide plenty of drive and run out of the back half for Fremantle. 6/10 (16) Murphy Reid: When he’s at his best, this young gun’s poise and creativity are off the charts. His playmaking was elite, especially in the first half, fashioning a fine bounceback from an under-par showing against the Hawks. 7.5/10 (17) Judd McVee: Called up to replace the injured Brandon Walker, he didn’t have much of an impact aside from a few glimpses in the second stanza. 4.5/10 (18) Mason Cox: He crashed packs, booted a goal, got in faces and provided occasional ruck relief for the rampant Jackson. He did his bit. 4/10 (20) Patrick Voss: What a return to form following his qualifying final shocker against Hawthorn. He booted four majors, exerted himself on the contest and ensured Tom Stewart’s hands were kept full. His goal right on three-quarter-time was massive. 8/10



View post on X (21) Oscar McDonald: He covered plenty of territory and his intercepting was important in the first half. He went to Ollie Henry in the fourth quarter, but generally had less impact as the evening wore on. Still, this was a better night for him than the rough one he had a week earlier against Jack Gunston. 5/10 (23) Karl Worner: He provided defensive pressure at the contest with calmness when exiting the backline was in his hands. His disposal efficiency was 100 per cent - you can’t ask much more than that from your half-backs. 7/10 (24) Jye Amiss: Thrashed by Tom Barrass a week ago, he was unsighted for long stretches against Geelong. He slotted an important goal in the second stanza and had a real crack. He was kept under wraps for most of the game by Jack Henry, but still managed 2.1 from his three kicks. 4.5/10 (25) Alex Pearce: His intercepting and decision-making on the last line was sound, as was his attack on the contest. His direct opponent Shannon Neale probably just took the honours, though. 5.5/10



(26) Hayden Young: That long goal he kicked out of the centre ball-up was one for the ages – as was his whole second quarter when he helped the Dockers get on top at stoppage. He had a game-high nine inside-50s to go with 556m gained. One of Fremantle’s real game-breakers. 8/10 View post on X (28) Neil Erasmus: He was solid on his wing, where he often found himself matched up with Jeremy Cameron. His ball use was sound and he played his role. 6/10 (32) Michael Frederick: He nailed a nice goal on the run during the Dockers’ sizzling opening-quarter surge, then another huge one in the fourth. In-between he was often unsighted, whether on a wing or at half-forward. 5/10 (34) Corey Wagner: The recalled utility was strong at the contest, mixing time on the wing with stints forward of centre. His tackling was immense but his ball use iffy. He made some amends with a magnificent long kick into attack for a strong Amiss mark and goal against the grain in the third quarter. 6/10



(35) Josh Treacy: Following his stinker against Hawthorn, the spearhead was much better against Geelong. He booted an important goal in the third term to restore Fremantle’s lead, while his powerful contested marking was a feature. 7/10 (39) Sam Switkowski: He provided his customary forward pressure and was involved in a number of the Dockers’ scoring chains. 5/10 (43) Isaiah Dudley: The little goalsneak bobbed up with two goals in a second-quarter cameo, but his disposal was rushed and imprecise at other times. 5/10 (44) Matthew Johnson: Bravely overcame a massive knee to the back from Dangerfield to have an impact after half-time. He spent some time in the centre-square as Fremantle tried something different during the Cats’ flurry. He followed a huge one-on-one win against Ollie Dempsey with a calm kick to Frederick for a crucial late goal. 6/10 Chris Scott could barely believe his eyes after a shot on goal from Ollie Dempsey was ruled a behind due to “inconclusive evidence” to overturn the umpire’s call. Seven



Geelong (2) Jay Polkinghorne: Dished the handball that led to Shaun Mannagh’s second-quarter goal, but had a quiet night overall. 1/10 (3) Bailey Smith: He was part of a beaten midfield early, but worked tirelessly and made his mark with his tackling before setting up consecutive goals to give the Cats their first lead in the third term. Won plenty of the Sherrin. 8.5/10 Patrick Voss and Bailey Smith aren’t exactly shrinking violets. AFL Photos



(4) Tanner Bruhn: Had a challenging night following Dudley around in defence, but fought back to have a better second half. 5/10 (5) Jeremy Cameron: Cameron’s night summed up his season. He still kicked two goals, but he has struggled to impact games like he did last year. 5/10 (7) Shaun Mannagh: Played a key role in keeping Geelong in the contest in the first half when few other Cats were firing. He generated several opportunities for himself and others, and even won four first-half clearances. 7/10 (9) Max Holmes: Looked poised to have a big second half after a strong finish to the second quarter, but his second game back from his ankle setback was largely muted by his standards. 6/10 Mitchell Edwards (pictured here competing with Voss) didn’t have his best night for the Cats. AFL Photos



(11) Mitch Edwards: Welcome to the finals cauldron. He hurt his pinky finger in the first quarter, but the flogging he received from Jackson would have been most painful of all. 3/10 (14) Connor O’Sullivan: He grabbed nine marks, and generally held his own in defence, even when the Cats were under siege early. 6.5/10 (17) Lawson Humphries: Like many Cats, Humphries had a slow start, but he warmed to the task and ended up being one of his team’s top contributors, using the ball neatly and repeatedly cutting off Docker forays. 7/10 (21) Ollie Wiltshire: Found space inside 50 to mark and goal in the first quarter, but was unable to have much of an impact. 3/10 (28) Ollie Dempsey: The All-Australian Cat couldn’t break loose for his typical game-breaking moments, but never stopped trying. 5/10



View post on X (30) Tom Atkins: A night to forget for the rugged Atkins, including conceding the last free kick and goal to Voss that sealed Fremantle’s victory. 2/10 (32) Gryan Miers: Miers’ work-rate spike in the third-quarter comeback, but where was he in the first half? Geelong needed more from him. 3/10 (33) Shannon Neale: Took a strong grab in the opening quarter and bobbed up for a pair of goals in the second term, including his 50th of the season, but was largely unsighted after half-time until a late goal. 5.5/10 (34) Oisin Mullin: The Irishman has become a very reliable AFL footballer who can be trusted in the biggest of matches. As always, he was strong defensively, but also won his share of the ball. 7/10



Patrick Dangerfield stood strong in the finals yet again. AFL Photos (35) Patrick Dangerfield: The champion Cat might not have been his match-winning self from a week ago, but still had some terrific moments, including an early 50-metre strike. “Danger” remains a force. 7.5/10 (36) Ollie Henry: The Cats’ best forward, and possibly best player, with a career-high five goals, including to keep them alive in the final term. He never stopped presenting and mostly finished his work. 8.5/10 (38) Jack Henry: Had a series of shaky first-half moments, including slipping to concede an easy goal to Cox. Improved in the second half and had EIGHT intercepts, but it wasn’t his best performance. 4/10 (39) Zach Guthrie: Guthrie was caught out of position a few times in the first half, but that wasn’t always his fault. Intercepted well and was very good in the third-quarter fightback, including two touches in one passage that led to an Ollie Henry goal. 7/10



(42) Mark O’Connor: Was used through the middle on occasion when the tide was against Geelong, and was solid without playing a major role. 5/10 (44) Tom Stewart: A rare finals downer for Stewart, who conceded two goals to direct opponent Voss in the opening quarter and was later outmarked by Treacy. He had nothing like his usual impact. 4/10 (45) Brad Close: He had two direct goal assists, including a clever pass to Shannon Neale, but went missing for large chunks of the game. 5/10 (46) Mark Blicavs: Another veteran Cat who struggled. Chris Scott used his star utility in his usual bevy of roles to try to get him going, including in the ruck against Jackson, but Blicavs didn’t fire a shot. 4/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Chalmers makes more tax tweaks to temper budget blow
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Chalmers makes more tax tweaks to temper budget blow Paul Sakkal September 12, 2026 — 4:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has made another tweak to fix the fallout from Labor’s budget tax rises, but a leading business group says the revised reforms remains harmful and sap confidence across the economy. The government moved on Friday to address concerns from a range of influential businesspeople and some Labor figures that Labor’s new inflation-adjusted model for taxing capital gains could hurt fast-growing new businesses and worsen Australia’s productivity and investment. Treasurer Jim Chalmers on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Under the changes, companies operating for up to 15 years will be able to qualify for a CGT concession, up from 10 years, while investors will need to hold eligible shares for three years, down from five. The concession will also no longer be capped. And a research and development refund scheme for biotech firms will be accessible for 15 years, up from 10. Tech Council of Australia chief executive Kate Cornick said the changes would “help ensure the risks that founders, talent and investors take to build and back early-stage companies are rewarded.”



“As a nation we have a lot of catching up to do on R&D, and the proposed [changes] ... are a solid step toward getting us back on track.” Related Article Exclusive

Federal budget ‘A problem for every single business’: Labor insider adds to backlash over CGT overhaul Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar said the overhaul did not alter the overall impact of Labor’s tax package on businesses. “We are almost four months on from the federal budget and the policy settings continue to move on a day-by-day basis, this is eroding confidence across the economy,” he said. A media release from Chalmers’ office said the changes were “all about supporting small businesses and start-ups, including in the biotechnology and medical technology sectors. These reforms will deliver more innovation, encourage more entrepreneurship and deliver certainty for investors.”



Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said Chalmers had been “forced by the prime minister into his fourth humiliating backdown over his budget”. “The backdown is welcome, but it is embarrassing that certainty and confidence has been jeopardised for so many businesses because we have an out-of-his-depth treasurer.” In the May budget, Labor scrapped negative gearing on existing properties and created new rules to stop tax minimisation by using trusts. It also moved from a flat 50 per cent CGT discount to an inflation adjusted model that could lead to lower taxes for investors in low-growth, high-dividend blue-chip shares but higher taxes on quicker growing firms that create dynamism. Labor promised before the last election it would not pursue such policies, but said it changed its position due to the urgency of solving the housing crisis. House prices have continued their pre-budget tumble due to a combination of high-interest rates and the tax changes. Labor has already walked back a tax on trusts that the Coalition weaponised into a “death tax” scare campaign, got rid of a tax that would have penalised people whose spouses died, and backtracked on elements of a new minimum tax on trusts. World.title: ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSeptember 11 attacks ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on Maria Tsvetkova , Idrees Ali and Joseph Ax Updated September 12, 2026 — 2:51am ,first published 11:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day. In New York, family members of the victims joined Vice President JD Vance, former president George W. Bush, who was in office on 9/11, and ex-presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8.46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Centre’s North Tower. A woman and child pause at the memorial on Friday morning. Spencer Platt/Pool Getty Images North America via AP The site of the World Trade Centre attacks, pictured on Friday, now the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, a sombre recitation that lasts for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001.



Elsie Caldwell carried a photograph of her son Kenny Caldwell to hear his name and all the others read aloud. She last spoke to him that morning a quarter-century ago. “Mom, I just want to let you know that I love you,” Caldwell said he told her in a final phone call. She is one of many relatives of victims whose remains never were recovered. Other moments of silence, marking when the other three planes hijacked by al-Qaeda terrorists crashed and the two towers collapsed, followed. For the first time, a seventh silence was observed to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward. Sombre ceremonies were held across the country to mark the 25th anniversary. Bloomberg New York City Fire Department (FDNY) members visit the memorial ahead of the ceremony. Bloomberg



An attendee with a tattoo of the Twin Towers at the memorial in New York on Friday. Bloomberg US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wiped away a tear as he revisited the place where the attacks killed 658 of his then-colleagues – including his brother, Gary Lutnick – at the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald. Gregory Carafello came to the ceremony to honour the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald. Carafello himself was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate. “Everyone should realise that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families,” he said. “These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work.” Former president Joe Biden, Vice President JD Vance and former president George W. Bush. AP Photo/Pamela Smith



Former President Bill Clinton, former First Lady Michelle Obama and former President Barack Obama listen to speakers at the memorial in New York. Olga Fedorova/POOL EPA via AP At the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, where American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building’s west flank, killing 184, senior military leaders gathered amid heavy rain to watch the unfurling of an American flag before US President Donald Trump chronicled some of the stories of those aboard who perished in the crash: a woman pregnant with her first child, a family of four headed to Australia, three sixth-graders on a field trip. “In those harrowing days after the attacks, we saw the authentic spirit of our nation,” Trump said at the ceremony. The president and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who also delivered remarks, both used their speeches to make the case for the Iran war, which they have defended as necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump at a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein



An American flag is unfurled at the Pentagon early on Friday morning. Bloomberg US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth watched the flag unfurling ceremony as rain fell at the Pentagon. Bloomberg “We salute our first responders and law enforcement, and we love them,” Trump said. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.” Trump added: “September 11th reminded us of the terrible power of hate. The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail, and to win.” A ceremony was also being held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington.



Related Article September 11 attacks The day that changed America and shaped the world we know today The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security. But for many whom the attacks directly affected – the victims’ families, first responders and rescue workers – the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter-century ago and the heartbreak that followed. Loading Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower.



Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him to her father’s grave last week and was attending a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday. “This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing that they won’t ever get to know each other,” Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. “My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather. Related Article September 11 attacks Australians remember lost loved ones 25 years on from September 11 attacks “We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added. The attacks initiated the “war on terror,” which led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements – a promise being tested by the current Iran war.



At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks. At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colours Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected. Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Rudy Giuliani, former mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony. Bloomberg Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died.



Patrick Whalen’s father, also named Patrick, was a New York City firefighter who responded to the attacks and continued working at Ground Zero for months amid the dust and rubble. In 2020, he was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer linked to exposure to toxic carcinogens, and died in 2021. Related Article September 11 attacks John Howard witnessed the 9/11 attacks as PM. It changed his leadership forever “The government told him it was safe to breathe, and, obviously, it was not true,” the younger Whalen said after a New York City Fire Department memorial service this week. Information that the air at Ground Zero was safe to breathe came from the US Environmental Protection Agency. Its former administrator, Christine Todd Whitman, apologised in a 2016 interview with The Guardian, saying the agency did its best with the knowledge it had. The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show. Twenty-six have died this year alone.



A woman mourns at the September 11 memorial plaza in Lower Manhattan. Dave Sanders/Pool The New York Times via AP A mourner places a flower on one of 2753 empty chairs in New York’s Bryant Park, each signifying a life lost in the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Centre. AP Photo/Heather Khalifa People walk in the Oculus near the memorial on the 25th anniversary of the attacks. AP Photo/Angelina Katsanis Reuters with AP Twenty-five years on from September 11

World.title: Bring on the the Zak attack: The Cats’ semi-final showed they sorely need it
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Bring on the the Zak attack: The Cats’ semi-final showed they sorely need it Andrew Wu September 12, 2026 — 2:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

There’s a good reason why Geelong are neck deep into getting Zak Butters. It was on show in Perth. Finals expose weaknesses and the Cats were found wanting again in the engine room, as they were when they were pounded by the Brisbane Lions in last year’s grand final. Their premiership dream unravelled last year against the power of Will Ashcroft, Lachie Neale and co. This time they were upended by the clean hands of Caleb Serong, the slick wheels of Shai Bolton and Hayden Young, and the might of Luke Jackson. Patrick Voss and Bailey Smith aren’t exactly shrinking violets. AFL Photos Geelong’s fate was ultimately decided by the belated tolling of the bells for “Wharfie Time” but the bursts at the start of the game and the final few minutes of a rollicking third quarter left them reeling.



Apart from that, as Geelong coach Chris Scott pointed out, the Cats matched the Dockers. The problem was Freo slammed seven goals in those periods. In a game decided by 14 points, those passages were critical. The opening spurt spat out three goals in four minutes for the Dockers, allowing the tension that had gripped their faithful last week to be released in a cacophony of roars and electronic hip-hop that accompanied each goal. Patrick Dangerfield stood strong in the finals yet again. AFL Photos Bolton, one of numerous star Dockers who were quiet in their qualifying final debacle, set them alight, getting out the front of stoppage twice for goals. It’s for games like these the Dockers paid the big price to lure him from Richmond. Bolton’s impact was dulled slightly after this – it had to be after such a fast start – but he still finished with 26 disposals. In his quieter patches, the Dockers had Serong, Young, Andrew Brayshaw and Murphy Reid running the show.



The Cats relied too heavily on Bailey Smith, who did not stop running, but lacked sufficient support. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The ‘Butters rule’ the AFL should introduce to fix a shonky system As brave as Max Holmes was to get up for two finals after ankle surgery, he did not produce the scything runs that make him a dangerous midfielder. He limped off just before half-time though played out the game for a modest 18 disposals. “So to come back and play two finals the way he did was ultra-impressive and speaks to his professionalism,” Scott said afterwards. “But I think it was more a matter of a couple more weeks would have had him closer to himself.” The Cats were walloped 23-13 out of the middle and conceded 12 goals from stoppage. They gave up 11 goals from this source in last year’s grand final.



Should Butters, one of the league’s best clearance winners, choose the hoops over the red, white and blue of his boyhood club the Western Bulldogs, he would stiffen a Cats on-ball brigade that often gets found out in big games. For periods in the second term, the Cats had taggers Oisin Mullin and Mark O’Connor in the centre square alongside Shaun Mannagh, who made his reputation as a dynamic half-forward. As honest as Mullin and O’Connor are, not many premiership contenders will fear Geelong’s midfield with both stoppers in there. “They’re a good centre bounce team. That’s an area we need to improve,” Scott said. Loading



“If you take out the first three to four minutes, and the centre bounces in general, and then that patch, it wasn’t even with three minutes to go in the third quarter, it was probably the last 90 seconds, we were probably on top for the rest of the game. They were two brief periods that really hurt us.” The Cats were also punished by Jackson, who made the most of his advantage in experience, size and strength against Mitch Edwards – a 21-year-old in just his 20th game and second final. When the coaches’ votes come out next week, it would be a surprise if he did not get the maximum of 10. View post on X The big man with the mullet gave his midfielders first use of the ball, won the ball himself at ground level, and kicked two clutch goals from ruck infringements when the Dockers surged late in the third quarter. There is little he cannot do.





As well-beaten as they were around the ball, the Cats hung tough, forcing the Dockers to win the game three times. Not much went right for them. They were stiff not to have Ollie Dempsey’s volley from close range ruled their way. Replays appeared to show the ball ricocheting off Matt Johnson’s arm onto Dempsey’s boot, but the ARC deemed there was insufficient evidence to overrule the goal umpire’s soft call. “From what I’m told, everyone has the same opinion that Ollie did,” Scott said diplomatically when asked for his assessment of the decision. The vision of Scott punching the window of the box in bemusement will become rich online meme material.



Chris Scott could barely believe his eyes after a shot on goal from Ollie Dempsey was ruled a behind due to “inconclusive evidence” to overturn the umpire’s call. Seven “Sometimes I punch the wall when I’m happy,” Scott said. “Sometimes I punch the wall when I’m annoyed.” Jeremy Cameron battled manfully for two goals and 15 disposals. He will undergo surgery to fix the lingering issues on the arm he broke in last year’s grand final and which has hampered him all year. Tom Stewart, the man who Scott rates as the best player at the club, was held to 14 disposals against the influential Patrick Voss – who energised the crowd with four goals, including the sealer with seconds left. Stewart did not take a mark in the first quarter when the Dockers surged. Along with Holmes’ struggles, that’s three of Geelong’s best players having midrange nights when more was needed from their top-liners.



Patrick Dangerfield was ominous at times but lacked the supply to dominate as he did last week, while Ollie Henry played his best game, booting five. If they win Toby Greene’s signature, their forward line will cause migraines for opposition defences. It is testament to their resilience that the game was still alive with 75 seconds on the clock, prompting the Dockers to toll the bell for Wharfie Time to spur their team home. “There are a lot of teams in history after a start like that who would’ve turned up their toes and been beaten badly,” Scott said. “Obviously, we were being outplayed. To hang in and give ourselves a chance late in the game, in some ways be a fraction unlucky at various times, I think is a credit to our players. “It’s less about our off-field stuff and much more the ability of those guys to hang in. They’ll all be really hurting at the moment.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wayne Bennett has never liked the bunker. He wants it gone after Friday night
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Wayne Bennett has never liked the bunker. He wants it gone after Friday night Christian Nicolussi September 12, 2026 — 12:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Wayne Bennett blasted the NRL bunker after Alex Johnston was ruled to have knocked on at a vital stage during the Rabbitohs’ 20-10 loss to Newcastle, and declared: “The quicker they get rid of the bunker, the happier I’ll be.” South Sydney lost Cody Walker to a calf injury, then lost to an impressive Knights who now march on to week two of the finals for a showdown against the loser of Saturday’s Warriors-Dolphins clash. Loading Approaching the hour mark at Allianz Stadium on Friday night, Latrell Mitchell squeezed a pass for Johnston who appeared to have the ball stripped from him by Knights backrower Jermaine McEwen. Play was allowed to continue, Johnston kneed the ball forward, then Jayden Sullivan kicked it further ahead before scoring.



Referee Ashley Klein awarded a try, but bunker official Chris Butler had other ideas, claiming McEwen was trying to make a tackle, and Johnston simply lost the ball. Rather than potentially go ahead 12-10, Souths were on the back foot, and 10 minutes later conceded a try to Dominic Young, who appeared to put his right foot on the touchline. Did Jeremaine McEwen strip the ball from Alex Johnston? Nine Bennett complimented Newcastle on playing a “tremendous game”, and was mindful to not deflect from the result, but he was also clearly frustrated with the bunker, which was meant to eliminate every contentious call. “Anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock-on,” Bennett said.



“The ball was knocked out of his [Johnston’s] hands. “The referee awards a try, then the bunker buys in and says it’s no try. “Ten minutes later, Newcastle winger Dom Young goes down the sideline, I’m not sure if he put his foot on the sideline, but the bottom line is the bunker comes back and says, ‘we’re going with the referee’s call’. “I want to know who is refereeing the game, that’s the first thing I want to know. “Is it the bunker or is it the referee?



“In the case of Alex Johnston ... you can look at that 50 times, everyone can come up with a different opinion. It’s just too technical. It’s not what the game needs. Cody Walker hobbles off with a calf injury. NRL “I’ve been in the game a long time, I’ve seen a lot of things, and I don’t think the bunker enhances our game to the [level] we believe it does.” Bennett said he was happy to live with referees’ making poor calls, just as he was prepared to cope with mistakes made by his own players. “But the bunker was meant to be 100 per cent bulletproof, and it’s not,” he said.



“It won’t stop here tonight. There will be more instances through the play-offs, I can promise you.” Related Video Video icon 1:05 Joey pleads with Rabbitohs to extend Walker Bennett was also confused by a call in the first half to penalise Mitchell when he appeared to be struck first by Knights centre Dane Gagai. The Mitchell-Gagai duel was one of the great match-ups of the evening. Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook thought “common sense prevailed” with the decision to strip Souths of the Johnston and Sullivan try, while Cameron Smith said during the live commentary it did not deserve to be a try.



The Knights looked like a team that was fresh from the bye the previous week, and looked in more sync in attack. Souths were not helped by Walker breaking down on the half hour, with the playmaker immediately signalling to the sideline for help. He would have been unlikely to play on next weekend had Souths progressed, but Bennett confirmed the club was keen for him to play on in 2027, even though a deal was yet to be formally struck. Aside from Walker, then Johnston failing to finish the game with a groin complaint, Souths had enjoyed a good run with injuries at this time of year. World.title: Dockers avoid a violet crumble, advance to a prelim final after Chris Scott left fuming from no-goal call
World.content:
Dockers coach Justin Longmuir says he has breathed a sigh of relief. His side was facing a straight-sets exit after finishing the season on top of the ladder.

They jumped out of the blocks at Optus Stadium with a six-goal opening term, but had to withstand a Geelong fightback during the third term. At one stage, Geelong held an eight-point lead.

But a four-goal burst to close out the third term set up their 14-point victory. It was a huge improvement from last week’s shock loss to Hawthorn.

“I thought we played a clearly much better brand of footy [than last week],” Longmuir told Channel 7.

“We played to win tonight, and you know, it got a bit hairy in the third quarter, and we clearly didn’t start the third quarter well. But I’m so proud of the way the players fought back at the back end of that third quarter.

“Clearly, it was an important part of the game. We lacked a bit of composure at times in the last quarter, but yeah, really proud of the week we had, and really proud of the effort.”

Longmuir will now begin preparing for next week’s preliminary final clash against the Swans in Sydney.

World.title: Fremantle v Geelong player ratings: ‘The Unicorn’ weaved his magic yet again, but these Cats guns will rue one that got away
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Fremantle v Geelong player ratings: ‘The Unicorn’ weaved his magic yet again, but these Cats guns will rue one that got away

Loading

All the pressure was on the Dockers as they desperately tried to avoid being the second top-of-the-ladder side in as many seasons (after the Crows last year) to bow out in straight sets. And in the Cats, they faced a proven finals foe that was never going to give in. That’s exactly what makes the Dockers’ 14-point win so impressive. Steve Barrett (Fremantle) and Marc McGowan (Geelong) run their eye over every player in from this semi-final. Josh Treacy lifted after his performance against the Hawks. AFL Photos



Fremantle (3) Caleb Serong: Predictably had Oisin Mullin for company, and eventually quelled the tag in a fine – and anticipated – return to form after he was below his usual standard against Hawthorn. His magnificent 55-metre goal in the fourth quarter all but sealed a preliminary final berth. 7.5/10 (5) Heath Chapman: Struggled to contain Ollie Henry, especially in the third term when the Cats were gathering steam, and his decision-making was shaky at times. He did salvage his night with a strong finish. 5.5/10 (6) Jordan Clark: One of Fremantle’s few bright spots in their qualifying final meltdown was industrious against the Cats, his old side. He generated tremendous run out of defence, racking up 621 metres gained and wasting almost none of his 25 touches. 7/10



(8) Andrew Brayshaw: One of the Dockers’ prime movers through the middle, his performance won’t create headlines, but he was as consistent as ever across four quarters and used the ball smartly. 7/10 Luke “the Unicorn” Jackson was nothing short of brilliant for the Dockers. AFL Photos (9) Luke Jackson: When Fremantle needed something special, their “Unicorn” delivered. After running amok in ruck in the opening term, he was becalmed in the second, before unleashing a match-winning third quarter for the ages. The big fella booted two goals for the term and contributed to three others. Titanic. 9/10 (10) Shai Bolton: The Dockers needed a bright start, but they couldn’t have dreamt of a better one than what their exciting No.10 crafted, twice bursting away from Bailey Smith in the middle and booting two goals in the opening 80 seconds. He continued to give Geelong fits, even when the disciplined Mark O’Connor ran with him. 8.5/10 View post on X



(13) Luke Ryan: Had his hands full with Patrick Dangerfield at times, but still managed to consistently provide plenty of drive and run out of the back half for Fremantle. 6/10 (16) Murphy Reid: When he’s at his best, this young gun’s poise and creativity are off the charts. His playmaking was elite, especially in the first half, fashioning a fine bounceback from an under-par showing against the Hawks. 7.5/10 (17) Judd McVee: Called up to replace the injured Brandon Walker, he didn’t have much of an impact aside from a few glimpses in the second stanza. 4.5/10 (18) Mason Cox: He crashed packs, booted a goal, got in faces and provided occasional ruck relief for the rampant Jackson. He did his bit. 4/10 (20) Patrick Voss: What a return to form following his qualifying final shocker against Hawthorn. He booted four majors, exerted himself on the contest and ensured Tom Stewart’s hands were kept full. His goal right on three-quarter-time was massive. 8/10



View post on X (21) Oscar McDonald: He covered plenty of territory and his intercepting was important in the first half. He went to Ollie Henry in the fourth quarter, but generally had less impact as the evening wore on. Still, this was a better night for him than the rough one he had a week earlier against Jack Gunston. 5/10 (23) Karl Worner: He provided defensive pressure at the contest with calmness when exiting the backline was in his hands. His disposal efficiency was 100 per cent - you can’t ask much more than that from your half-backs. 7/10 (24) Jye Amiss: Thrashed by Tom Barrass a week ago, he was unsighted for long stretches against Geelong. He slotted an important goal in the second stanza and had a real crack. He was kept under wraps for most of the game by Jack Henry, but still managed 2.1 from his three kicks. 4.5/10 (25) Alex Pearce: His intercepting and decision-making on the last line was sound, as was his attack on the contest. His direct opponent Shannon Neale probably just took the honours, though. 5.5/10



(26) Hayden Young: That long goal he kicked out of the centre ball-up was one for the ages – as was his whole second quarter when he helped the Dockers get on top at stoppage. He had a game-high nine inside-50s to go with 556m gained. One of Fremantle’s real game-breakers. 8/10 View post on X (28) Neil Erasmus: He was solid on his wing, where he often found himself matched up with Jeremy Cameron. His ball use was sound and he played his role. 6/10 (32) Michael Frederick: He nailed a nice goal on the run during the Dockers’ sizzling opening-quarter surge, then another huge one in the fourth. In-between he was often unsighted, whether on a wing or at half-forward. 5/10 (34) Corey Wagner: The recalled utility was strong at the contest, mixing time on the wing with stints forward of centre. His tackling was immense but his ball use iffy. He made some amends with a magnificent long kick into attack for a strong Amiss mark and goal against the grain in the third quarter. 6/10



(35) Josh Treacy: Following his stinker against Hawthorn, the spearhead was much better against Geelong. He booted an important goal in the third term to restore Fremantle’s lead, while his powerful contested marking was a feature. 7/10 (39) Sam Switkowski: He provided his customary forward pressure and was involved in a number of the Dockers’ scoring chains. 5/10 (43) Isaiah Dudley: The little goalsneak bobbed up with two goals in a second-quarter cameo, but his disposal was rushed and imprecise at other times. 5/10 (44) Matthew Johnson: Bravely overcame a massive knee to the back from Dangerfield to have an impact after half-time. He spent some time in the centre-square as Fremantle tried something different during the Cats’ flurry. He followed a huge one-on-one win against Ollie Dempsey with a calm kick to Frederick for a crucial late goal. 6/10 Chris Scott could barely believe his eyes after a shot on goal from Ollie Dempsey was ruled a behind due to “inconclusive evidence” to overturn the umpire’s call. Seven



Geelong (2) Jay Polkinghorne: Dished the handball that led to Shaun Mannagh’s second-quarter goal, but had a quiet night overall. 1/10 (3) Bailey Smith: He was part of a beaten midfield early, but worked tirelessly and made his mark with his tackling before setting up consecutive goals to give the Cats their first lead in the third term. Won plenty of the Sherrin. 8.5/10 Patrick Voss and Bailey Smith aren’t exactly shrinking violets. AFL Photos



(4) Tanner Bruhn: Had a challenging night following Dudley around in defence, but fought back to have a better second half. 5/10 (5) Jeremy Cameron: Cameron’s night summed up his season. He still kicked two goals, but he has struggled to impact games like he did last year. 5/10 (7) Shaun Mannagh: Played a key role in keeping Geelong in the contest in the first half when few other Cats were firing. He generated several opportunities for himself and others, and even won four first-half clearances. 7/10 (9) Max Holmes: Looked poised to have a big second half after a strong finish to the second quarter, but his second game back from his ankle setback was largely muted by his standards. 6/10 Mitchell Edwards (pictured here competing with Voss) didn’t have his best night for the Cats. AFL Photos



(11) Mitch Edwards: Welcome to the finals cauldron. He hurt his pinky finger in the first quarter, but the flogging he received from Jackson would have been most painful of all. 3/10 (14) Connor O’Sullivan: He grabbed nine marks, and generally held his own in defence, even when the Cats were under siege early. 6.5/10 (17) Lawson Humphries: Like many Cats, Humphries had a slow start, but he warmed to the task and ended up being one of his team’s top contributors, using the ball neatly and repeatedly cutting off Docker forays. 7/10 (21) Ollie Wiltshire: Found space inside 50 to mark and goal in the first quarter, but was unable to have much of an impact. 3/10 (28) Ollie Dempsey: The All-Australian Cat couldn’t break loose for his typical game-breaking moments, but never stopped trying. 5/10



View post on X (30) Tom Atkins: A night to forget for the rugged Atkins, including conceding the last free kick and goal to Voss that sealed Fremantle’s victory. 2/10 (32) Gryan Miers: Miers’ work-rate spike in the third-quarter comeback, but where was he in the first half? Geelong needed more from him. 3/10 (33) Shannon Neale: Took a strong grab in the opening quarter and bobbed up for a pair of goals in the second term, including his 50th of the season, but was largely unsighted after half-time until a late goal. 5.5/10 (34) Oisin Mullin: The Irishman has become a very reliable AFL footballer who can be trusted in the biggest of matches. As always, he was strong defensively, but also won his share of the ball. 7/10



Patrick Dangerfield stood strong in the finals yet again. AFL Photos (35) Patrick Dangerfield: The champion Cat might not have been his match-winning self from a week ago, but still had some terrific moments, including an early 50-metre strike. “Danger” remains a force. 7.5/10 (36) Ollie Henry: The Cats’ best forward, and possibly best player, with a career-high five goals, including to keep them alive in the final term. He never stopped presenting and mostly finished his work. 8.5/10 (38) Jack Henry: Had a series of shaky first-half moments, including slipping to concede an easy goal to Cox. Improved in the second half and had EIGHT intercepts, but it wasn’t his best performance. 4/10 (39) Zach Guthrie: Guthrie was caught out of position a few times in the first half, but that wasn’t always his fault. Intercepted well and was very good in the third-quarter fightback, including two touches in one passage that led to an Ollie Henry goal. 7/10



(42) Mark O’Connor: Was used through the middle on occasion when the tide was against Geelong, and was solid without playing a major role. 5/10 (44) Tom Stewart: A rare finals downer for Stewart, who conceded two goals to direct opponent Voss in the opening quarter and was later outmarked by Treacy. He had nothing like his usual impact. 4/10 (45) Brad Close: He had two direct goal assists, including a clever pass to Shannon Neale, but went missing for large chunks of the game. 5/10 (46) Mark Blicavs: Another veteran Cat who struggled. Chris Scott used his star utility in his usual bevy of roles to try to get him going, including in the ruck against Jackson, but Blicavs didn’t fire a shot. 4/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.
